Banerji, 2018 ABCA 176, 2018 CarswellAlta 890, 73 Alta. L.R. (6th) 213, 424 D.L.R. (4th) 656, [2018] 10 W.W.R. 22, [2018] A.J. No. 591, Justices Paperny and Slatter discussed the two categories into which summary judgment and summary dismissal applications fall: 36 Summary judgment and summary dismissal applications usually fall into one of two categories: (a) Those where the “merit” of the claim is said to rest on the facts and the evidence. In that sort of case, if the moving party can prove on a balance of probabilities that it has proven the facts needed to support its claim or defence, it is entitled to summary disposition: Stefanyk v Sobeys Capital Incorporated, 2018 ABCA 125 at paras. 14–6. (b) Those where the “merit” is said to rest on the legal basis for the claim. This type of summary dismissal application proceeds on the assumption either that the plaintiff (i) will be able to prove the facts alleged, or (ii) has proven the relevant facts, but those facts do not support any claim in law. The analytical approach in these two types of cases, and the standard of review, are subtly different. 37 The suitability of the summary judgment procedure in the first category of case is often tied back to whether “there is a genuine issue requiring a trial”. The test in factually based summary judgment applications is naturally tied back to “issues requiring trial”, because trials are designed to find facts. Material disputed facts will often preclude summary judgment. Where none of the material facts are unknown or uncertain, a trial is not called for. 38 Parties to a summary disposition application are expected to put their “best foot forward”, meaning that gaps in the record do not necessarily prevent summary disposition: Canada (Attorney General) v Lameman, 2008 SCC 14 at para. 11, [2008] 1 SCR 372. A summary judgment motion must be decided on the record before the Court, and not by speculation about what evidence may be adduced in the future if the matter is allowed to proceed to trial: Lameman at para. 19. 39 On the other hand, where the summary dismissal application is based on questions of law, a trial will less frequently be necessary. If the factual basis of the claim is established on the record, or if the plaintiff's claim discloses no merit even if the underlying facts are assumed to be true, summary judgment is generally the appropriate procedure: Lameman at para. 12; Jackson v Canadian National Railway, 2013 ABCA 440 at para. 29, 91 Alta LR (5th) 401, 566 AR 247. There is usually no need for a trial, because as noted trials are for finding facts. There are cases where the legal issues are complex and intertwined with the facts, in which event a trial still may be necessary: Tottrup v Clearwater (Municipal District No. 99), 2006 ABCA 380 at para. 11, 68 Alta LR (4th) 237, 401 AR 88. However, litigation that depends primarily on the applicable law is ideally suited for summary disposition. In Axcess Mortgage Fund Ltd. v. 1177620 Alberta Ltd., 2018 ABQB 626, 2018 CarswellAlta 1764, Justice Renke said that after determining the type of summary judgment application before it, the court must consider the case made by the party seeking summary judgment and the case made by the party opposing the application. His Lordship said: 45 In addition to distinguishing the two types of summary judgment cases, within a particular application, two cases must be assessed—the case of the moving party and the case of the non-moving party. 46 A moving party should not be entitled to succeed in a summary judgment application if, on the record, it cannot establish its case on a balance of probabilities. Summary judgment is a procedure for proving a case on the balance of probabilities. The standard of proof resting on the moving party should neither be reduced nor elevated because of the procedure through which it seeks judgment: Stefanyk v Sobeys at para 15; Pioneer Exploration Inc (Trustee of) v Euro-Am Pacific Enterprises Ltd, 2003 ABCA 298 at para 18: [18]…[T]he plaintiff bears the evidentiary burden of proving its cause of action on a balance of probabilities. Each and every fact necessary to support the claim must be proven: Bank of Montreal v. Kalin (1992), 131 A.R. 397 (C.A.). 47 Proof on a balance of probabilities is a necessary condition for success but not a sufficient condition. Summary judgment may be resisted by a non-moving party if it shows that there is a genuine issue requiring trial. The case of the non-moving party must be assessed. 3. — “Merit” Resting on the Legal Basis for the Claim 48 In a summary judgment application turning on whether a non-moving party has a legally enforceable claim or defence, a fair disposition on the record may be available if the critical legal issue or issues may be determined on the assumption that the nonmoving party's evidence is established. See Arndt v Banerji at para 39: “If the factual basis of the claim is established on the record, or if the plaintiff's claim discloses no merit even if the underlying facts are assumed to be true, summary judgment is generally the appropriate procedure.” See also 776826 Alberta Ltd v Ostrowercha at para 10. 49 Nonetheless, even if the critical issue is a matter of law, a trial may be necessary if the legal issues are unsettled, complex, and intertwined with the facts (fact-specific and nuanced): Arndt v Banerji at para 39; Stefanyk v Sobeys at paras 16, 17; Condominium Corporation No. 0321365 v Cuthbert, 2016 ABCA 46 at para 29; Templanza v Wolfman, 2016 ABCA 1 at para 20; Amack v Wishewan, 2015 ABCA 147 at para 36; Tottrup at paras 11-12. 4. — “Merit” Resting on the Facts and Evidence 50 In a summary judgment application turning on the facts and evidence, The suitability of the summary judgment procedure … is often tied back to whether “there is a genuine issue requiring a trial”. The test in factually based summary judgment applications is naturally tied back to “issues requiring trial”, because trials are designed to find facts. Material disputed facts will often preclude summary judgment. Where none of the material facts are unknown or uncertain, a trial is not called for: Arndt v Banerji at para 37. When does an issue genuinely require trial, in the sense of being an issue with “merit” in the language of r. 7.3? Merit has two aspects. (a)—“Materiality” of the Issue 51 First, the issue must be significant or important to the litigation, an issue that should be resolved before judgment may be granted: 776826 Alberta Ltd v Ostrowercha at para 11; Rotzang v CIBC World Markets Inc at para 67. An issue of merit is not insignificant or collateral to the issues between the parties. Resolution of the issue must have some non-trivial bearing on the resolution of the dispute. (b)—Non-Moving Party's Prospect of Success 52 Second, for an issue to have “merit,” the non-moving party must have a “sufficient” prospect of success on the issue to warrant resolution through trial as opposed to resolution on the summary judgment record. Given the current state of the jurisprudence, it is necessary to move cautiously in specifying the standard of sufficiency that a non-moving party must meet to avoid summary judgment and in specifying the reciprocal standard that a moving party must meet to succeed in the application. See 330626 Alberta Ltd v Ho & Laviolette Engineering at paras 39-40: [39] One issue as yet unresolved is the standard of proof to be met by the moving party. The Court of Appeal in Stefanyk said proof must be made on a balance of probabilities (paras 15 & 16; see also Angus Partnership at paras 41 & 42). It specifically rejected the standard of proof that the moving party's position is “unassailable” such that it is so compelling that the “likelihood of success [at trial] is very high”. In doing so, the Court distinguished Beier, [2013] A.J. No. 707 and the concurring reasons in Can v Calgary Alberta (Police Service), 2014 ABCA 322 at para 20, 584 AR 147. (See also Composite Technologies Inc v Shawcor Ltd, 2017 ABCA 160 at para 2.) [40] One month later, the Court of Appeal returned to the Beal, [2018] A.J. No. 827, Can, Composite Technologies standard of proof in Rotzang v CIBC World Markets… at para 15, and Whissell Contracting Ltd v Calgary (City), 2018 ABCA 204 at paras 2 & 3. 53 I suggest that there is consensus respecting the following aspects of merit. 54 Merit does not mean (no longer means) that the record supports a finding that there is a “triable issue” that might go in the non-moving party's favour. “Summary judgment is therefore no longer to be denied solely on the basis that the evidence discloses a triable issue:”WP v Alberta, 2014 ABCA 404 at para 26; see 776826 Alberta Ltd v Ostrowercha at para 13. That is, merit is not established a finding that it is possible that an issue might be resolved at trial in the non-moving party's favour or on the acknowledgement of a doubt about whether an issue might be resolved at trial in the non-moving party's favour. It follows that the mere fact that the record discloses some admissible evidence that provides inferential support to the non-moving party's position is not necessarily sufficient to resist a summary judgment application. (Were there gaps in the evidential support for the non-moving party's position, that would be an independent basis for summary dismissal of its claim as a matter of law.) 55 Merit, though, cannot require the non-moving party to prove its case on a balance of probabilities. That is the standard of proof to be met at trial. 56 As indicated above, establishing lack of merit should not require the moving party to prove its case to some standard higher than the balance of probabilities. 57 An issue has merit, and should be decided at trial, if the issue cannot fairly and justly be decided on the summary judgment record. That, again, is what Hryniak v Mauldin teaches at para 49. When is it not fair and just to decide an issue on the record? At this point, I depart from safe consensus. 58 It would not be fair and just to decide an issue if, on the record, in light of both the evidence of the moving party and the evidence of the non-moving party, the decision-maker is not satisfied that the moving party has satisfied its case on the balance of probabilities. On the record, the moving party's evidence cannot be fairly and justly found to be more likely than the evidence of the non-moving party. 59 It would not be fair and just to decide against the non-moving party if, on the record, the non-moving party had a “real chance of success” or genuine chance of success on the issue, as rule 7.3 suggests: Hercules Managements Ltd v Ernst & Young, [1997] 2 SCR 165 at para 15; Guarantee Co of North America v Gordon Capital Corp, [1999] 3 SCR 423 at para 27. From the perspective of the moving party, the question is whether it has shown that the non-moving party does not have a real or genuine chance of success at trial. 60 On this approach, the moving party bears no standard of proof higher than the balance of probabilities. The question is whether, on the record, the probative value of the non-moving party's evidence is so low that it does not preclude the inferences sought by the moving party. In that sense, the non-moving party's likelihood of success must be “very low:”Whissell Contracting Ltd v Calgary (City), 2018 ABCA 204 at para 2; Rotzang v. CIBC World Markets Inc at para 15. The current uncertainty relates to the description of the standard governing the assessment of the merits of the non-moving party's case as opposed to the ultimate burden borne by the moving party. 61 A typical example of when deciding an issue on the record would not be fair and just would concern conflicting affidavit evidence on an important issue. The record itself may not permit a finding that one account should be preferred over the other. Both the non-moving party's claims and the moving party's claims are in affidavit form. There is no basis for choosing between the two accounts. There are no objective indicia, no foundations in the evidence that would permit a decision-maker to find that the non-moving party does not have a real or genuine chance of success at trial, a chance of success at least equal to the chance of the moving party. To obtain an evidential foundation for finding that one set of claims has greater weight than the other, further evidence is needed, such as through viva voce evidence and trial. See 776826 Alberta Ltd v Ostrowercha at para 11; Price-Goulet v Transamerica Life Canada, 2017 ABCA 156 at para 8 (“The key is whether viva voce evidence is required to resolve the dispute”). Rotzang v CIBC World Markets Inc at para 68. See also Nafie v Badawy, 2015 ABCA 36 at para 106; Rensonnet v Uttl, 2014 ABCA 304 at para 10; Charles v Young, 2014 ABCA 200 at paras 3–5; Nieuwesteeg v Barron, 2009 ABCA 235 at paras 9–11. Thus we read in Cuthbert at para 28 that [28] Summary judgment is not possible if opposing parties' affidavits and evidence conflict on material facts because a chambers judge cannot weigh evidence or credibility on a summary judgment application … and in Stefanyk v Sobeys at para 15: In other words, is the record such that it is fair and just to decide summarily if the moving party has proven the case on a balance of probabilities? That generally comes down to deciding if there is any material issue of fact on which a trial is justified, or whether the chambers judge can make any required fact findings from the summary dismissal record in a fair and just manner. A trial may be the preferred and proportional procedure where there is a reasonable expectation that a better evidentiary record will be created by a trial, for example because there are disputed issues of material fact, or issues of credibility, that cannot fairly be resolved summarily. 62 However, summary judgment is not precluded just because affidavits conflict. Decision-makers have some latitude for fact-finding and assessing the chance of success at trial even in the face of conflicting affidavit evidence—if the record provides a foundation for substantially discounting the probative value of a party's claims. Facts may be found and chance of success determined despite conflicting affidavit evidence if, for example, (i) the conflicts do not concern essential or material facts; (ii) the conflicts do not concern facts, but only litigants' opinions—especially legal opinions—about the facts (often affidavits contain thinly disguised argument as opposed to facts); (iii) a party's affidavit evidence contains internal conflict or contradiction, including evidence that supports an opponent's factual allegations—such evidence would amount to admissions against interest; (iv) a party's affidavit evidence is inconsistent with evidence provided in Questioning on affidavit; or (v) issues can be resolved on the basis of evidence that is not in dispute. See Sandhu v Siri Guru Nanak Sikh Gurdwara of Alberta, 2015 ABCA 101 at para 81 and Janvier v 834474 Alberta Ltd, 2010 ABQB 800, Macklin J at para 15. 63 Furthermore, the weight of affidavit evidence may properly be found to be reduced if, for example, the evidence is not consistent with other evidence and known circumstances: Compton Petroleum Corporation v Alberta Power Ltd, 1999 ABQB 42 at para 14; see N. V. Reykdal & Associates Ltd, 2000 ABCA 330 at para 5; Janvier v 834474 Alberta Ltd at para 15; Faryna v Chorny, 1951 CanLII 252 (BC CA), 1951 CarswellBC 133, [1952] 2 DLR 354, O'Halloran JA at para 8 (CarswellBC). Common sense need not be abandoned in the face of an allegation in an affidavit. Allegations are not entitled to weight just because they are included in an affidavit. 64 Finally, claims in an affidavit have no weight if the statements are “self-serving,” in the sense of being “merely conclusory,”“argumentative,” or having no evidence supporting the claims made besides the claims themselves; that is, if the claims are “bare assertions” or “mere assertions.” See Guarantee Co of North America v Gordon Capital, [1999] 3 SCR 423 at para 31. 65 If, on the record and despite conflicting affidavits, a decision-maker has a foundation for concluding that there is no real or genuine chance that the non-moving party would be able to establish its claims, that the weight of the non-moving party's claims is so impaired that the decision-maker can find that the moving party has established its claims on a balance of probabilities, then the decision-maker may grant summary judgment to the moving party. 66 These reflections are consistent, I suggest, with the “road map” for summary judgment set out by Master Schlosser at para 17 of 1214777 Alberta Ltd v 480955 Alberta Ltd, 2014 ABQB 301. 4. Summary Judgment is still available in actions set for a jury trial In Wenzel v. Nenshi, 2015 ABQB 742, Justice Gates stated: 25 I accept the Plaintiff's argument that resort to the summary judgment process set out in the Alberta Rules of Court is not specifically precluded by s 17 of the Jury Act. Further, I accept the approach adopted in both Manitoba and Ontario, which promotes access to speedy justice through summary judgment, while protecting the jury mode of trial for those matters that actually proceed to trial. It follows that I do not accept the Defendant's contention that the Plaintiff's summary judgment application is precluded by the order of Yamauchi J directing that this matter proceed to trial before a jury. I agree with the Plaintiff that the right to a jury trial does not preclude the bringing of a summary judgment application. 5. Summary Judgment and Points of Law In Cardinal v. Alberta Motor Association Insurance Company, 2018 ABCA 69, 2018 CarswellAlta 293, the Court said: [10]… Summary judgment may be appropriate even in cases involving a significant legal issue which is novel and unsettled: Encana Corp v Devon Canada Corp, 2012 ABCA 271 at para 20, 536 AR 199. A point of law does not have to be beyond doubt before summary judgment can be granted. Rather, a novel or unsettled legal issue can be decided on a summary judgment application where the material facts are not in dispute and the issue can be fairly determined on the existing record: Tottrup v Clearwater (Municipal District No. 99), 2006 ABCA 380 at para 11, 401 AR 88. In LNR v. Mountview Pharma Corp., 2017 ABQB 730, 2017 CarswellAlta 2646, Justice Phillips discussed situations in which it would not be appropriate to grant summary dismissal when there is an unsettled legal issue: 31 A summary dismissal application will often be appropriate where the main issue is a legal issue: Windsor at para 16. However, where a judge is not confident that the issues can be fairly decided on the record before the Court where legal issues are unsettled, complex or intertwined with facts, a full trial should be held: Templanza v Wolfman, 2016 ABCA 1 at para 20; Amack v Wishewan, 2015 ABCA 147 at para 36; Tottrup v Clearwater (Municipal District No 99), 2006 ABCA 380 at para 11. 32 In Amack v Wishewan, 2015 ABCA 147 at paragraph 36 the Court stated the following: Accordingly, a full trial will still be required where a summary record cannot fairly be used to decide legal issues which are unsettled, complex or intertwined with the facts: see Gayton, [2010] A.J. No. 399 supra at para 11; Condominium Corporation No. 0321365 v MCAP Financial Corporation, 2012 ABCA 26 at para 5, 519 AR 322; Elbow River Marketing Limited Partnership v Canada Clean Fuels Inc., 2012 ABCA 328 at para 6, 539 AR 68. This is consistent with the principle set out in Hryniak[2014] 1 S.C.R. 87 that summary judgment is appropriate where the motion judge is confident that he or she can fairly resolve the dispute: see paras 50, 57. If not so confident, then a trial is in order. 33 In Beier v Proper Cat Construction Ltd., 2013 ABQB 351 at para 69, Wakeling J. (as he then was) summarized the principles governing summary judgment in cases where the law is unclear: Fourth, if the law is unclear, either because the moving party is seeking to extend the scope of a well established proposition or to make new law, a chambers judge may decline to resolve the dispute. This is so even though the trial judge is, arguably, in no better position to decide this challenging legal issue than the chambers judge. The chambers judge may legitimately conclude that her proper role is to identify unassailable positions, which assumes the law on the issue is settled, not develop the law in the course of a summary judgment chambers application. See Romano v. D'Onofrio, 262 D.L.R. (4th) 181, 184 (Ont. C.A. 2005) (motion judge erred in deciding “a significant question of law … in the context of a Rule 20 motion”); R.D. Belanger & Associates Ltd. v. Stadium Corp., 5 O.R. (3d) 778, 782 (C.A. 1991) (“Matters of law which have not been settled fully in our jurisprudence should not be disposed of at this [early] stage of proceedings”; Richter v. Chemerinski, 2010 ABQB 302, para 20 (“Judgment should not be given … if there are difficult or intricate legal issues”); Barrett v. Enfield London Borough Council, [2001] 2 A.C. 550, 557 (1999) &Farah v. British Airways plc, The Times (January 26, 2000) (C.A. 1999). But the chambers judge is entitled to decide the novel legal issue if she wishes to do so. A willingness to decide such a legal issue would be consistent with the goal of expedited justice. See Rules of Civil Procedure, R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 194, rule 20.04(4) (the court may determine the question of law). 34 In Can v. Calgary Police Service, 2014 ABCA 322, Wakeling J.A. at para 80 reiterated this principle in his concurring reasons. 6. Shifting Onus and Conflicting Evidence (and where it can come from) In First Calgary Holdings (Alb) Corp. v. Metropolitan Ventures Inc., 2015 ABQB 54, 2015 CarswellAlta 108 (Master), the defendants applied for summary dismissal of the plaintiff's claim. The plaintiff did not file an affidavit that supported its claim; the plaintiff submitted that the documents produced and excerpts from the questioning of the applicants (defendants) (there was no cross-examination of the defendants on their affidavits filed in support of the application) showed that the defendants' affidavit evidence in support of the application was unreliable, and that the application must therefore fail. The defendants submitted that without cross-examination on the affidavits, the content of them should be accepted by the Court. Master Robertson said, at paragraph 68: 68 In my view the resolution of this application rests on whether “the record permits a fair and just adjudication”, based upon the approach indicated by the Alberta Court of Appeal in Windsor v. Canadian Pacific Railway, 2014 ABCA 108, 2014 CarswellAlta 395. If the affidavit evidence put forward in support of the application does not appear to be true, or there is a reasonable basis for doubting the veracity of the affidavit evidence on material points of fact, the onus does not shift to the respondent to reply. Only when the applicant has met its obligation does the onus shift to the respondent, as described in Pioneer Exploration Inc. v. Euro-Am Pacific Enterprises Ltd., 2003 ABCA 298 at para. 18 and 19, Murphy Oil Co. v. Predator Corp., 2006 ABCA 69, and Tottrup v. Clearwater, 2006 ABCA 380 at para. 10. The learned Master then addressed the absence of cross-examination on the affidavits: 76 The defendants say that neither Mr. Tomanik nor Mr. Luppi were cross-examined on their affidavits, and therefore their affidavit evidence should be accepted by the Court. 77 However, citing Beier v. Proper Cat Construction Ltd., 2013 ABQB 351 at para. 61, First Capital says that the defendants have not demonstrated that their position is “unassailable” and “so compelling that the likelihood of success is very high.” Since the evidence is not clear, and may not be accurate, … the affidavits cannot be relied upon for summary dismissal. If it is shown that their evidence may not be true because of inconsistencies they themselves have presented, their position cannot be described as “unassailable”. 78 Nonetheless, the defendants say First Capital cannot take this position without cross-examining. 79 They refer to section 23 of the Alberta Evidence Act. That section addresses presenting contradictory evidence to a witness who is in cross-examination. Before giving proof of a contradictory statement, where the witness has not already admitted that he made the statement, the witness is to be asked whether he made the contradictory statement. It assumes that there actually is a cross-examination in which this would be done. It does not appear to apply here so as to require a cross-examination take place where this witness has previously given evidence under oath in the same proceedings that contradicts his later evidence, and the issue before the court is not whether his evidence is true—that is, the court is not weighing his evidence—but whether there is some basis for concluding that his evidence should be weighed by a trial judge. 80 Counsel for the defendants also relies on the Rule in Browne v. Dunn, and says that on this summary judgment application his clients have not been given an opportunity to explain their prior inconsistent statements. Accordingly, the statements should not be referred to, and the evidence in their affidavit should be treated as uncontroverted and simply accepted by the Court regardless of their prior inconsistent testimony in the same proceedings. 81 I drew to counsel's attention (as had counsel for First Capital) that I had recently concluded that the Rule in Browne v. Dunn does not apply in summary judgment applications, because it is a rule that applies to allow the proper weighing of evidence, and evidence is not weighed at a summary judgment application: Chandos Construction Ltd. v. Buildtech Framing Inc., 2014 ABQB 597. 82 Furthermore, the realities of a trial are simply not the same as they are on a chambers application, as counsel for First Capital pointed out. In light of the fact that the previous inconsistent statements were given under oath in these proceedings, and they were clearly identified in First Capital's brief, there could have been a request for an adjournment for a further affidavit by either Mr. Luppi or Mr. Tomanik, or both, to provide an explanation, but there was none. These deponents are not third party witnesses who may no longer be available to swear new affidavits; they are the litigants instructing counsel, and who are trying to persuade the Court to dismiss the claim as against them. There is not the same prejudice here as there is at trial when a witness has long left the witness stand, and then some prior allegedly inconsistent statement that he made, but to which he was not referred in his evidence, is raised in order to call his credibility into question or to prove that his evidence was wrong. In that case, the witness has not been given an opportunity to explain. 83 As well, no suggestion was made here as to what Mr. Luppi's and Mr. Tomanik's explanations might possibly be. … 85 In my view, a part of a party's duty to “put its best foot forward” is its duty to allow relevant information to be placed before the court. It cannot object to relevant evidence, and then argue that the evidence is not before the court because the other side did not compel it to provide it. The court is entitled to consider whether evidence, or a topic of enquiry, is relevant when the issue comes before it, not just on an application to compel. 86 First Capital had been met with the objections based on relevance at questioning. Conducting a cross-examination on an affidavit simply to get the same objections would have been pointless. 87 Objections based on relevance at questioning can backfire on the party making the objection. A party who objects to questions by the opposing party may find himself estopped from tendering evidence on the same topic at trial, having taken the position that it was irrelevant at questioning. The objection may be binding on the objecting party at trial if it is not challenged by the opposing party. But his objection does not bind the opposing party from continuing to assert that the evidence is relevant. Master Robertson concluded: 97 All of this leaves the evidence in a very unsatisfactory state for a summary dismissal of the claim against the individuals. … 98 The burden on an applicant for summary judgment is to present a case that is “unassailable”. If it appears to be unassailable, the respondent can provide evidence that demonstrates that it is not. 99 However, where the respondent can demonstrate that the applicant's own evidence is not “unassailable”, the onus does not shift to the respondent to tender any evidence. 100 As explained above, the questioning can be relied upon to show discrepancies in the applicant defendants' own evidence, and the documents listed in the parties' affidavits of records may be referred to for at least the limited purposes of showing that they exist and are authentic, and that they have been transmitted. 101 The application for summary judgment dismissing the claim against some of the defendants is dismissed. In Mackey v. Squair, 2015 ABQB 329, Justice Topolniski discussed summary judgment applications and the onus of proof: 21 Rule 7.3 of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010 permits a party to apply for summary judgment on all or part of a claim where there is no merit to a claim or part of it, or where the only real issue is quantum …. 22 A party's position is without merit if the facts and law make the moving party's position unassailable and entitle it to the relief it seeks. In this regard, “unassailable” means if it is so compelling that the likelihood of success is very high: Access Mortgage Corporation (2014) Limited v Arres Capital Inc, 2014 ABCA 280 at para 45 (Access Mortgage). 23 The Supreme Court of Canada and Alberta Court of Appeal have mandated a cultural shift to promote timely and affordable access to our civil justice system which affects applications for summary judgment: Hryniak v Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, [2014] 1 SCR 87 (Hryniak); Windsor v Canada Pacific Railway Ltd, 2014 ABCA 108, 371 DLR (4th) 339 (Windsor). Today, if the Court is able to reach a fair and just determination on the merits on a motion for summary judgment then there is no meritorious issue which requires a trial. Windsor at paras 12-13 and 49 indicates there are three criteria to apply Rule 7.3 and order summary judgment; if the summary judgment application: 1. allows the judge to make the necessary findings of fact, 2. allows the judge to apply the law to the facts, and 3. is a proportionate, more expeditious and less expensive means to achieve a just result. 24 The supporting principles governing summary judgment applications are described in Beier v Proper Cat Construction, 2013 ABQB 351 at paras 66–69, 564 AR 357, and reiterated in several appellate authorities including Stout v Track, 2015 ABCA 10 at para 53, 9 Alta LR (6th) 341 and Access Mortgage at para 45: 1. The onus of proof is on the moving party who must present the facts, which in combination with the applicable law, make its position unassailable if the non-moving party does not contest the facts and the law. 2. The non-moving party has no legal or persuasive burden to discharge although that may practically place him at risk. 3. The Court may not make findings of credibility and resolve contested facts. However, controversy over nonmaterial fact is irrelevant. 4. The Court considers the evidence before it the not that which might later be adduced. In Amack v. Wishewan, 2015 ABCA 147, the Court commented on the meaning of the phrase “no genuine issue for trial” after the Supreme Court of Canada's decision in Hryniak v. Mauldin: 26 Rule 7.3(1)(b) allows a court to grant summary judgment to a defendant where there is “no merit” to a claim. Where the claim is by a plaintiff, it is referred to as summary judgment; and where it is by a defendant, it is typically referred to as summary dismissal. The point is that for purposes of this Rule, summary judgment includes summary dismissal. Following the recent Supreme Court of Canada decision in Hryniak v Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, [2014] 1 SCR 87 [Hryniak], this Court has held that summary judgment can be granted if a disposition that is fair and just to both parties can be made on the existing record: Windsor v Canadian Pacific Railway Ltd., 2014 ABCA 108 at para 13, 572 AR 317 [Windsor]; Maxwell v Wal-Mart, 2014 ABCA 383 at para 12. This does not, however, detract from the requirement that there be “no genuine issue for trial”: Hryniak, supra at para 34; Windsor, supra at para 13; 776826 Alberta Ltd. v Ostrowercha, 2015 ABCA 49 at para 11 [Ostrowercha]; Can v Calgary (Police Service), 2014 ABCA 322 at para 10, 315 CCC (3d) 337. Rather, the two concepts are themselves linked, as noted in Hryniak, supra at para 49: • There will be no genuine issue requiring a trial when the judge is able to reach a fair and just determination on the merits on a motion for summary judgment. This will be the case when the process (1) allows the judge to make the necessary findings of fact, (2) allows the judge to apply the law to the facts, and (3) is a proportionate, more expeditious and less expensive means to achieve a just result. Justice Yungwirth put it this way in Robinson v. Lewis, 2015 ABQB 385: 25 In relation to an application for summary dismissal pursuant to Rule 7.3(1)(b), Read J confirmed in the case of Harding v Hudsons Canadian Hospitality Ltd, 2015 ABQB 38 at para 9, [2014] AWLD 1488, that summary judgment is no longer to be denied solely on the basis that the evidence discloses a triable issue. She confirmed that the question is whether there is in fact any issue of merit that genuinely requires a trial. 7. Affidavits in Summary Judgment Applications In H2 Canmore Apartments LP v. Cormode & Dickson Construction Edmonton Ltd., 2023 ABKB 659, Justice Marion discussed what should, and should not, be in an affidavit filed in a summary judgment application: [18] It is appropriate in a well drafted affidavit to describe an allegation to provide the reader with context to better understand the evidence in the affidavit, but the statements must not go beyond that purpose and amount to inadmissible advocacy: Kissel at para 62, citing Alberta Treasury Branches v Leahy, 1999 ABQB 185 at para 84. See also Kudzin v APM Construction Services Inc, 2023 ABKB 425 at para 121; Rau v Edmonton (City), 2015 ABCA 5 at para 19. 2. Factual Conclusions in Affidavits [19] Conclusions are the function of the court and affidavits should be confined to evidence: Alberta (Human Rights Commission) v Alberta Blue Cross Plan, 1983 ABCA 207 at para 6; Rau at para 19. [20] As per McDonald, [McDonald v. Sproule 2023 ABKB 587] at para at 96: [96] Fourth, bald, conclusory, argumentative or self-serving statements, personal opinion, allegations, speculation, conjecture or assertions made in affidavits or questioning transcripts, in the absence of detailed facts and supporting evidence, should be given little or no weight and cannot establish a genuine issue requiring a trial: Fitzpatrick at para 23; Wetaskiwin Animal Clinic Ltd v Hartley, 2021 ABQB 144 at para 41; Murray v Ford Motor Company of Canada, 2020 ABQB 729 at para 103; Rudichuk QB at paras 16-17 and 21; Clark Builders at para 157; County of Vulcan at para 81; Stankovic v 1536679 Alberta Ltd, 2019 ABCA 187 at para 46; ANC Timber at paras 32 and 98; Goodswimmer at paras 38-45; Malhotra v 1743134 Alberta Ltd, 2017 ABQB 34 at para 32; Shefsky v California Gold Mining Inc, 2016 ABCA 103 at para 113; Brookfield at para 18; Rau v Edmonton (City), 2015 ABCA 5 at para 19; R Floden Services Ltd v Solomon, 2015 ABQB 450 at para 23; Guarantee Co of North America v Gordon Capital Corp, 1999 CanLII 664 (SCC), [1999] 3 SCR 423 at para 31; Attila Dogan at para 52; Minex Minerals Ltd v Walker, 2019 ABQB 460 at para 148; Pyrrha Design Inc v Plum and Posey Inc, 2016 ABCA 12 at para 22; Kudzin v APM Construction Services Inc, 2023 ABKB 425 at para 121; Spady at para 57. [21] It is also important, again, to remember the summary judgment context. Given that the applicant has both the threshold and ultimate burden to establish that summary judgment is appropriate and that there are no genuine issues for trial, the court must be careful in considering a pre-emptive motion to strike evidence. For example, the court must be alive to the fact that only the initial elements of a defence must be proven in order to trigger the duty of the respondent to put its best foot forward. In some cases, this may require an applicant affiant to open themselves up to questioning by simply saying: “the allegations against me are not true”. Courts must be careful about striking, as a bald or bare assertion, a factual statement required to put the applicant over the threshold burden. [22] Further, Courts must be wary of requiring an affiant to provide detailed supporting facts to support a negative proposition. For example, where it is alleged a defendant did X, it may not be reasonable to expect an affidavit to say more than: I did not do X as alleged. It may not be reasonable to expect an affiant to provide detailed evidence of everything they did do that was not X. In some instances, a lack of detailed back-up to a conclusory statement in an affidavit should be addressed in the context of all the evidence. This point is particularly relevant where an applicant for summary dismissal is responding to broad or conclusory allegations in a Statement of Claim. 3. Legal Conclusions or Legal Opinion in Affidavits [23] Conclusions are the function of the court and affidavits should be confined to evidence: Alberta (Human Rights Commission) at para 6; Rau at para 19. To the extent a lay witness with no legal expertise ventures into providing legal opinions, it is trite that such opinions are also inadmissible. 4. Opinion Evidence in Affidavits [24] The general rule is that witnesses may not express opinions, because opinion evidence is presumptively inadmissible: R v DD, 2000 SCC 43 (CanLII), [2000] 2 SCR 275 at para 49; Kon Construction Ltd v Terranova Developments Ltd, 2015 ABCA 249 at para 20; White Burgess Langille Inman v Abbott and Haliburton Co, 2015 SCC 23 at paras 14-15. [25] There are at least two exceptions to this rule: (1) the compendious statement of facts exception; and (2) the witness with expertise exception: O'Kane v Lillqvist-O'Kane, 2021 ABQB 925 at para 6. [26] The first exception was summarized in O'Kane [footnotes omitted]: [8] The leading case on the admissibility of lay opinion evidence under the compendious statement of facts exception is Graat v R. The Supreme Court of Canada admonished courts faced with lay opinion evidence not to place too much weight on the “tenuous, and frequently false, antithesis between fact and opinion. The line between “fact” and “opinion” is not clear.” The Court went on to prescribe a principled approach. The Court explained that “[a]dmissibility is determined, first, by asking whether the evidence sought to be admitted is relevant. This is a matter of applying logic and experience to the circumstances of the particular case. The question which must then be asked is whether, though probative, the evidence must be excluded by a clear ground of policy or of law.” [9] The Court in Graat admitted lay opinion evidence from police officers as to whether the accused was too drunk to drive. The lay opinion evidence was neither excluded by a clear ground of policy nor law because it fell under what is known as the “compendious statement of facts” exception to the rule against opinion evidence. Under the compendious statement of facts exception, the opinion functions as a shorthand for expressing all of the small facts that are implicit in the opinion. For example, the conclusion that a person is drunk may be taken to be comprised of the factual observations that an ordinary person would use to conclude that a person was drunk, such as slurred words and a lack of coordination. [10] Following Graat, leading texts have distilled four criteria for admitting lay evidence under the compendious statement of facts exception that have, in turn, been accepted by courts. Lay opinion evidence may only be accepted if: (1) the lay witness is in a better position than the trier of fact to form the conclusion; (2) the conclusion is one that persons of ordinary experience are able to make; (3) the witness, although not expert, has the experiential capacity to make the conclusion; and (4) the opinions being expressed are merely a compendious mode of stating facts that are too subtle or complicated to be narrated as effectively without resort to conclusions. [11] The four criteria are sometimes styled the “lay evidence rule.” [27] The second exception was addressed by the Court of Appeal in Kon Construction. In that case, the Court of Appeal identified three types of witnesses with expertise, at para 35: (a) Independent experts who are retained to provide opinions about issues in the litigation, but were not otherwise involved in the underlying events. This is the category of expert witness contemplated by White Burgess and Mohan. (b) Witnesses with expertise who were involved in the events underlying the litigation, but are not themselves litigants. An example is the family physician in a personal injury case who is called upon to testify about his or her observations of the plaintiff, and the treatment provided. (c) Litigants (including the officers and employees of corporate litigants) who have expertise, and who were actually involved in the events underlying the litigation. [28] The Cormode Employee Defendants argue that they fall within the third category: litigants with expertise who were involved in the underlying litigation. In Kon Construction, the Court of Appeal said this about these types of witnesses: [40] Secondly, it is generally not necessary to qualify the last class of witnesses with expertise as “experts” under the Mohan procedure. As parties to the litigation they are entitled to testify, and generally they will have the most direct and relevant evidence about the issues. The truth finding function of a trial requires that their evidence be received. Since they were often only involved in the underlying events because of their expertise, it makes no sense to hold that they cannot explain why they acted as they did, if they stray into their expertise. Their opinions explain why they acted as they did. Since these witnesses are available for pre-trial questioning, formal advance notice of their opinions or their evidence is not needed. [29] It may be difficult in determining exactly when such witnesses stray outside of their expertise, or when they are giving opinions that are not based on their involvement in the underlying events. If it is not clear, it may be more appropriate for such issues to be dealt with as in the context of all the evidence on the summary judgment application. Where it is clear that such witnesses are giving opinions outside of their expertise or are given opinions that are not based on their personal involvement in the matter, then such evidence may be inadmissible. 5. Hearsay in Affidavits [30] As per McDonald, at paras 91-92: [91] First, with respect to applicant affidavits, they should generally be based on personal knowledge: rule 13.18(3): Magnuson Estate, 2023 ABKB 305 at paras 35-38; Consolidated Civil Enforcement Inc v Shipalesky, 2022 ABKB 718 at para 30; Moore v Wetaskawin Friends and Horizons Training, 2022 ABKB 617 at para 34; Van Grinsven v Kortbeek, 2022 ABQB 138 at para 32; Malkhassian Estate v Scotia Life Insurance Company, 2020 ABQB 173 at para 40; From Estate, 2019 ABQB 988 at para 103; Clark Builders and Stantec Consulting Ltd v GO Community Centre, 2019 ABQB 706 at para 40; DD v Calgary Counselling Centre, 2017 ABQB 95 at para 44; Attila Dogan Construction v AMEC Americas Limited, 2015 ABQB 120 at para 52 affirmed 2015 ABCA 406. [92] However, there is some flexibility in the application of rule 13.18(3) in the context of summary judgment applications – sometimes evidence not based on personal knowledge can be admitted. For example, courts may be more flexible where the applicant is a corporation or estate, where there are no people left with personal knowledge, or where the evidence would be admissible at trial as an exception to hearsay: Magnuson Estate at para 38; Moore at paras 35 and 38-40; Spady v Spady Estate, 2022 ABQB 591 at para 56; Barry v Industrial Alliance Insurance and Financial Services Inc (IAF), 2022 ABQB 265 at para 53; Pure Environmental Waste Management Ltd v Lonquist Field Service (Canada), ULC, 2022 ABQB 30 at para 47; Saito v Lester Estate, 2021 ABCA 179 at paras 11-12; County of Vulcan v Genesis Reciprocal Insurance Exchange, 2020 ABQB 93 at paras 70-71; Goodswimmer v Canada (Attorney General), 2017 ABCA 365, leave to appeal ref'd [2018] SCCA No 1 at para 33; Klein v Wolbeck, 2016 ABQB 28 at para 15; Attila Dogan at paras 64-75; Murphy v Cahill, 2012 ABQB 793 at paras 26-30. […] [31] Even if hearsay is permitted, it should only be admitted if would be admissible at trial; or if it meets the requirements for a principled exception to hearsay (when it meets the necessity and threshold reliability criteria): R v Philip, 2022 ABCA 39 at para 22, citing R v Bradshaw, 2017 SCC 35 at para 1. 8. (b) Alternatively, if the conflicting affidavit evidence is irrelevant to a particular issue that must be decided and the Court can make a determination in the dispute that is fair and just, it will do so. This jurisprudence states that where resolving such disputes entails weighing evidence, summary judgment normally ought not to be granted. 11 There are some exceptions to this general rule, for example: (i) where the chambers judge/master assumes that the evidence of the non-moving party is correct, (as was done in Sherwood Steel, supra). (ii) where the evidence of the non-moving party is either destroyed by cross-examination on affidavit or the introduction of other evidence rendering that party's evidence completely non-credible: Janvier v. 834474 Alberta Ltd., 2010 ABQB 800. (iii) Where the conflicting evidence is on matters which are irrelevant to the ground upon which summary judgment is being sought (for example, where there is conflicting evidence as to which driver caused a collision between two automobiles but the summary dismissal application is being brought on a limitations defence). 12 No exceptions apply here. In Goodswimmer v. Canada (Attorney General), 2017 ABCA 365, 2017 CarswellAlta 2299, 60 Alta. L.R. (6th) 226, the Court said: 38 The appellants argue that the case management judge erred in granting summary relief in the face of conflicting affidavits. They argue that the only way to resolve disputed issues of fact is with a trial. There are admittedly cases that point out the dangers of attempting to resolve disputed issues, especially those that rely on findings of credibility, based on conflicting affidavits and documents that would support either party's position. 39 The modern summary judgment case law, however, marks a shift away from seeing the trial as the default method of proving disputed facts. Hryniak v Mauldin at para. 4 confirms that a trial is not needed to resolve disputed facts if a summary judgment motion can achieve a fair and just adjudication, and that the prospect of the trial judge obtaining a better appreciation of the evidence at a trial should not be overemphasized. Not every conflict in the evidence precludes the chambers judge from drawing inferences from the admitted facts, the undisputed evidence, the conduct of the parties, and the corroborating evidence (such as documents with objective reliability): Sandhu v Siri Guru Nanak Sikh Gurdwara of Alberta, 2015 ABCA 101 at paras. 79–81, 12 Alta LR (6th) 299, 599 AR 267. The Alberta Rules permit a judge to make findings of fact on an application for summary judgment: Windsor v Canadian Pacific Railway Ltd., 2014 ABCA 108 at para. 14, 94 Alta LR (5th) 301, 572 AR 317. 40 The mere fact that there might be some conflicting evidence on the record does not mean that a “fair and just adjudication” is not possible. The case law was summarized in Shefsky v California Gold Mining Inc., 2016 ABCA 103 at para. 113, 31 Alta LR (6th) 1, 616 AR 290: 113 Not every piece of disputed evidence requires a trial. For example, a “bare denial” or bald allegation does not raise a triable issue: Canada (Attorney General) v Lameman, 2008 SCC 14 at para. 11, [2008] 1 SCR 372; Goldman v Devine, 2007 ONCA 301 at para. 23; R. Floden Services Ltd. v Solomon, 2015 ABQB 450 at para. 23, 24 Alta LR (6th) 76; Confederation Trust Co. v Alizadeh, [1998] OJ No 408 (QL) (Gen Div). Nor does a self-serving affidavit unsupported by other evidence: Guarantee Co. of North America v Gordon Capital Corp., [1999] 3 SCR 423 at pp. 436-37. Nor does evidence that flies in the face of the balance of the record: Dagher v Glenn, 2016 ABCA 38 at paras. 30–2; Pioneer Exploration Inc. (Trustee of) v Euro-Am Pacific Enterprises Ltd., 2003 ABCA 298 at para. 25-6, 27 Alta LR (4th) 62; Rogers Cable TV Ltd. v 373041 Ontario Ltd. (1994), 22 OR (3d) 25 (Gen Div); Klein v Wolbeck, 2016 ABQB 28 at para. 26; Pizza Pizza Ltd. v Gillespie (1990), 75 OR (2d) 225 at p. 253 (Gen Div). Whether there is truly a “genuine issue requiring resolution at a trial” requires a nuanced balancing of the weight and perceived reliability of the evidence, the importance of the issue, the likelihood of there being a better record at trial, and any other relevant considerations. There are other manifestations of this principle, including Leis v Leis, 2014 ABCA 36 at para. 45, where the affidavit said to raise a conflict was “unsupported or outright contradicted by the litigation history”, and Lydian Properties Inc. v Chambers, 2009 ABCA 21 at paras. 2, 22-3, 100 Alta LR (4th) 39, 457 AR 211 where the conflicting evidence was not material to the outcome. 41 The presumption against deciding summarily based on conflicting affidavits is primarily concerned with situations where the conflict raises issues of credibility. None of the historical evidence in this case raises issues of credibility. Assertions by those who actually participated in the settlement negotiations that are plainly contradicted by the contemporaneous documents do not necessarily bar summary disposition. Further, the presumption against deciding summarily based on conflicting affidavits assumes that the affidavits are relevant and admissible. Where the identified disputes are not on matters of fact, but are really legal opinions, inferences, or subjective views on the interpretation of documents, there is not necessarily an impediment to a summary disposition. In Liberty Mortgage Services Ltd. v. Shaw, 2024 ABKB 92, Justice Aloneissi said: [39] Summary judgment is not limited to cases where the facts are not in dispute: Weir-Jones at para 21. Put otherwise, not every conflict in evidence gives rise to a genuine need for a trial: Weir-Jones at para 38. That said, some factual disputes can create a need for trial, like conflicts of evidence on material issues or conflicts of evidence that require findings of credibility to be resolved: Weir-Jones at paras 35 and 38. [40] Conflicts between affidavit evidence may require credibility findings to resolve. It is an error to disregard conflicting affidavit evidence entirely when that evidence could, if assessed for credibility, have a material impact on the outcome of the case: LRS v SSD, 2020 ABCA 206 at paras 17 and 19 citing to Nieuwesteeg v Barron, 2009 ABCA 235. [41] However, conflicts in affidavit evidence do not necessarily preclude summary judgment. The circumstances in which facts may be found in despite conflicting affidavit evidence were described by Bielby JA in Sandhu v Siri Guru Nanak Sikh Gurdwara of Alberta, 2015 ABCA 101 [Sandhu]: 1. Where the conflicts in the evidence do not concern essential facts. 2. Where the apparent conflict is a conflict of opinions or interpretations, rather than a factual conflict. 3. Where the issues can be resolved based only on facts that are not disputed. 4. Where one party relies on several affidavits which contain internally conflicting evidence, including some evidence which agrees with or supports the opposing party's evidence and thus amounts to an admission against interest. Sandhu at para 81. [42] In R Floden Services Ltd v Solomon, 2015 ABQB 450 [Floden], Justice Renke added an additional category: 5. Where the issues can be resolved on the basis of admissible evidence other than the conflicting affidavit evidence. Floden at para 21 citing to Compton Petroleum Corp v Alberta Power Ltd, 1999 ABQB 42 [Compton] at para 14 and N V Reykdal & Associates v 571582 Alberta Ltd, 2000 ABCA 330 at para 5 [Reykdal]. [43] Furthermore, not all affidavit evidence is equally weighty. In Floden at para 22, Justice Renke listed the circumstances in which a Judge may properly give less weight to particular affidavit evidence: 1. The Judge is satisfied the deponent was attempting to engineer circumstances which precluded being tested on credibility (e.g. by avoiding questioning): Sandhu at para 83. 2. The affidavit evidence is “destroyed by cross-examination”: Janvier v 834474 Alberta Ltd, 2010 ABQB 800 at para 15 [Janvier]. 3. The evidence is not consistent with other evidence and known circumstances: Compton at para 14; Reykdal at para 5; Janvier at para 15. [44] Affidavit evidence that is general, vague, or superficial may also be given reduced weight: Geophysical Service Inc v Falkland Oil and Gas Ltd, 2020 ABCA 21 at para 61; MNP Ltd (Eco-Industrial Business Park Inc) v Symmetry Asset Management Inc, 2023 ABKB 429 at para 87. Affidavit evidence that is self-serving and otherwise unsupported can be given no weight and does not give rise to a genuine need for trial: Guarantee Co of North America v Mr. Tayloron Capital Corp, 1999 CanLII 664 (SCC), [1999] 3 SCR 423 at 436-437 [Mr. Tayloron] at 436-437. Other descriptions of this type of evidence include a “bare denial”, a “bald assertion”, or having no “air of reality”: Goodswimmer v Canada (Attorney General), 2017 ABCA 365 at para 40 citing to Lameman at para 11 and Floden at para 23; Fitzpatrick v The College of Physical Therapists Alberta, 2020 ABCA 164 at para 22. 9. His Lordship said: 7 The appeals are allowed for the following reasons. Parties to litigation may bring an application for summary judgment or summary dismissal prior to and regardless of whether or not they have taken the pre trial steps of questioning and document production. The question raised in this instance is whether or not the default position, in the face of such proceedings, is that the obligations or powers under Part 5 of the Alberta Rules of Court [Rules] are stayed or held in suspense. 8 The starting point in this analysis has to be the Rules themselves. As our Court of Appeal has said in Canadian Natural Resources Ltd v ShawCor Ltd, 2014 ABCA 289 at para 30, the Rules have a status comparable to a statute and must be read in their entire context and in their grammatical and ordinary sense, harmoniously with the overall scheme of the legislation. 9 Part 5 makes an affidavit of records mandatory (rule 5.5). Timing of Summary Judgment Applications with Class Proceedings Applications In P. (W.) v. Alberta, 2014 ABCA 404, 2014 CarswellAlta 2152, 7 Alta. L.R. (6th) 319, 62 C.P.C. (7th) 111, 378 D.L.R. (4th) 629, the plaintiffs applied for certification of their action under the Class Proceedings Act. The defendants applied for summary judgment on the basis that the claim was brought out of time. The learned Chambers judge granted the summary judgment application, and then made a provisional ruling on the Class Proceedings application in case the summary judgment ruling was reversed on appeal. The plaintiffs appealed the summary judgment decision and provisional ruling as they contended that the learned Chambers judge should have certified the proceedings before ruling on the summary judgment application. The Court of Appeal ruled that the order in which the applications are determined is within the discretion of the judge. At paragraphs 18–23, the Court said: 18 As already noted, this ground has—as the appellants have framed it—two aspects. They say, first, that the chambers judge should have deferred hearing and deciding on Alberta's summary judgment application until deciding on certification. And, secondly, they argue that summary judgment should not have been granted at all, since whether the ultimate limitation period applied here was a “triable issue”. 19 The appellants assert (but really do not argue) that this sequencing of dispositions is preferable. Indeed, they say that the jurisprudence shows that limitations issues are “overwhelmingly” decided by a full trial, rather than by summary judgment. Yet, the briefest review of the case law demonstrates that this is not so. Subject to the Rules of Court (which, by operation of section 41 of the CPA, apply to class proceedings), and to a court exercising its case management discretion to direct otherwise, a party defending against an action may apply at any time for summary judgment. Usually, an application for certification will be heard first: Hoffman v Monsanto Canada Inc, 2002 SKCA 120 at paras 28-29, 220 DLR (4th) 542; Kwicksutaeineuk/Ah-Kwa-Mish First Nation v British Columbia (Agriculture and Lands), 2009 BCSC 1593 at paras 59–62, 84 CPC (6th) 170. This is principally the effect of the short timeframe contemplated by the CPA for obtaining certification of a class proceeding.2 20 The appellants say that this timeframe amounts to a statutory “direction” that all other matters are to be held in abeyance pending certification. This is incorrect. Proceeding with a certification application first is “primarily a matter of convenience rather than necessity”: Kowch v Gibraltar Mortgage Ltd, 2013 ABQB 317 at para 10, 536 AR 112 (Master in Chambers). The CPA does not preclude a judge from exercising his or her discretion to hear and decide a summary judgment application prior to certification on the basis that it is an efficient and cost-effective way of disposing of an issue that might bring an end to the litigation altogether. It does not matter whether the purportedly unmeritorious claim is sought to be advanced as a class proceeding or not. Trying unmeritorious claims is per se unreasonable, because it imposes an unnecessary and often onerous burden upon parties and our system of civil justice: Hryniak at paras 23–28; Canada v Lameman, 2008 SCC 14 at para 10, [2008] 1 SCR 372; Windsor at para 13; Beier v Proper Cat Construction Ltd, 2013 ABQB 351 at paras 56–71, 564 AR 557 [Beier]; Orr v Fort McKay First Nation, 2014 ABQB 111 at paras 24–26. 21 Simply put, a class proceeding is just one procedural mode of advancing a claim. The mere fact that a claim is advanced by way of a class proceeding does not endow it with special status allowing it to survive where the same claim would otherwise be doomed. More particularly, it remains subject to all the tools furnished by Part 7 of the Rules of Court for resolving claims without a full trial, including summary judgment. As the Supreme Court observed in Bisaillon v Concordia University, 2006 SCC 19 at para 17, [2006] 1 SCR 666, “[t]he class action is … a procedural vehicle whose use neither modifies nor creates substantive rights[.]… It cannot serve as a basis for legal proceedings if the various claims it covers, taken individually, would not do so[.]” (See also Stevenson Estate v Bank of Montreal, 2011 SKCA 51 at para 12, 371 Sask R 198; Thorpe v Honda Canada Inc, 2011 SKQB 72 at para 29, 373 Sask R 71; and Thorpe v Honda Canada Inc, 2009 SKQB 488 at para 14, 357 Sask R 1.) 22 The foregoing applies with equal force where the summary judgment application is based upon the expiry of a limitation period relative to the claim of a proposed representative plaintiff: Stone v Wellington County Board of Education, 1999 CanLII 1886 (ONCA) at para 10, [1999] OJ No 1298 (QL) [Stone]. Where a proposed representative plaintiff's claim is shown to be time-barred, there is no good reason for permitting the issue of certification to continue consuming judicial and litigants' resources. Indeed, there is good reason for not doing so, since the representative plaintiff must be a member of the class: Section 2(1) of the CPA.3 Allowing a representative plaintiff's clearly time-barred claim to proceed further would defy the Legislature's intent that the class proceeding be brought only by someone with a personal stake in the outcome: Stone at paras 9-10; Hughes v Sunbeam Corp (Canada) Ltd (2002), 61 OR (3d) 433, 165 OAC 68 at para 15, leave to appeal refused [2002] SCCA No 446 (QL). 23 While the chambers judge in this case actually expended the time needed to hear and provisionally decide the certification application after having heard the summary judgment application, concerns about costs to litigants and to the civil justice system nonetheless arise here given the appellants' argument that limitations should have been determined by a full trial. Further, the chambers judge's decision as case manager to order the applications as he did is entitled to substantial deference. That decision was not appealed. And, in any event, it was not unreasonable for him to exercise his discretion by hearing and deciding on Alberta's summary judgment application before deciding on the appellant's certification application.
