Rule Applies to Unliquidated Claims In Espey v. Chapters Inc. (1998), 225 A.R. 68 (Q.B.), the plaintiff sued the defendant alleging wrongful dismissal. In its statement of defence, the defendant did not allege termination for cause, but did allege that the plaintiff had not properly mitigated her damages. The plaintiff applied for summary judgment. In holding that summary judgment could be granted in such a case, Fruman J., (as she then was), said, at p. 69: Ms. Espey applied for summary judgment under rule 159. She filed a comprehensive affidavit that provided detailed information about her personal situation, employment history and responsibilities, circumstances of the termination of her employment, her post termination employment search and the losses she incurred. Ms. Epsey was cross-examined on her affidavit. Chapters chose to file no affidavit in connection with the summary judgment application Then, at pp. 71-73, Her Ladyship said: As I understand the defendant's principal argument, because an action for wrongful dismissal require[s] a judge to make a determination as to whether the period of notice was sufficient and then to quantify the damages and consider mitigation, and because these issues requires [sic] the exercise of judicial discretion, the case is not an appropriate one for summary judgment. They say this even though both the facts and the law are clear. All that is required is an application of the law to the facts, which requires the exercise of judicial discretion. There is nothing in rule 159 which prevents such a judicial exercise. In its earlier formulation, rule 159 was restricted to actions in debt with liquidated damages. That is no longer the case. . . . . . Given that both the facts and law are clear, I cannot see how a court would be assisted by requiring a trial to take place merely because the matter involves wrongful dismissal and an exercise of judicial discretion. . . . . . I see no advantages in having a trial. The facts and law are clear and credibility is not in issue. People are entitled to their day in court but not their decade. I do not suggest that there have been undue delays in this case; rather we must recognize that not every case merits a trial. A summary judgment procedure is swift, cheap and efficient, with the same neutral evaluation before an imparital judge. It is particularly well-suited to a case like this, where a judge applies undisputed facts to settled law. Requiring a trial in these circumstances is not in the interests of the administration of justice. As to the assessment of the damages, Fruman J. said, at pp. 73-74: The next stage then is the assessment of damages. As I read rule 159(5), a court may direct that the action proceed only to assess the amount of damages or may direct a reference or accounting. These are permissive. A Master does not have jurisdiction to assess unliquidated damages. A Court of Queen's Bench justice does. I have reviewed the matter carefully and I am in a position to make an assessment of damages. I see no benefit in delaying this matter by referring it to another justice to be considered on another day. I find that the appropriate period of notice should have been 11 months. If the parties cannot resolve the amount of salary and value of the benefits, I direct a reference to the Master, as referee, to determine the value of the salary and benefits received in the month preceding the date of termination of Ms. Espey's employment. 15. Rule can apply to Judicial Review applications In Bergman v. Innisfree (Village), 2020 ABQB 661, 2020 CarswellAlta 2024, 10 M.P.L.R. (6th) 183, Justice Feth said: [96] Rule 7.3(1)(b) allows a party to apply to the Court for summary judgment (including dismissal) in respect of all or part of a claim if “there is no merit to a claim or part of it.” [97] In considering a summary judgment application, the Court utilizes the test from Hryniak v Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7. Summary judgment is appropriate where the record allows the Court to make the necessary findings of fact, apply the law to the facts, and summary judgment is “a proportionate, more expeditious and less expensive means to achieve a just result” than a trial or full hearing: Hryniak at para 4. [98] If summary dismissal of an application for judicial review requires a merits review, the application to dismiss is duplicative of the judicial review proceeding itself and generally does not promote a more expeditious and less expensive means to achieve a just result. Summary dismissal is therefore rarely available in judicial review proceedings. [99] Summary dismissal of a judicial review proceeding may be appropriate in some limited situations, particularly where a fatal flaw strikes at the foundation of the Court's authority to hear the application. [100] In Tolksdorf v Canada (Attorney General), 2019 FCA 158 at para 7, the Federal Court of Appeal held that “the summary dismissal of the application for judicial review before the Federal Court was justified on the basis that the application for judicial review was so clearly improper as to be bereft of any chance of success.” The Federal Court of Appeal referred to its earlier decision in Canada (National Revenue) v JP Morgan Asset Management (Canada) Inc, 2013 FCA 250 at para 47: There must be a “show stopper” or a “knockout punch”—an obvious, fatal flaw striking at the root of this Court's power to entertain the application: Rahman v. Public Service Labour Relations Board, 2013 FCA 117 at paragraph 7; Donaldson v. Western Grain Storage By-Products, 2012 FCA 286 at paragraph 6; cf. Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc., 1990 CanLII 90 (SCC), [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959. [101] In Morris v 1934809 Alberta Ltd, 2018 ABQB 299 at paras 9–14, in the context of an application to strike under Rule 3.68, this Court “dismissed” an application for judicial review “on a summary basis,” where the “Applicants failed to file an application for leave to appeal within the time limits provided for in section 688” of the MGA and tried instead to utilize judicial review. The Court reasoned that “incorrect legal advice” about the time to appeal did not constitute a special circumstance inviting the Court to exercise its inherent jurisdiction of judicial review. While the application was dismissed pursuant to Rule 3.68, summary dismissal under Rule 7.3(1)(b) might have been available as well. In Neilson v. Leduc (County), 2021 ABQB 735, 2021 CarswellAlta 2201, Justice Rothwell said: [22] Courts in Alberta have granted summary judgment/dismissal of applications for judicial review. In Bergman v Innisfree (Village), 2020 ABQB 661 [Bergman], Justice Feth noted that summary dismissal of a judicial review proceeding is only available in limited circumstances, but may be appropriate when “a fatal flaw strikes at the foundation of the Court's authority to hear the application”: see paras 99–101. [23] Summary judgment/dismissal has been granted when the judicial review application has not been commenced within the 6 month time frame mandated by Rule 3.15: see Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation v Alberta (Minister of Energy), 2009 ABQB 576, upheld on appeal 2011 ABCA 29, Enmax Corporation v Alberta Labour Relations Board, 2018 ABQB 431; and Boll v Woodlands County, 2021 ABQB 406 [Boll]. 16. Rule May Be Applied In Provincial Court In Savoie v. AUPE, 2012 ABQB 575, Madam Justice Moreau concluded that a summary judgment application under Rule 7.3 was available in civil actions conducted in the Provincial Court of Alberta. At paragraphs 12–14, her Ladyship said: 12 Mr. Savoie took issue at the hearing of the appeal with the jurisdiction of the Provincial Court to grant summary judgment dismissing his Civil Claim on the basis that the Provincial Court Act, RSA 2000, C. P-31 and amendments thereto (“the Act”) and regulations thereunder contain no provision for making the application. The learned Provincial Court judge referred to s. 8(2) of the Act, which provides: Rules of Court 8. (1) The practice and procedure of the Court shall be as provided in this Act and the regulations. (2) Where this Act or the regulations do not provide for a specific practice or procedure of the Court that is necessary to ensure an expeditious and inexpensive resolution of a matter before the Court, the Court may (a) apply the Alberta Rules of Court, and (b) modify the Alberta Rules of Court as needed. 13 As noted by the Supreme Court of Canada in Canada (Attorney General) v. Lameman, 2008 SCC 14, at paras. 11-12: The summary judgment rule serves an important purpose in the civil litigation system. It prevents claims or defences that have no chance of success from proceeding to trial. Trying unmeritorious claims imposes a heavy price in terms of time and cost on the parties to the litigation and on the justice system. It is essential to the proper operation of the justice system and beneficial to the parties that claims that have no chance of success be weeded out at an early stage. Conversely, it is essential to justice that claims disclosing real issues that may be successful proceed to trial. 14 In light of these comments, the summary judgment procedure is “necessary to ensure an expeditious and inexpensive resolution of a matter before the Court” within the meaning of s. 8(2) of the Act. As neither the Act nor the regulations provides for a summary judgment application, it was within the powers of the PTC judge and the judge who ultimately heard the application to permit AUPE to proceed with a summary dismissal application pursuant to Rule 7.3 of the Alberta Rules of Court. 17. Medical Malpractice Actions—Expert Evidence In Sima v. Hui, 2008 ABQB 104, 2008 CarswellAlta 178, 90 Alta. L.R. (4th) 360, Ross J. discussed the use of expert evidence in summary judgment applications. At pp. 366–368, her Ladyship said: 21 The initial onus in a summary judgment application is on the applicant to show that there is no genuine issue for trial. Once the applicant has made this case, the onus then shifts to the respondent to “establish his claim as being one with a real chance of success”: Guarantee Co., at para. 27. The respondent cannot simply rely on the allegations in his pleadings, or on the possibility that further evidence may be available at trial. If the respondent fails to come forward with evidence to prove a meritorious case, summary judgment will be given against him: Jager Industries Inc. v. Canadian Occidental Petroleum Ltd., [2000] A.J. No. 994, 2000 ABQB 592, at para. 20–25. 22 In the context of medical malpractice claims, this means there may be an onus on a plaintiff/respondent who is facing a summary judgment application to provide expert evidence to support his claim. There will be such an onus where the claim by its nature depends on expert evidence, and where the defendant/applicant produces expert evidence that the claim is without merit: Stoddard v. Montague, [2006] A.J. No. 446, 2006 ABCA 109 (“Stoddard”). 23 In Stoddard, the plaintiff had commenced action against several doctors for failing to diagnose or treat illnesses or conditions from which he suffered, alleging that he suffered injuries and complications as a result. In applications for summary dismissal, the defendant doctors filed evidence detailing the medical concerns the plaintiff presented to them, and the treatment they provided. They also filed expert evidence that the care they provided “easily met the standard of care attributable to each of them, and that the care provided did not cause any of the injuries” that the plaintiff allegedly suffered from. The plaintiff did not file expert evidence to support his claim. He filed a pharmacologist's report, but the pharmacologist stated that his expertise did not extend to the complaints made about the doctors. 24 The Court of Appeal stated as follows regarding the need for expert evidence on the application: It is not always necessary for plaintiffs in medical negligence cases to adduce expert evidence, since in some cases the relevant standard of care or whether a breach caused an injury will be within the knowledge of the court. However, this is not such a case, as the standards of care at issue are not obvious … … The need for expert evidence for [the issues of causation and standard of care] is obvious. In a medical negligence action, where the allegation of negligence involves issues outside the ordinary knowledge and experience of the trier of fact, summary dismissal of the plaintiff's claim is appropriate when the plaintiff has failed to adduce any supportive expert opinion: Claus v. Wolfman (1999), 52 O.R. (3d) 673, at para. 12 S.C.J.; aff'd (2000), 52 O.R. (3d) 680 (C.A.) (“Claus”); Tamimi v. Toronto Hospital (Western Division) (1999), [1999] O.J. No. 2632, 123 O.A.C. 182, at para. 2; leave to appeal to S.C.C. ref'd (2000), [1999] S.C.C.A. No. 464, 256 N.R. 198. If all the plaintiff does is assert that evidence will or may come out at trial and that the pleadings and allegations made during argument support issues for trial, he or she will not be successful in preventing summary dismissal in the face of overwhelming evidence that the alleged perpetrators were not negligent, did not cause the injuries complained of, and met the relevant standard of care … 25 This principle has been applied in cases in which the plaintiff suffered a complication resulting from medical care. For example, in Kravontka v. Capital Region Health Authority, [2002] A.J. No. 876, 2002 ABQB 652 (“Kravontka”), the plaintiff sued regarding complications following surgery. The defendant doctors applied for summary judgment dismissing the action. Their application was supported by affidavits of physicians who provided expert opinion evidence that “the Plaintiff had an unfortunate complication and that the level of care was superb” (para. 14). The Plaintiff responded with a personal affidavit describing his perception of his post-surgery care. He did not provide any expert evidence in response. 26 Master Funduk granted summary judgment, holding that “[w]ithout any expert evidence in his favour the Plaintiff's case is doomed” (para. 18). It was not enough for the Plaintiff to argue that the defendants' experts might not be believed; even if they were, that alone would not make out a prima facie case for the plaintiff. It was also not enough for the Plaintiff to say the “lawsuit should remain alive to let the Plaintiff try to get an expert who will favour him” (para. 21). This did not meet the defendant doctors' case that the Plaintiff had no reasonable prospect of success, and that the claims against them should be dismissed. 27 In Claus, the plaintiff suffered an injury to her right femoral nerve during the delivery of a healthy child. The defendants submitted evidence in support of their application for dismissal of the claim that they had met the required standard of care. The plaintiff did not have an expert opinion to support her contention to the contrary. Pitt J. held that, unless the issues are within the ordinary knowledge and experience of the trier of fact, a plaintiff faced with a summary dismissal application must provide expert evidence to support her case. He granted the defendants' application, noting that while the injury was a lamentable occurrence, “such an action cannot be allowed to proceed to trial in the absence of an expert opinion supportive of the plaintiffs' position, especially in light of the powerful opinion provided by the defence” (para. 23). In Carbone v. Whidden, 2013 ABQB 434, the plaintiff sued her surgeon in relation to a liposuction procedure performed on her by the defendant. The defendant brought an application for a summary dismissal of the claim. The defendant filed an affidavit sworn by him to which was attached a letter from another physician (Dr. Lobay). Justice Poelman discussed the use of such a “report” in the summary dismissal application. At paragraphs 16, 17, 21–25, his Lordship said: 16 As can be seen from my brief summary of the pleadings, Ms. Carbone's allegations against Dr. Whidden fall into two broad categories. First, she pleads that the liposuction procedure was to be on her hips only, and specifically not on her buttocks, but that in fact her buttocks were involved in the surgery. Second, she pleads that Dr. Whidden should not have conducted any procedure without adequately exploring the existence of possible body dysmorphic disorder. 17 Thus, for Dr. Whidden to be granted summary dismissal, he must first establish that there is no genuine issue of material fact requiring trial. This requires consideration of his affidavit, the only evidence he submitted on this application. … 21 Dr. Whidden's counsel submitted that I should infer from Dr. Lobay's report that there was no involvement of the buttocks in the surgery. I am unable to see a basis for that inference in the very general statements Dr. Lobay makes in his letter. 22 Further, it would be unsafe and improper for me to generously draw inferences from Dr. Lobay's report in favour of Dr. Whidden's position. Dr. Lobay's letter is not sworn or affirmed when Ms. Carbone requested Dr. Whidden's counsel to make Dr. Lobay available for cross-examination, she was met with the response that “we will not produce Dr. Lobay for cross-examination on his expert report as there is no obligation to do so, having not filed an affidavit.” When she applied to the court under rule 5.37 to cross-examine Dr. Lobay, Dr. Whidden argued that the rule only applies to the questioning of experts before trial, on expert reports prepared and served as required by the Alberta Rules of Court—a position which was, based on the plain wording of the rule, accepted by the case management justice. 23 If an applicant relies on an opinion as a central part of his case, but chooses not to have it adduced as sworn evidence and objects to all attempts to have it tested, it is not worthy of generous interpretation. Perhaps on questioning Dr. Lobay would have clarified his opinion on Ms. Carbone's chief complaint that the surgery extended to her buttocks. Now we can only guess. 24 In my view, Dr. Whidden has failed to meet the onus of showing that there is no genuine issue of material fact requiring trial. Ms. Carbone's claim is very simple: she agreed with Dr. Whidden to have liposuction surgery performed on her hips, but expressly excluded any surgery on her buttocks. Contrary to her instructions and their agreement, Dr. Whidden allegedly operated on her buttocks. That claim is met by Dr. Whidden's statement of defence that he did not perform surgery on her buttocks. However, he adduced no evidence on this point. 25 The defendants are not entitled to rely on the simple fact that they have attached an expert letter as shifting the evidentiary onus. For that to occur they must adduce expert evidence that squarely and credibly addresses the plaintiff's specific claims. In my view, while I have not relied on this point, it is even doubtful that Dr. Lobay's opinion is evidence of the nature a defendant must bring to meet the first stage of the summary judgment test. It is unsworn, hearsay fact and opinion tendered through Dr. Whidden, who does not even affirm its truth or his agreement with it. Further, Dr. Whidden's affidavit is general and conclusory, failing to set out sufficient facts to be of much probative value. As the Supreme Court of Canada has stated, “a self-serving affidavit is not sufficient in itself to create a triable issue in the absence of detailed facts and supporting evidence.” [Footnotes omitted] 18. Third Party Notices In Anderson v. Canadian Western Trust Company, 2019 ABQB 413, 2019 CarswellAlta 1114, Justice Eamon said: [27] Where the moving party is a third party defendant, there are additional risks to be considered: whether it is fair and reasonable to determine third party claims without a detailed record of the factual circumstances in the main action; whether it is fair and reasonable to force a defendant to make a case against itself in order to justify its own claim for contribution or indemnity; and, whether attempting to resolve the third party claims would give rise to a risk of inconsistent findings (330626 Alberta Ltd v Ho & Laviolette Engineering Ltd, 2018 ABQB 478 (CanLII) at paras 44–46, 65). With respect to the third consideration, the mere risk of inconsistent findings is not determinative. The Court has a residual discretion to reject third party proceedings where the overall interests of justice require it and the residual risk of inconsistent findings does not always predominate (O'Connor Associates Environmental Inc v MEC OP LLC, 2014 ABCA 140 (CanLII) at para 43). 19. Applicant Must Prove Every Fact to Support Claim A summary judgment requires an applicant to prove each and every fact necessary to support his claim. Bank of Montreal v. Kalin (1992), 131 A.R. 397 (C.A.), at 397, per Conrad J.A. In Wild Rose School Division No. 66 v. Bert Pratch Construction Co. (1998), 238 A.R. 339 (Q.B.), a contractor (Pratch) sued a school division and an engineering firm (Bearden) for damages resulting from a fire at a construction project. The engineering firm filed a third party notice against the school division. The contract between the school division and Pratch required Pratch to obtain a policy of insurance for the very type of loss which formed the subject matter of Pratch's claim against the school division. The school division applied for summary judgment dismissing the third party proceedings. An issue arose as to whether the court could rely on the pleadings as evidence of what claim was being made by the contractor. The engineering firm which filed the third party notice contended that the court could only look at the filed affidavits, and that if the type of claim was not disclosed in the affidavits, the court could not look at the pleadings to ascertain the nature of the claim (that information was essential so that the court could determine if the claim fell within the contractor's insurance obligation). Sanderman J. held that he could rely on the pleadings as evidence of the nature of the contractor's claim. At pp. 343-44, his Lordship said: Bearden takes the position that the affidavits relied upon by the School Division do not establish to the degree required that the claim of Pratch is caught by the covenant to insure in the construction contract in existence between Pratch and the School Division. Bearden asserts that there is no positive statement establishing this fact. Therefore there remains unresolved a genuine question of fact and consequently a genuine question of law. Put simply, Bearden submits that there is nothing in the affidavit that indicates that that which is claimed by Pratch against the School Division falls within the ambit of the covenant to insure. There is nothing from Pratch that asserts this in a conclusive manner. Bearden submits that the court is left in the position of not knowing what the covenant to insure relates to. Absent this information being provided in a positive fashion in that affidavit, Bearden takes the position that the application must be dismissed in its entirety regardless of the analysis that the court has found compelling. Bearden insists that the court cannot look at the pleadings filed by Pratch in order to determine whether or not there is evidence before the court that indicates with a degree of particularity what Pratch's claim is for. Bearden takes the position that the court is restricted to looking at the affidavit evidence filed on behalf of the parties in relation to this application. I disagree with the position taken by Bearden. Pratch is not involved in this application. No materials have been filed on behalf of Pratch. Pratch is a major participant in this lawsuit. It is through Pratch's statement of claim that Bearden has asked for indemnity or contribution from the School Division. The document that allows Bearden to make this claim is Pratch's statement of claim. It is the defining document. Not to be allowed to look at it for the purposes of deciding this application would be foolish and irresponsible on the part of the court. It is presumed that the pleadings of a party set out with precision the claim made or defence offered. They must be taken to set out the position of the party filing them with the court. The court must be able to rely upon pleadings as being an accurate assertion of the position of the party filing them unless they are amended. To come to some other conclusion would be sheer folly. The pleadings of a party delineate with particularity the remedy being sought. A court's jurisdiction to grant a remedy is limited by the pleadings of the party. The remedy granted cannot go beyond that which is sought in the pleadings… Surely, the court must be able to rely upon the pleadings of a party when attempting to ascertain what a claim is for. When one reads clause 17 of the statement of claim of Pratch, it is obvious what is being claimed. Pratch is claiming for “expense in the amount of $297,059.81 to repair and replace direct physical damage to property in the course of construction, installation, reconstruction or repair”. One could not but come to the conclusion that this was work contemplated by the construction contract between Pratch and the School Division. It is caught by the covenant to insure. It is not necessary for a positive assertion of this to be placed in the affidavit filed in support of this application. The court must be able to rely upon the pleadings of the party that Bearden joins in its claim against the School Division. 20. Denial of the Debt Is Insufficient In Montreal Trust Co. of Canada v. Sagars Investments Inc. (1995), 167 A.R. 290 (Master); [affirmed on reconsideration [1995] A.W.L.D. 831], Master Funduk heard an application for summary judgment based on guarantees granted by the defendants. In considering the evidence tendered by the defendants opposing the application, the learned Master said at pp. 294-95: I do not agree that a creditor who swears that a certain amount is owing must, without more, “exhibit” the books and provide a “calculation” as to how the amount claimed is arrived at. This is a loan that was made in 1986. It is quite absurd to say that, without more, the plaintiff must provide an eight year accounting. The amount owing is a question of fact so there must be evidence to show a triable issue as to amount. It is not enough for a defendant to just plead that there is no debt “as alleged or at all and put the plaintiff to the strict proof thereof” and say that that discloses a triable issue. The plaintiff's evidence must be impeached or contradicted. The first is done by a cross-examination … and the second is done by contrary evidence … The point is put succinctly in Brown v. Northey and Killian's Restaurant (1987) Ltd. (1991), 115 A.R. 321 (C.A.) at para. 11: … Here the appellant defendants (plaintiffs by counterclaim) made out a strong prima facie case for summary judgment. Therefore, the respondent plaintiff who alleges there is a triable issue and resists summary judgment, had to produce evidence to show a triable issue (as the pleadings did not raise a purely legal arguable issue). It is not enough for such a respondent merely to argue that there may be facts somewhere which might emerge at trial and might turn out to be relevant. The court can direct a plaintiff to provide an accounting, but not just by the asking. There must be some evidence which justifies that being directed. 21. Payments on Account Rule 7.3 does not permit “payments on account”. In action #8903-14622, this is a motion for summary judgment by a woman who, following an automobile accident, has grave medical problems. She is also extremely short of money and she has no prospect of an early trial. She therefore moves for summary judgment. Unfortunately I have concluded that I should not give her that remedy. The first thing to note is that what is in issue here is not liability, and therefore the fact that liability is not in dispute is beside the point. The issue is quantum and quantum is disputed, so therefore the issue is whether there is a genuine triable issue as to any part of quantum … So therefore for these reasons I have come to the conclusion that on each part of the claim of the plaintiff there is a genuine issue to be tried, not in the sense of liability but in the sense of quantum. Therefore it naturally follows that there cannot be, or rather should not be, summary judgment here. This does not leave the plaintiff in a happy situation. In England and, I think, some of the other Canadian provinces, the Rules of Court or the statutes have been amended to allow a plaintiff to claim before trial a compulsory payment of an amount on account. When the plaintiff's counsel here argues that she is obviously going to get an assessment at least X dollars, he has a good point. Unfortunately, however, Alberta still has the common law rule which says that damages are to be assessed once and for all, and does not provide for a compulsory payment on account. It is obvious from what I have said that I do not read rule 159 on summary judgment, which was really designed for totally different matters, as extending to that sort of thing. Chernichen v. Armitage (1991), 122 A.R. 387 (Q.B.), at 388-89, per Côté J. 22. Summary Judgment versus Striking Out Statement of Defence Striking out a statement of defence and summary judgment are mutually exclusive. Fernwood Construction of Canada Ltd. v. Century 21 Birch Realty Ltd. (1982), 48 A.R. 147 at 148 (Master). The same comment was made by Wittmann J.A. in H. (V.A.) v. Lynch, 2000 ABCA 97, 2000 CarswellAlta 277, 255 A.R. 359, 78 Alta. L.R. (3d) 1; reconsideration refused 2000 ABCA 213, 2000 CarswellAlta 795, 266 A.R. 150, 85 Alta. L.R. (3d) 51; additional reasons at 2001 ABCA 37, 2001 CarswellAlta 148, 277 A.R. 104, 91 Alta. L.R. (3d) 1; reconsideration refused 2001 ABCA 211, 2001 CarswellAlta 1196, 293 A.R. 395, 95 Alta. L.R. (3d) 299, at p. 8 [Alta. L.R.]. The two remedies are mutually exclusive because R. 3.68 (Striking Out a Statement of Defence) requires the court to find that no defence at law is to be found in the statement of defence, whereas R. 7.3 relates not to theoretical defences pleaded, but to defences that exist, or do not exist, on the merits. 23. Applications Based on a Statutory Defence … a defendant who wants summary dismissal of a lawsuit based on a statutory defence must come in under rule 159, not rule 129. Hill v. Richert (1996), 180 A.R. 156 (Master), at 160, per Master Funduk. Old R. 159 is new R. 7.3. Old R. 126 is new R. 3.68. 24. Standard of Proof and Burden of Proof In Stefanyk v. Sobeys Capital Incorporated, 2018 ABCA 125, 2018 CarswellAlta 587, 67 Alta. L.R. (6th) 215, [2018] 5 W.W.R. 654, the Court stated that the standard of proof for summary judgment applications is on a balance of probabilities. The Court said: 12 An action may be summarily dismissed where “there is no merit to a claim or part of it”: R. 7.3(1)(b). Summary judgment is an appropriate procedure where there is no genuine issue requiring a trial. There will be no genuine issue requiring a trial when the judge is able to reach a fair and just determination on the merits on a motion for summary judgment. This will be the case when the process (a) allows the judge to make the necessary findings of fact, (b) allows the judge to apply the law to the facts, and (c) is a proportionate, more expeditious and less expensive means to achieve a just result: Hryniak v Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7 at para. 49, [2014] 1 SCR 87; Windsor v Canadian Pacific Railway, 2014 ABCA 108 at para. 13, 94 Alta LR (5th) 301, 572 AR 317. Parties to a summary disposition application are expected to put their “best foot forward”, meaning that gaps in the record do not necessarily prevent summary disposition: Canada (Attorney General) v Lameman, 2008 SCC 14 at para. 11, [2008] 1 SCR 372. 13 In this case the reasons under appeal stated the test for summary judgment as being whether the moving party's position was “unassailable”, and stated it would be unassailable if it is so compelling that the “likelihood of success [at trial] is very high”: reasons at para. 9. This statement of the law was extracted from the concurring reasons in Can v Calgary Police Service, 2014 ABCA 322 at para. 20, 584 AR 147, which extracted that test from the earlier reasons of the author in Beier v Proper Cat Construction Ltd., 2013 ABQB 351 at para. 61, 564 AR 357. The obiter dicta in Can do not accurately state the law. Under the rules of stare decisis, decisions of the Court of Appeal reflect the law of the province. The binding ratio decidendi of a Court of Appeal decision, however, is to be found in the majority reasons. Obiter dicta in concurring and dissenting reasons do not reflect the law, and they should not be followed to the extent that they are inconsistent with binding authority. 14 First of all, it is now established that there is only one civil standard of proof and it is proof on a balance of probabilities. The rule was definitively stated in F.H. v McDougall, 2008 SCC 53 at para. 40, [2008] 3 SCR 41: “… I think it is time to say, once and for all in Canada, that there is only one civil standard of proof at common law and that is proof on a balance of probabilities”. That is the standard the summary judgment rule engages when it talks about “merit”: proof on a balance of probabilities. “Unassailable” and “very high likelihood” are not recognized standards of proof. 15 Secondly, the test for summary judgment is stated in the binding cases like Hryniak v Mauldin and Windsor v Canadian Pacific Railway. Summary judgment is one procedure for deciding whether the moving party has proven its case on a balance of probabilities. Summary judgment is the appropriate procedure where the record is such that a fair and just disposition can be made on it: 776826 Alberta Ltd. (c.o.b. Budweiser Motorsports Park) v Ostrowercha, 2015 ABCA 49 at paras. 9-10, 593 AR 391. In other words, is the record such that it is fair and just to decide summarily if the moving party has proven the case on a balance of probabilities? That generally comes down to deciding if there is any material issue of fact on which a trial is justified, or whether the chambers judge can make any required fact findings from the summary dismissal record in a fair and just manner. A trial may be the preferred and proportional procedure where there is a reasonable expectation that a better evidentiary record will be created by a trial, for example because there are disputed issues of material fact, or issues of credibility, that cannot fairly be resolved summarily. 16 It follows that a plaintiff cannot resist summary dismissal merely by raising a “doubt”, although the plaintiff is not required at that stage to prove its case on a balance of probabilities: McDonald v Brookfield Asset Management Inc., 2016 ABCA 375 at para. 13. The plaintiff can obviously resist summary dismissal by showing that the applicant has not, at that stage, proved its defence on a balance of probabilities. Summary dismissal can also be resisted when the record or the issues mean that summary dismissal is not a fair and just procedure for both parties: Abbey Lane Homes v Cheema, 2015 ABCA 173 at para. 22. A dispute about material facts that cannot be resolved on the existing record, or that fairly and reasonably call for a trial will be sufficient: Ostrowercha at para. 11. 17 Therefore, in this appeal the issue is not whether the appellant's position is “unassailable”. The first question is whether the record is sufficient to decide if the appellant is liable for the plaintiff's injuries. There are no material facts in dispute, no overwhelming issues of credibility, and the court is able to apply the law to the facts. It is unlikely that the cost and expense of a trial is justified because of an expectation of a significantly better record. In this case summary judgment is a proportionate, more expeditious and less expensive means to achieve a just result, and therefore it is an appropriate procedure. The ultimate issue is whether the appellant has proven on a balance of probabilities that it is not liable for the plaintiff's injuries. In Angus Partnership Inc. v. Salvation Army (Governing Council), 2018 ABCA 206, 2018 CarswellAlta 1049, 70 Alta. L.R. (6th) 79, 422 D.L.R. (4th) 721, 90 R.P.R. (5th) 175, [2018] 8 W.W.R. 440, the Court said: 42 In Stefanyk v Sobeys Capital Incorporated, 2018 ABCA 125, 2018 CarswellAlta 587 (WL Can) the unanimous panel confirmed that the standard of proof on a summary disposition application is on the balance of probabilities. Here, the chambers judge's finding that the Salvation Army was required to present uncontroverted facts which make it “highly unlikely” that Angus will succeed at trial was an error. However, there seems to be a contrary view held by at least two members of the Court of Appeal. In Whissell Contracting Ltd. v. Calgary (City), 2018 ABCA 204, 2018 CarswellAlta 1032, 71 Alta. L.R. To require that the standard be high that a claim or defence is (or has been) proved on a balance of probabilities is not to incorporate two civil standards of proof but only to require a higher standard for what the Court thinks of the record, or the quality of the evidence at this stage of the proceedings. No Affidavit of Responding Defendant Is Required The defendant can utilize any evidence the plaintiff puts forward. The Rule does not require the defendant to put in an affidavit. He can satisfy the court “or otherwise”. Jason Development Corp. v. Robertoria Properties Ltd. (1980), 42 A.R. 369 at 370 (Master). And Master Quinn said: The defendant is not obligated to file an affidavit in opposition to the summary judgment application, as he may “otherwise” satisfy the court that a trial on the merits is required. A defendant might find some flaw in the plaintiff's affidavit, or the defendant may cross-examine the plaintiff on his affidavit and obtain some evidence from the mouth of the plaintiff which would indicate that the matter is not beyond doubt and must go to trial. Royal Bank v. Facto Homes Ltd. (1983), 54 A.R. 228 at 229 (Master). Therefore a defendant may rely upon exhibits before the court (e.g., contracts) to show that a triable issue exists. However, the key point to remember is that there must be “evidence” before the court. These cases simply reaffirm that one party may rely upon evidence which comes from the other party. Indeed, if one does not file an affidavit, one runs the risk of the court drawing an adverse inference. In Trosin v. Sikora, 2002 ABQB 132, 2002 CarswellAlta 160, 311 A.R. 162, two of the defendants applied under old Rule 159 for summary judgment dismissing the claim against them on the ground that the claim was without merit. The Plaintiffs did not file an affidavit in defence of the application. At pp.166-167, Lee J., having found that the applicants' affidavit “fulfills the requirements of Rule 159(2)” and “seems to make out their case” with the result that “the onus shifts to the Plaintiffs to establish his (sic) claim as being one with a real chance of success”, made the following observations: The fact that no Affidavit was filed by the Plaintiffs in defence of the application with evidence regarding their claim against ASC and Kimack is troubling, as pleadings alone are not evidence for the purposes of summary judgment applications: Alberta (Treasury Branches) v. Wenley Enterprises & Sales Ltd. et al. (1985), 66 A.R. 232 (Q.B.) at para. 51, and although there are pages of “evidence” in the Plaintiffs' brief, submissions of counsel are not evidence either: Halwa v. Phillips (1987), 81 A.R. 182 (Q.B. Master). It is open to the Court to draw an adverse inference where the respondent of a summary judgment application does not swear an Affidavit: see Chaba v. Alberta (Provincial Treasurer), [1988] A.J. No. 304, and Wenley, supra. The Alberta Rules of Court also seem to support this use of an adverse inference as Rule 314.1(1) clearly provides that “where an affidavit is to be used at a hearing in opposition to a motion or application or in reply, that affidavit shall be filed …”. These rules exist so that everyone, including the judge, knows what evidence is to be relied upon, and where to find it. However, Rule 313 of the Alberta Rules of Court provides that “[a]ny affidavit which has been made and filed in any cause or matter may be referred to and used at any stage of the proceedings in any application in chambers.” Counsel for the Plaintiff, in their brief, makes specific references to previously filed Affidavits and cross-examination on Affidavits. In Alberta (Provincial Treasurer) v. Gordey Construction Ltd. et al. (1991), 120 A.R. 282, 8 W.A.C. 282, 83 Alta. L.R. (2d) 48 (C.A.), the Alberta Court of Appeal held that, although the plaintiff had not filed an affidavit specifically in response to the defendant's application, the chambers judge did not err when he considered evidence from previously filed Affidavits from both parties to decide an issue. The Plaintiffs have previous to this motion, filed several Affidavits in support of this action, and, as summary judgment is harsh, it was my view that these Affidavits should be examined to determine whether there was evidence showing there is some merit to their claim. I caution, however, that other brothers and sisters of the Court may not be as forbearing. 26. The rule in Browne v. Dunn In Chandos Construction Ltd. v. Buildtech Framing Inc., 2014 ABQB 597, 2014 CarswellAlta 1770 (Master), Master Robertson concluded that the rule in Browne v. Dunn does not apply to summary judgment applications. At paragraphs 19–21, the learned Master said: [19] In oral argument, I put to counsel for Chandos whether the Rule should be applied in summary judgment applications generally, because if so then a respondent to a summary judgment application would, in many cases, be required to cross-examine the applicant on the applicant's affidavit before filing his own affidavit, even though the evidence may be starkly in contrast and it is obvious that a trial is necessary. If the respondent did not cross examine, then the applicant would urge the court not to accept respondent's reply affidavit. That would unduly complicate what would otherwise be straightforward unsuccessful summary judgment applications, contrary to the Foundational Rules now in our Rules of Court. [20] The Rule in Browne v. Dunn is intended to put the trier of fact in the best position to weigh evidence. Should the witness' evidence at trial be accepted notwithstanding that he said something inconsistent previously? Or should the evidence of one witness be accepted when the evidence of later witness gave conflicting testimony? The Rule exists for the benefit of weighing evidence. The court does not weigh evidence on a summary judgment application. That is what trials are for. The court may decide that there is a conflict in the evidence that it does not affect the outcome, but if the credibility of a witness is part of the real dispute, there must be a trial. [21] In my view, with all respect for the Ontario Master, it is hard to see how the Rule in Browne and Dunn would apply to a summary judgment application. That is not to say that witnesses should not be cross-examined on evidence that will be contradicted by another witness, or on their prior inconsistent statement. The witness may realize that the evidence he or she initially gave is wrong and admit that, or there may be an explanation that eliminates the apparent conflict. 27. Applications Judge Jurisdiction A master may grant summary judgment. The Master does not hear the application because he is a judge but because under [the Rules] he has the powers of a judge in such matters. Polson Iron Works v. Munns (1915), 9 W.W.R. 231 (Alta. T.D.), at 232, (approved in S.B.I. Management Ltd. v. 109014 Holdings Ltd. (1981), 32 A.R. 6 at 22-23 (C.A.).) However: A Master in Chambers does not have jurisdiction to grant a judgment for damages, as that involves an assessment. Athan Holdings Ltd. v. Merchant Holdings Ltd. (1982), 40 A.R. 199 at 205 (Master). And Fruman J. said: The next stage then is the assessment of damages. As I read rule 159(5), a court may direct that the action proceed only to assess the amount of damages or may direct a reference or accounting. These are permissive. A Master does not have jurisdiction to assess unliquidated damages. A Court of Queen's Bench justice does. Espey v. Chapters Inc. (1998), 225 A.R. 68 at 73 (Q.B.). Further: … in any proceedings before a Master, even though it be purely an interlocutory procedural matter and not a substantive application, the Master has no jurisdiction if there are disputed or contentious questions of fact. The legislature has seen fit to limit the Master's jurisdiction to those cases where the application is either ex parte, is unopposed, or if opposed where there are no facts which have to be weighed, i.e. pro and con evidence. Barrowman v. Ranchland Asphalt Services Ltd. (1981), 29 A.R. 306 at 345 (Master). In O'Donnell v. Soldan Fence and Metals (2009) Ltd., 2015 ABQB 764 (Master), the Plaintiff's employment was terminated without cause, and he was paid eight weeks salary. The Plaintiff, who had been employed by the Defendant, or its predecessor, for 34 years and 11 months, sued for damages for wrongful dismissal. The Defendant admitted liability; the remaining issues related to the proper length of notice, the adequacy of the Plaintiff's mitigation efforts, and entitlement to vacation pay. The Plaintiff applied before a Master for summary judgment. Master Schlosser concluded that a Master had jurisdiction to determine unliquidated damages in a summary judgment application. The learned Master said: 8 The Respondent argues that I cannot determine this matter because a master is constitutionally barred from weighing evidence. Wrongful dismissal damages are unliquidated damages, and, they argue, unliquidated damages cannot be determined unless evidence is weighed. 9 In SBI Management Limited v 109014 Holdings Ltd., 1981 ABCA 235, Lieberman, J.A., writing for the Court, said at para. 57: • The master would be exceeding his jurisdiction if he assessed damages in the sense that he weighed evidence in order to arrive at an amount. 10 The Respondent suggests that because of the constitutional impediment, I should simply dismiss Mr. O'Donnell's application, with costs. Alternately, I could refer the matter to a judge pursuant to section 13 of the Court of Queen's Bench Act, RSA 2000, c. C-31 which provides: • A master in chambers may refer any matter before the master to a judge for decision and the judge may dispose of or refer back the matter in whole or in part. However, I am not going to do that. 11 The Court of Queen's Bench Act, a Provincial Statute, constitutes this Court and defines the powers of masters and judges. Section 9(1)(a) of the Act says that subject to certain qualifications, a master has the same powers as a judge sitting in chambers. It does not say anything about liquidated damages. Summary judgment applications in wrongful dismissal actions are not obviously caught by any of the exceptions in the Act. There are no disputed or contentious questions of fact. 12 The issue has not been properly framed as a constitutional issue and neither the Provincial nor the Federal Attorneys General are involved or on notice. For the reasons that follow, it is my view that this case is within my jurisdiction. As pleasurable as an esoteric constitutional debate might be, I do not have to weigh any evidence to decide Mr. O'Donnell's severance. • What does it mean to weigh evidence, and how does this fit into the Summary Judgment context? 13 The starting point for a summary judgment application is often said to be: “to make findings of fact”. There are many authorities to the effect that the Court should not weigh evidence in chambers to get there: Sherwood Steel Ltd. v Odyssey Construction Inc., 2014 ABCA 320 (at paras 7, 8) and the cases cited there; Orr v Fort McKay First Nation, 2014 ABQB 111 at para. 19, per Brown, J. (as he then was); Whitecourt Power Limited Partnership v Interpro Technical Services Ltd., 2014 ABQB 135, at paras. 31, 40 and 41, Muhammad v Canlanka Ventures Limited, 2015 ABQB 145, per Jones, J. and the SBI case (above), for example. i)—Weight and Probative Value 14 In its ordinary sense (and I have in mind The Concise Oxford Dictionary meaning) “to weigh” is to “estimate relative value or importance”, or, “to consider with the view to choice, rejection, or preference”. In the trial context this usually means an estimation of probative value. In the trial context, weight has to do with ranking admissible evidence to find facts or to decide whether one fact is more or less probable than a competing fact. In this case, I do not have to decide between competing facts. There are no facts in dispute. There are no questions of admissibility in this case. ii)—Weight and Admissibility 15 Weight and admissibility are two different things. Admissibility has to do with whether you can consider evidence, or even hear it at all. Like truth or the quality of being unique, admissibility does not admit of degree. iii)—Weighting Factors 16 There may be another sense in which evidence might be weighed. Bardal (below) sets out a non-exhaustive list of factors for determining the length of reasonable notice. It might be said that ranking the factors (by attaching more weight or importance to length of service than to age, for example) is, in some sense, weighing or weighting evidence. However, (and subject to what follows), the law of reasonable notice is so well travelled, the determination is largely a question of attaching equal weight to what the decided cases tell us are the important points and then applying the decided cases to them like an algorithm. There might be an unusual case that takes us outside this exercise. But this is not one of them. iv)—Summary Judgment 17 A master (or for that matter, a judge), in a summary judgment application is playing a very different role from a trier of fact at a trial. 18 Masters, or chambers judges, hearing summary judgment applications are not acting as “triers of fact”. They determine the sufficiency of the evidence to make a summary disposition. The Court is saying: “If the matter were to go to trial, this would be the result”. The Court is reaching its decision that a matter need not go that far on a level of certainty that is usually (and perhaps necessarily) higher than balance of probability certainty. And this is done on the assumption that both sides are putting their best case forward. 19 If the weight of evidence is in question at a summary judgment application, it might be necessary to see the witnesses and send the evidence for “forensic testing at trial”: 776826 Alberta Ltd. v Ostrowercha, 2015 ABCA 49. 20 Conflicts in the evidence usually mean that the matter must go to trial. It is not an option to resolve conflicts in the evidence at a summary judgment application, unless the parties agree and the matter is being heard by a master (section 9(3)(b) of the Court of Queen's Bench Act), or unless the conflict has been resolved in some other fashion. 21 The distinction is subtle but important. In Orr v Fort McKay First Nation, 2014 ABQB 111, Brown J. said: [17] The line between weighing evidence, and deciding that the evidence merits granting (or not granting) summary judgment, may seem elusive when it is considered that both parties to a summary judgment application will typically put evidence before the master in order to show that the test is (or is not) met. Again, Harvey CJ's decision in Polson Iron Works, [1915] A.J. No. 106 offers guidance: The order under consideration is perhaps the nearest approach to determining the rights of parties by trial that the rules authorize the Master to make. But in reality, he is not trying the rights of the parties. He is determining that there is no real issue to be tried. It is only when such a situation is found to exist that the Master is authorized to give a judgment … (Polson Iron Works at 235.) [18] In short, while masters may not weigh evidence to resolve disputed or contentious questions of fact, they may examine the evidence to determine whether an issue remains to be tried or to otherwise determine (by applying the facts to the law) whether a party's position is so compelling that the likelihood it will succeed is so high that it merits granting summary judgment. (Janvier v 834774 Alberta Ltd, 2010 ABQB 800 at para 15.) I recognize that, at some level, all evidence—even extremely compelling evidence—requires weighing. (Brown, “The Possibility of “Inference Causation”: Inferring Cause-in-Fact and the Nature of Legal Certainty” (2010) 55 McGill LJ 1 at 31–35.) To carry that proposition to its logical conclusion would, however, defeat the constitutional purpose served by appointing masters of facilitating the administration of justice. This conundrum need not be resolved here. It suffices for present purposes to reiterate that masters may not carry out the weighing of evidence contemplated in Ontario's Rule 20.04(2.1), which is the first reason why the guidance in Hryniak v Mauldin regarding the standard of review is inapplicable to an application for summary judgment under Rule 7.3. 22 The question is whether this case meets the threshold for summary determination. In this post—Hryniak culture, I take comfort in the fact that at least one other Master has made similar observations in the wrongful dismissal context: Watkins v Willow Park Golf Course Ltd., 2015 ABQB 127, per Prowse, M at para. 6. (and see also: Beatty v Best Theratronics Ltd, 2015 ONCA 247 and Espey v Chapters Inc, (1998) 225 AR 68). Conclusion on Jurisdiction 34 I agree with Master Schlosser and I disagree with Master Farrington's oral decision in Slatni. The assessment of the appropriate period of notice in a wrongful dismissal summary judgment, when the facts otherwise are not materially in dispute, is an example of “applying the facts to the law” as discussed in Orr v Fort MacKay. As Master Schlosser said in Harper: • This is an application for summary judgment in a wrongful dismissal action. Apart from the delay in booking Master's Specials, summary judgment is an ideal vehicle for the determination of such disputes. The law is well settled and the facts are rarely in dispute. 35 On an opposed summary judgment application where the applicant otherwise satisfies its initial burden, a reluctant respondent should be able to articulate what facts are in dispute that need to be resolved at trial: Tottrup v Clearwater (Municipal District No. 99), 2006 ABCA 380 at para. 11-12. If there are material facts in dispute, summary judgment in a wrongful dismissal claim may not be available. 36 If a party believes the master was in error, there is a clear right of appeal. An appeal is largely a rehearing, although the standard of review is “correctness”, which presumes the need for some argument as to why a master in chambers was incorrect in reaching the decision that he or she did. The master's reasons are part of the record that is to be placed before the justice hearing the appeal: rule 6.14. 37 The approach expressed long ago in the unanimous judgment of the Supreme Court of Alberta, Appellate Division enunciated in Advance Rumely Thresher Co v LaClair, 10 Alta. L.R. 446, [1917] 1 W.W.R. 875, 32 D.L.R. 609 (1916) seems definitive, where the Court said: • It is to be remembered that the jurisdiction of the Master is not given by statute although the office is provided for in that way. The jurisdiction is given by the Rules of Court which are the rules of procedure only. It simply amounts to this that by rules of procedure certain matters are referred to the Master to decide. The judgment entered is not the judgment of the Master but the judgment of the Court arrived at by means of certain rules of procedure. These matters can always be taken to a Judge if any party so desires and the hearing by the Judge though called an appeal is really merely a review and a rehearing. In this case the decision of the Master was confirmed by a Judge and even another affidavit was introduced before the Judge for the first time. In view of the decision in Polson Iron Wks v Munns and of those considerations I have mentioned it would appear that we ought to hear no more of this objection. In Coffey v. Nine Energy Canada Inc., 2018 ABQB 898, 2018 CarswellAlta 2553, 78 Alta. L.R. (6th) 379, 51 C.C.E.L. (4th) 104, 2019 C.L.L.C. 210-014, Justice K. Nixon concluded that “the assessment of damages for pay in lieu of reasonable notice is not appropriate for summary judgment” (paragraph 11) which means that it would fall outside the Masters' summary judgment jurisdiction. Justice Nixon said: [26]S.B.I. remains the leading and correct statement of the master's jurisdiction. There is no doubt that masters have jurisdiction to grant summary judgment in appropriate cases. However, the summary judgment rule must be interpreted within the context of the jurisdiction of the master. In Orr v Fort McKay First Nation, 2014 ABQB 111 (CanLII), referring to Polson Iron Works, Brown J (as he then was) reminded us the purpose of the summary judgment rule is not to try the rights of parties but to examine the evidence to determine whether there is an issue to be tried (at para 17). When evidence must be weighed and contentious issues of fact determined, summary judgment, whether before a master or a judge, is inappropriate (see, Condominium Corporation No. 0321365 v Cuthbert, 2016 ABCA 46 (CanLII), at para 11). The proper summary procedure where evidence must be weighed, but when a full trial is not necessary, is rather a summary trial. [27] The core issue in my view is whether an assessment of reasonable notice involves weighing evidence, whether by a master or by a justice. … … [35] It is clear from the leading texts and the leading authorities in Bardal and Machtinger that the assessment of the “catalogue” of factors for reasonable notice involves the weighing of evidence, and is not a simple mechanical application of legal principles to established facts. “[T]he question of what is reasonable notice is a question of fact to be determined in the circumstances and is no different than any other question to be resolved in the contractual context, such as reasonable price or value” (Rahmath v. Louisiana Land & Exploration Company, 1989 ABCA 100 (CanLII), at para 3, Stevenson JA, as he then was, for the Court). In concluding that a master does not have jurisdiction to grant summary judgment for a reasonable notice period, Master Funduk stated, “[w]hat constitutes a reasonable notice period is a question of fact in each case” (Smith v R.L. Crain Inc., [1990] A.J. No. 309 (ABQB)(QL)). The assessment of damages for wrongful dismissal is distinguishable from the “simple computation” in S.B.I. (cited in Cote and Stevenson, Civil Procedure Encyclopedia (Edmonton: Juriliber, 2003), at 3–7). … [41] In my opinion, the Master was correct in finding that the assessment of damages for pay in lieu of reasonable notice for wrongful dismissal is not appropriate for summary judgment under Rule 7.3. It involves the determination of contentious issues of fact that requires evidence to be weighed to determine the rights of the plaintiff. This is outside the jurisdiction of the master and beyond the scope of the summary judgment rule. 28. Summary Judgment and Wrongful Dismissal Claims In Coffey v. Nine Energy Canada Inc., 2018 ABQB 898, 2018 CarswellAlta 2553, 78 Alta. L.R. (6th) 379, 51 C.C.E.L. (4th) 104, 2019 C.L.L.C. 210-014, Justice K. Nixon concluded that “the assessment of damages for pay in lieu of reasonable notice is not appropriate for summary judgment” (paragraph 11) (see the annotation “Masters' Jurisdiction” under this rule). However, in Rudichuk v. Genesis Land Development Corp., 2019 ABQB 133, the defendants brought an application for summary dismissal of the plaintiffs' wrongful dismissal claim. Justice Marriott discussed summary judgment applications relating to wrongful dismissal claims: [28] The party moving for summary judgment has the burden of proving, by adducing their own evidence, that there is no genuine issue for trial on a balance of probabilities: Weir-Jones at paras 32, 47; Windsor at para 13; Stefanyk v Sobeys Capital Incorporated, 2018 ABCA 125 (CanLII) at para 4 [Stefanyk]; Murphy Oil Co Ltd v Predator Corp, 2006 ABCA 69 (CanLII) at para 25 [Murphy Oil]. [29] Once the moving party has met its burden, the responding party must then demonstrate from the record that there is a genuine issue for trial: Weir-Jones at para 47. This may be done in a number of ways, including that “the responding party may adduce evidence to persuade the court that there remains a genuine issue to be tried”: Murphy Oil at para 25. [30] The Court of Appeal noted in Weir-Jones that there is “no symmetry of burdens”: at para 32. Once the party moving for summary judgment has established the factual elements of its case on a balance of probabilities and that there is no genuine issue requiring a trial, then the respondent must “only demonstrate that the record, the facts, or the law preclude a fair disposition”: at para 32. [31] Summary judgment is still possible even when there is some conflict in the affidavit evidence of the opposing parties, provided it is possible to fairly resolve the dispute summarily: Weir-Jones at para 47. “The key is whether the necessary findings of fact can be made on the record. The chambers judge may make inferences of fact based on the undisputed facts before the court, as long as the inferences are strongly supported by the facts”: Malhotra at para 31, citing Guarantee Co at para 31. The Court only assesses credibility and weighs evidence at trial, not when considering an application for summary judgment. However, the Court may properly reduce the weight of affidavit evidence for several reasons including when the judge is satisfied that “the evidence is not consistent with other evidence and known circumstances”: Malhotra at para 33. Furthermore, the conflict between the affidavits may not be on essential facts, or the issues may be resolvable based on the portions of the affidavits which are not in conflict: Sandhu v Siri Guru Nanak Sikh Gurdwara of Alberta, 2015 ABCA 101 (CanLII) at para 81, leave to appeal to SCC refused, 36426 (13 August 2015). [32] As stated above, it is well established that the party bringing the motion for summary judgment bears the onus to prove that there is no issue of merit requiring trial. What is less clear is which party bears the onus for proving or disproving Genesis' just cause defence. [33] The parties appear to disagree as to which party bears the onus with respect to just cause. The Plaintiffs concur with Master Robertson, who held that even in an employee's application for summary judgment, “the primary burden is on the employer to prove that there was just cause” if he raises it as a defence. This follows the principle that “he who asserts must prove” unless there is a specific reverse onus: Rudichuk at paras 27–29. [34] Genesis disagrees, citing a wrongful dismissal summary judgment decision of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, which held: “[t]he onus is on a Plaintiff to establish that there is no triable issue with respect to its claims or any defence raised with respect to those claims”: Lewis v Lavern Heideman & Sons Ltd, 2015 ONSC 3752 (CanLII) at para 43. However, this statement in Lewis is, in my view, simply the condensed version of the plaintiffs' and moving party's initial onus of establishing wrongful dismissal, a further two part process that is fully described in Anderson v Cardinal Health, 2013 ONSC 5226 (CanLII) which Lewis cites for authority. [35] As held in Anderson, the onus rests on the non-moving employer to establish their defence of mitigation against the employee's claim. It is then up to the employee to counter the alleged defence with sufficient evidence to demonstrate that the defence is not a genuine issue requiring a trial: Anderson at para 7. Although the onus is on the moving party to show that the issue of the defence can be determined on a summary basis, the non-moving party must first establish that there is merit to its alleged defence. Recent case law confirms that this is the approach taken by the Ontario Superior Court of Justice: Merritt v Tigercat Industries Inc, 2016 ONSC 1214 (CanLII) at para 25; Edmond v Algonquin College, 2018 ONSC 1898 (CanLII) at para 95; Visaggio v Joynt-Dent Inc, 2018 ONSC 1911 (CanLII) at para 123. [36] In East Winds Caribbean Limited Partnership v Reti, 2016 ABQB 536 (CanLII) at para 42, Master Hanebury clearly described the onuses and evidentiary burdens on each party as follows: … it is important to note that this [the test for summary judgment] does not affect the established legal burdens. If an applicant discharges the initial evidentiary burden imposed upon it on a balance of probabilities, the evidentiary burden then falls to the respondent to show that there is arguable merit to the case and that there is a compelling reason that it should go to trial. Only when the applicant has met its initial obligation does the onus shift to the respondent to reply, and the legal or persuasive burden is on the applicant throughout. [37] The reasoning behind this assignment of onus is two-fold. First, as identified by Master Robertson, absent guidance in a specific rule or statute, the general rule is that “he who asserts must prove”, and that the moving party needs evidence. Otherwise, the moving party may have to prove a negative in response to a defence raised by the other party, “which is normally next to impossible”: Garry v Canada, 2007 ABCA 234 (CanLII) at para 8; Slater v Burgoin, 2001 ABCA 213 (CanLII) at para 13. [38] Second, in response to the significant economic and self-worth consequences to an employee who is terminated for cause, the law has developed to protect employees in these vulnerable situations, in part by placing the onus to prove just cause on a balance of probabilities on the employer: Molloy v EPCOR Utilities Inc, 2015 ABQB 356 (CanLII) at para 140. It would not, therefore, be reasonable to strip the employee of the protection of an employer's onus simply because the employee applies for summary judgment. [39] In Hryniak, the Supreme Court recognised the importance of the summary judgment procedures (in appropriate cases) for access to justice: at paras 1–6. Contrary to the intent of the Court, wrongfully dismissed employees would be discouraged from making use of summary judgment if the just cause onus was reversed. The employer's rights are still protected, because, to succeed at summary judgment, the employee must still rebut the evidence in support of just cause to the extent that they can show that just cause is not an issue of merit that requires a full trial to justly determine. [40] To conclude, in the case at bar, the Plaintiffs, Rudichuk and Scott, bear the onus of proving, on a balance of probabilities, that there is no genuine issue for trial with respect to their employment contract, and whether Genesis wrongfully terminated their employment contract. Once the Plaintiffs have satisfied this burden, it is up to Genesis to demonstrate from the record enough evidence in support of its defence of just cause to show that there is a dispute that cannot be justly resolved by summary judgment. If Genesis is successful in the preceding step, then the Plaintiffs, to be successful in their summary judgment application, bear the burden of countering Genesis' just cause evidence to demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that there is no issue of merit for trial. In Kubersky v. Pomeroy (Pomeroy Group), 2021 ABQB 173, 2021 CarswellAlta 499, 25 Alta. L.R. (7th) 354, affirmed 2021 CarswellAlta 3387 (Q.B.) (Master), Master Schlosser concluded that a Master did have jurisdiction to grant summary judgment in a wrongful dismissal action. The learned Master said: [3] It might be worthwhile to begin by clearing up a few misconceptions about Summary Judgment. From a Master's perspective, the law is in an unsatisfactory state. Much of the problem stems from the decision in Coffey v Nine Energy Canada Inc. That case holds that neither a Master nor a Judge can weigh evidence in Chambers (Master's because of the constitutional impediment) and, consequently, a wrongful dismissal case must proceed at least to a summary trial. The learned Justice in that case acknowledges that there are at least nine decisions against this position (at paras 14, 15): listing seven Masters' decisions and two Judges' decisions. To that list we can add Bier v Proper Cat Construction Ltd, 2013 ABQB 351 at paras 63, 64 per Wakeling (then) J which holds out wrongful dismissal as an example of a type of case suitable for Summary Judgment. And there are others. … [16] In S.B.I. (at para 57) Justice Lieberman, writing for the Court, said: The Master would be exceeding his jurisdiction if he assessed damages in the sense that he weighed evidence to arrive at an amount … Here, however, there was no weighing of evidence … . The damages in that case were essentially liquidated damages. [17] In the Coffey decision at first instance (2017 ABQB 417), Master Farrington declined to determine pay in lieu of notice and found that a claim for damages and the counterclaim were not suitable for summary disposition. His decision was affirmed on appeal (2018 ABQB 898). The appeal decision came out before Weir-Jones and Hannam, at a time when there was division in the decided cases about the approach to Summary Judgment and the correct test to be used. It is the appeal decision that gives us trouble. [18] Coffey makes a number of pronouncements: 1. That it is inappropriate to weigh evidence at a Summary Judgment application whether it is before a Master or a Judge (para 45); 2. Weighing evidence is outside the jurisdiction of the Master and beyond the scope of the Summary Judgment rule (para 41); and 3. A Master is precluded by Section 9 of the Court of Queen's Bench Act and Section 96 of the Constitution Act from weighing evidence in reaching a determination of damages (para 21). [19] First of all, (and with respect) these pronouncements fail to grasp the ‘elusive distinction’ between summary disposition and trial referred to in paragraph 13, above. Summary disposition is neither a trial nor an adjudication (in the Section 96 sense). Second, and perhaps understandably, the case failed to anticipate the path of the law both in terms of the approach to summary disposition and the appropriate test to be used; though I acknowledge that the appeal decision did not turn on the correct test to be used (Coffey, para 20). As such, it now conflicts with the leading authorities from the Court of Appeal. Third, and again with respect, no stock can be placed in the constitutional pronouncements made in that case. Much of the dicta in Coffey seems to be premised on the assumption that summary disposition is an adjudication. Summary disposition does not try the rights of the parties. A Master hearing a summary disposition application is not weighing evidence in an adjudicative sense as a Judge would at trial. … [29] The truth of the matter is that there is no one type of case that is now inherently unsuitable for summary disposition. There is no one type of case that requires a summary trial. The analysis has to be performed on a case-by-case basis according to the principles set out below, and, to the extent that I am forced to choose between the conflicting decided cases, I am not persuaded that the Coffey decision properly decides the central issue raised by the Court. My vote goes to the opposite team. See also: Nixdorf v. Broadstreet Properties Ltd., 2017 ABQB 132, 2017 CarswellAlta 297 (Master), where Master Robertson similarly concluded that a Master does have jurisdiction to hear a plaintiff's application for summary judgement in an action for wrongful dismissal (paragraphs 3-4 and 32-33). 29. Must Defence Referred to in R. 7.3 Be in Statement of Defence? The answer seems to be “no”. In Bartle & Gibson Co. v. Spicer (1982), 35 A.R. 324 (Q.B.), Master Funduk says at pp. 332-33: Although Rule 159(2) states a defendant must satisfy the court that he has a good defence on the merits it does not necessarily follow that it must in all events be a defence which has been raised by the pleadings. The question the court must address is whether the defence might succeed with an amendment. 30. Counterclaims May Not Prevent Summary Judgment Counsel for the defendants submits that summary judgment on the debt claim should not go because of the counterclaim. A counterclaim does not without more prevent a plaintiff from getting a summary judgment on his claim. It depends on what is advanced in the counterclaim. If a counterclaim advances a defence of legal set-off or equitable set-off it may prevent a summary judgment going. That is because legal set-off and equitable set-off are defences. These defences are raised in a counterclaim (rather than a statement of defence) because rule 93(2) requires it. However, it does not follow that because legal set-off and equitable set-off are raised by way of counterclaim that all counterclaims are defences. They are not. A counterclaim which does not raise legal set-off or equitable set-off is at best a “procedural set-off”, which is not a defence: Abacus Cities Ltd. v. Aboussafy (1981), 29 A.R. 607 (C.A.). McBride v. Kolenko (1990), 115 A.R. 348 (Master), at 351, per Master Funduk. Similarly, a set-off claim does necessarily defeat a summary judgment application. One must always go back to the rule. The fact a defendant raises a claim of set-off in his pleading does not of itself mean summary judgment should not be granted to the plaintiff. A claim by the defendant, whether raised in a statement of defence or a counterclaim, still must meet the test imposed on a defendant by Rule 159 if summary judgment is to be avoided. What it comes down to is that a pleading is not evidence …Bank of Montreal v. Rolseth (1986), 66 A.R. 381 at 387 (Master). 31. Summary Judgment for Part of Claim In some cases it is appropriate to give summary judgment for part of a claim with the balance of the claim going to trial: Steeplejack Services (Canada) Ltd. v. Access Scaffold and Ladder Co. (1989), 98 A.R. 311 (Q.B. Master). The cases where that is appropriate are situations where the defendant will be liable for one or the other, that is, the lesser or the greater. It is a two possibilities situation. Summary judgment for part of a claim is not appropriate where it is a three possibilities situation, the three possibilities being: (a) no liability; (b) liability for the lesser amount; (c) liability for the greater amount. See, for example, Rajani v. Mandel Group Inc. (1987), 75 A.R. 309 (Q.B. Master), p. 312 on this point. Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce v. Godziuk (1996), 182 A.R. 145 (Master), at 148, per Master Funduk. In Borhaven v. Brookwood Catering, 2002 ABQB 79, 2002 CarswellAlta 79, 306 A.R. 308, the plaintiff applied for summary judgment for the minimum amount of damages she expected to be awarded in the action. The plaintiff alleged that she required the money to alleviate financial hardship. Burrows, J. held that Rule 159 (6.1) (now R. 7.3) does not permit such an order. At pp. 310-312, His Lordship said: Her [the plaintiff's] goal, in this application, is to obtain some relief from that financial hardship before the trial of this action. She argues that unless her application succeeds, the financial pressures weighing upon her may force her to accept a settlement for an amount far less than is just. She submits the defendants should be required to make a partial advance payment of her damages because it is obvious they will eventually be found liable to her for substantial damages. . . . . . Of these cases, only Chernichen v. Armitage[(1991), 122 A.R. 387 (Alta. Q.B.)] dealt with the subject in a context similar to the present case. There the defendant had admitted liability. Côté J.A. sitting in the Queen's Bench, said: When the Plaintiff's counsel here argues that she is obviously going to get an assessment at least X dollars, he has a good point. Unfortunately, however, Alberta still has the common-law rule which says that damages are to be assessed once and for all, and does not provide for a compulsory payment on account. It is obvious from what I have said that I do not read Rule 159 on summary judgment, which was really designed for totallydifferent matters, as extending to that sort of thing. Rule 159 (6.1) was enacted in 1999. … In my view, even with the addition of subrule (6.1), Rule 159 still does not provide for a compulsory payment on account. It may be helpful to read and understand Rule 159 as a whole Subrule (1) sets out three situations where an order under the rule may be granted: a) where there is no defence to a claim b) where there is no defence to a part of a claim, and c) where the only genuine issue is as to amount. Subrule (6) adds a fourth situation: d) where the only genuine issue is a question of law. The order granted will depend on which situation exists. Where there is no defence to a claim, the court may order summary judgment (subrule (3)). Where the only genuine issue is as to amount, the court may order an assessment (subrule (5)). Where the only genuine issue is a question of law, the court may order the trial of that issue (subrule (6)). Subrule (6.1) applies in the remaining situation—where there is no defence in respect of part of claim or in respect of an amount less than the full amount of the claim. Where there is a defence as to the other part of the claim, the court may order summary judgment for the first part and a trial for the second. Where the only genuine issue with respect to the other part of the claim is as to amount, the court may order summary judgment for the first part and an assessment for the second. But, in my view, subrule 6.1 has no application where, for the whole of the claim, the only genuine question is as to amount. This is the situation which Ms. Borhaven has sworn she believes exists in this case. Subrule (5) applies in that situation. It would require that an assessment be directed. It does not contemplate summary judgment being granted for a portion of the damages to be assessed—not even a portion clearly small enough to be certainly less than the eventual assessment. In my view in this case none of the situations which Rule 159 contemplates is present. There are genuine issues as to liability and amount in this case… There is no part of Ms. Borhaven's claim for which there is clearly no defence. An order under Rule 159 (6.1) cannot be granted. Counsel referred to Ontario cases where summary judgment for part of a claim was granted in circumstances similar to this case: Moore v. Vandenbosch, [1989] O.J. No. 1987 (Ont. H.C.); Johnson v. Bates (1994), 20 O.R. (3d) 751 (Ont. Gen. Div.). The Ontario Court of Appeal commented on those cases in Ford Motor Co. of Canada v. Ontario (Municipal Employees Retirement Board) (1997), 36 O.R. (3d) 384 (Ont. C.A.).
