Under the new Rule, no genuine issue for trial exists where the judge is able to make a fair and just determination on the merits without a trial, because the summary judgment process allows him or her to make the necessary findings of fact, to apply the law to those facts and is a proportionate, more expeditious and just means to achieve a just result.

Under the new Rule, summary judgment may be granted if a disposition that is fair and just to both parties can be made on the existing record: see Windsor v Canadian Pacific Railway Ltd., 2014 ABCA 108 at para 13
Combined Air Mechanical Services Inc v Flesch, 2011 ONCA 764 at paras 45–55, 108 OR
In Whitecourt Power Limited Partnership v.

Elliott Turbomachinery Canada Inc., 2015 ABCA 252, the Court said: 9 In light of the Supreme Court's decision in Hryniak v Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, [2014] 1 SCR 87 and decisions of this court since Hryniak, summary judgment is no longer denied solely on the basis that the evidence discloses a triable issue.

Rather, the court asks whether there is any issue of merit that genuinely requires a trial or, conversely, whether the claim or defence is so compelling that the likelihood it will succeed is very high such that it should be determined summarily.
A second consideration is whether examination of the existing record can lead to an adjudication and disposition that is fair and just to both parties.
See generally W.P v Alberta, 2014 ABCA 404 at para 26, 7 Alta LR (6th) 319; Windsor v CPR, 2014 ABCA 108 at para 16, 572 AR 317.
10 The decision to grant or deny summary judgment is an exercise of the chambers judge's discretion.
The standard of appellate review was summarized in 776826 Alberta Ltd v Ostrowercha, 2015 ABCA 49 at para 7 (available on CanLII): His decision was an exercise of discretion.

While the culture shift in Canadian law towards using alternative but fair and just methods of adjudication is well established in Alberta, front line judges are entitled to deference on their decisions as to whether summary judgment under Rule 7.3 is a fair and appropriate means for adjudication in a given case: W.P. v Alberta, 2014 ABCA 404 (CanLII) at para 15 (“Appellate intervention is warranted only if the judge has clearly misdirected himself or herself on the facts or the law, proceeded arbitrarily, or if the decision is so clearly wrong as to amount to an injustice: Balogun v Pandher, 2010 ABCA 40 (CanLII) at para 7, 474 AR 258.”) In practical terms, this means that appeals from denials of motions for summary judgment will be difficult to establish.
In Condominium Corp.
No.
Cuthbert, 2016 ABCA 46, 2016 CarswellAlta 222, the Court said: 27 When deciding a summary judgment application, there are two considerations.

With respect to the process, the court must ask, “whether examination of the existing record can lead to an adjudication and disposition that is fair and just to both parties”: Whitecourt at para 9; see also Ostrowercha at para 9
WP at para 26
Windsor at para 16.

With respect to the substantive issues, the court must ask “whether there is any issue of merit that genuinely requires a trial or, conversely, whether the claim or defense is so compelling that the likelihood it will succeed is very high such that it should be determined summarily”: Whitecourt at para 9; see also Ostrowercha at para 10.

An issue of merit is established when the respondent's (non-moving party) case discloses a “genuine issue of a potentially decisive material fact in the case which cannot be summarily found against the non-moving party on the record revealed by the ‘fair and just [summary] process’”: Ostrowercha at para 11.

28 Summary judgment is not possible if opposing parties' affidavits and evidence conflict on material facts because a chambers judge cannot weigh evidence or credibility on a summary judgment application: Sherwood Steel at paras 7-8
Whitecourt at paras 31, 40-41.
29 Complex legal questions may be sufficient to deny summary judgment.

A full trial is required when the summary record cannot be used to decide legal issues that are unsettled, complex or intertwined with facts: Templanza v Wolfman, 2016 ABCA 1 at para 20; Amack at paras 36–37.
A trial is also required when an applications judge is not satisfied she can fairly resolve the dispute on the record before her: Templanza at para 20.
In Malhotra v.

1743134 Alberta Ltd., Re, 2017 ABQB 34, 2017 CarswellAlta 65, Justice Goss provided this summary of the law on summary judgment: 23 Modern civil procedure has come to recognize that a full trial is not always the sensible and proportionate way to resolve disputes: Windsor v Canadian Pacific Railway Ltd, 2014 ABCA 108, 94 Alta LR
(5th) 301, citing Hryniak v Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, [2014] 1 SCR 87.
Summary judgment is one option for parties to consider where a fair and just disposition for both parties can be made on the existing record.

In Hryniak, Karakatsanis J. held that the evidence on a summary judgment motion need not be equivalent to that at trial, but must be such that the judge is confident that s/he can find the necessary facts and apply the relevant legal principles so as to resolve the dispute.
In summary judgment applications, the record is critical.
24 Summary judgment applications must be considered from the perspectives of both process and substance: 776826 Alberta Ltd v Ostrowercha, 2015 ABCA 49, [2015] A.J.
No 118 at paras 9–13.
25 From the process perspective, summary judgment can be given if the Court can make a disposition that is fair and just to both parties on the existing record.
The Court is to look at the record and the dispute to decide whether it is essential that the Court hear viva voce evidence in order to resolve the dispute.

If so, the matter must go to trial: Papaschase Indian Band No 136 v Canada (Attorney General), 2008 SCC 14 at paras 10 to 11, [2008] 1 SCR 372, 1214777 Alberta Ltd v 480955 Alberta Ltd, 2014 ABQB 301 at para 17, [2014] A.J.

26 From a substantive perspective, summary judgment can be granted if, within that fair and just process, it is revealed that the non-moving party's position has no merit in law or in fact, even assuming the accuracy of its position.
The test is whether the claim is so compelling that the likelihood it will succeed is very high such that it should be determined summarily: WP v Alberta, 2014 ABCA 404 at para 26, [2014] A.J.
No 1320, leave denied [2015] SCCA No 41.

The moving party's position must be unassailable or so compelling, on the facts and law, that the likelihood of success is very high: Access Mortgage Corp (2004) Ltd v Arres Capital Inc, 2014 ABCA 280 at para 45, 584 AR 68.
27 As Slatter J.A. observed in Tottrup v Clearwater (Municipal District) No 99, 2006 ABCA 380 at paras 11-12, [2006] A.J.
No 1532, in some cases the application is simply based on the factual merits of the case.
In such a case, the plaintiff must prove, on a balance of probabilities, each and every fact necessary to support its claim.
The evidentiary burden then shifts to the defendant.

28 A party faced with an application for summary judgment must put its best foot forward, and present evidence on the record to show sufficient merit to establish a genuine issue requiring a trial with respect to the outstanding issues: Canada (Attorney General) v Lameman, 2008 SCC 14 at para 11, [2008] 1 SCR 372
Windsor at para 21.
However, the ultimate burden remains, as always, with the plaintiff.
If the defendant proves there is a genuine issue for trial, the plaintiff fails to meet its ultimate burden.
The plaintiff must establish that it is beyond doubt that no genuine issue for trial exists.
29 In analyzing the evidence, the chambers judge need not determine whether the respondent's evidence actually proves the fact sought to be proven.

A party can defeat a summary judgment application by showing on the record the existence of evidence that could be sufficient to defeat the applicant at trial: Bemum Petroleum Ltd v Birch Lake Energy Inc, 2014 ABQB 652, [2014] A.J.
No 1199 at paras 19-20; AT Films Inc v AT Plastics Inc, 2014 ABQB 422, [2014] A.J.
No 731 at para 22.
However, a summary judgment motion cannot be defeated by vague references to what may be adduced in the future, if the matter is allowed to proceed: Lameman at para 19.

The mere assertion of a position by the non-moving party in a pleading or otherwise, or the mere hope or speculation of the non-moving party that something will turn up at a trial, does not suffice: Ostrowercha at para 11, Windsor at para 21.

Raising issues of fact in a statement of defence is insufficient to meet the burden imposed on the defendant on a summary judgment application: Quinney v 1075398 Alberta Ltd, 2015 ABQB 452, [2015] A.J.
No 790 at para 43.

30 In Hryniak, the Supreme Court determined that some conflict in affidavit evidence of opposing parties in an application for summary judgment does not mandate setting the matter for trial in every situation.
The key is whether the necessary findings of fact can be made on the record.

The chambers judge may make inferences of fact based on the undisputed facts before the court, as long as the inferences are strongly supported by the facts: Guarantee Co of North America v Gordon Capital Corp, [1999] 3 SCR 423, [1999] SCJ No 60 at para 30
Lameman at para 11.
31 Where the judge finds that s/he can make a fair and just determination on the merits, the matter should proceed without oral evidence even in the face of alleged factual conflicts.
It may be that the conflicts do not arise on essential facts.
It may be that analysis shows no factual conflict exists, but only a conflict of the litigants' separate opinions.
It may be that issues can be resolved on the basis of those portions of the affidavits which are not in dispute.

It may be that one party relies on several affidavits containing internally conflicting evidence, including some evidence which agrees with or supports the evidence led by the opposite party, amounting to admissions against interest: Sandhu v Siri Guru Nanak Sikh Gurdwara of Alberta, 2015 ABCA 101, [2015] A.J.
No 271 at paras 79–81, leave denied [2015] SCCA No 184.

32 A self-serving affidavit is not sufficient in itself to create a triable issue in the absence of detailed facts and supporting evidence in the record: Guarantee Co v Gordon Capital, [1999] 3 SCR 423, [1999] SCJ No 60 at para 31.
Self-serving opinion evidence is inadmissible and is properly ignored by the chambers judge on a summary judgment application: Pyrrha Design Inc v Plum and Posey Inc, 2016 ABCA 12, [2016] A.J.
No 129 at para 22.
33 On a summary judgment application, the chambers judge does not weigh the evidence or assess credibility; that is the function of a trial judge.

However, the weight of affidavit evidence may properly be found to be reduced if the judge is satisfied that the deponent was attempting to engineer circumstances so as to preclude testing on credibility, one party's evidence on material facts is destroyed by cross-examination on affidavit, or the evidence is not consistent with other evidence and known circumstances.

Further, statements in an affidavit have no weight if the statements are self-serving in the sense of being merely conclusory, argumentative, a bare assertion with no evidence supporting the claim: R Floden Services Ltd v Solomon, 2015 ABQB 450, [2015] A.J.
No 771 at paras 22-23.
34 Slatter J.A. in Tottrup noted that in other cases, the facts are clear and undisputed.
The ultimate outcome of the case may depend on the interpretation of some statute or document, or on some other issue of law that arises from undisputed facts.
In such cases, the test for summary judgment is not whether the issue of law is “beyond doubt”, but whether the issue of law can fairly be decided on the record before the court.
If the legal issue is unsettled or complex or intertwined with the facts, it is sometimes necessary to have a full trial to provide a proper foundation for the decision.
In other cases, it is possible to decide the question of law summarily.
Trials are not generally held to find out the answers to questions of law; they are primarily to determine questions of fact.
Two Categories of Application In Arndt v.
Banerji, 2018 ABCA 176, 2018 CarswellAlta 890, 73 Alta.
L.R.
No.

591, Justices Paperny and Slatter discussed the two categories into which summary judgment and summary dismissal applications fall: 36 Summary judgment and summary dismissal applications usually fall into one of two categories:
(a) Those where the “merit” of the claim is said to rest on the facts and the evidence.

In that sort of case, if the moving party can prove on a balance of probabilities that it has proven the facts needed to support its claim or defence, it is entitled to summary disposition: Stefanyk v Sobeys Capital Incorporated, 2018 ABCA 125 at paras.
(b) Those where the “merit” is said to rest on the legal basis for the claim.

This type of summary dismissal application proceeds on the assumption either that the plaintiff (i) will be able to prove the facts alleged, or (ii) has proven the relevant facts, but those facts do not support any claim in law.
The analytical approach in these two types of cases, and the standard of review, are subtly different.
37 The suitability of the summary judgment procedure in the first category of case is often tied back to whether “there is a genuine issue requiring a trial”.
The test in factually based summary judgment applications is naturally tied back to “issues requiring trial”, because trials are designed to find facts.
Material disputed facts will often preclude summary judgment.
Where none of the material facts are unknown or uncertain, a trial is not called for.

38 Parties to a summary disposition application are expected to put their “best foot forward”, meaning that gaps in the record do not necessarily prevent summary disposition: Canada (Attorney General) v Lameman, 2008 SCC 14 at para.

A summary judgment motion must be decided on the record before the Court, and not by speculation about what evidence may be adduced in the future if the matter is allowed to proceed to trial: Lameman at para.
39 On the other hand, where the summary dismissal application is based on questions of law, a trial will less frequently be necessary.

If the factual basis of the claim is established on the record, or if the plaintiff's claim discloses no merit even if the underlying facts are assumed to be true, summary judgment is generally the appropriate procedure: Lameman at para.
12; Jackson v Canadian National Railway, 2013 ABCA 440 at para.
There is usually no need for a trial, because as noted trials are for finding facts.
There are cases where the legal issues are complex and intertwined with the facts, in which event a trial still may be necessary: Tottrup v Clearwater (Municipal District No.
99), 2006 ABCA 380 at para.
However, litigation that depends primarily on the applicable law is ideally suited for summary disposition.
In Axcess Mortgage Fund Ltd. v.

1177620 Alberta Ltd., 2018 ABQB 626, 2018 CarswellAlta 1764, Justice Renke said that after determining the type of summary judgment application before it, the court must consider the case made by the party seeking summary judgment and the case made by the party opposing the application.

His Lordship said: 45 In addition to distinguishing the two types of summary judgment cases, within a particular application, two cases must be assessed—the case of the moving party and the case of the non-moving party.
46 A moving party should not be entitled to succeed in a summary judgment application if, on the record, it cannot establish its case on a balance of probabilities.
Summary judgment is a procedure for proving a case on the balance of probabilities.
The standard of proof resting on the moving party should neither be reduced nor elevated because of the procedure through which it seeks judgment: Stefanyk v Sobeys at para 15

Pioneer Exploration Inc (Trustee of) v Euro-Am Pacific Enterprises Ltd, 2003 ABCA 298 at para 18: [18]…[T]he plaintiff bears the evidentiary burden of proving its cause of action on a balance of probabilities.
Each and every fact necessary to support the claim must be proven: Bank of Montreal v.
47 Proof on a balance of probabilities is a necessary condition for success but not a sufficient condition.
Summary judgment may be resisted by a non-moving party if it shows that there is a genuine issue requiring trial.
The case of the non-moving party must be assessed.

3. — “Merit” Resting on the Legal Basis for the Claim 48 In a summary judgment application turning on whether a non-moving party has a legally enforceable claim or defence, a fair disposition on the record may be available if the critical legal issue or issues may be determined on the assumption that the nonmoving party's evidence is established.

See Arndt v Banerji at para 39: “If the factual basis of the claim is established on the record, or if the plaintiff's claim discloses no merit even if the underlying facts are assumed to be true, summary judgment is generally the appropriate procedure.” See also 776826 Alberta Ltd v Ostrowercha at para 10.

49 Nonetheless, even if the critical issue is a matter of law, a trial may be necessary if the legal issues are unsettled, complex, and intertwined with the facts (fact-specific and nuanced): Arndt v Banerji at para 39
Stefanyk v Sobeys at paras 16, 17
Condominium Corporation No.
0321365 v Cuthbert, 2016 ABCA 46 at para 29; Templanza v Wolfman, 2016 ABCA 1 at para 20; Amack v Wishewan, 2015 ABCA 147 at para 36; Tottrup at paras 11-12.

4. — “Merit” Resting on the Facts and Evidence 50 In a summary judgment application turning on the facts and evidence, The suitability of the summary judgment procedure … is often tied back to whether “there is a genuine issue requiring a trial”.
The test in factually based summary judgment applications is naturally tied back to “issues requiring trial”, because trials are designed to find facts.
Material disputed facts will often preclude summary judgment.
Where none of the material facts are unknown or uncertain, a trial is not called for: Arndt v Banerji at para 37.
When does an issue genuinely require trial, in the sense of being an issue with “merit” in the language of r.
Merit has two aspects.

(a)—“Materiality” of the Issue 51 First, the issue must be significant or important to the litigation, an issue that should be resolved before judgment may be granted: 776826 Alberta Ltd v Ostrowercha at para 11
Rotzang v CIBC World Markets Inc at para 67.
An issue of merit is not insignificant or collateral to the issues between the parties.
Resolution of the issue must have some non-trivial bearing on the resolution of the dispute.

(b)—Non-Moving Party's Prospect of Success 52 Second, for an issue to have “merit,” the non-moving party must have a “sufficient” prospect of success on the issue to warrant resolution through trial as opposed to resolution on the summary judgment record.

Given the current state of the jurisprudence, it is necessary to move cautiously in specifying the standard of sufficiency that a non-moving party must meet to avoid summary judgment and in specifying the reciprocal standard that a moving party must meet to succeed in the application.
See 330626 Alberta Ltd v Ho & Laviolette Engineering at paras 39-40: [39] One issue as yet unresolved is the standard of proof to be met by the moving party.
The Court of Appeal in Stefanyk said proof must be made on a balance of probabilities (paras 15 & 16; see also Angus Partnership at paras 41 & 42).
It specifically rejected the standard of proof that the moving party's position is “unassailable” such that it is so compelling that the “likelihood of success [at trial] is very high”.
In doing so, the Court distinguished Beier, [2013] A.J.
No.
707 and the concurring reasons in Can v Calgary Alberta (Police Service), 2014 ABCA 322 at para 20, 584 AR 147.
(See also Composite Technologies Inc v Shawcor Ltd, 2017 ABCA 160 at para 2.) [40] One month later, the Court of Appeal returned to the Beal, [2018] A.J.
No.
827, Can, Composite Technologies standard of proof in Rotzang v CIBC World Markets… at para 15, and Whissell Contracting Ltd v Calgary (City), 2018 ABCA 204 at paras 2 & 3.
53 I suggest that there is consensus respecting the following aspects of merit.

54 Merit does not mean (no longer means) that the record supports a finding that there is a “triable issue” that might go in the non-moving party's favour. “Summary judgment is therefore no longer to be denied solely on the basis that the evidence discloses a triable issue:”WP v Alberta, 2014 ABCA 404 at para 26; see 776826 Alberta Ltd v Ostrowercha at para 13.

That is, merit is not established a finding that it is possible that an issue might be resolved at trial in the non-moving party's favour or on the acknowledgement of a doubt about whether an issue might be resolved at trial in the non-moving party's favour.

It follows that the mere fact that the record discloses some admissible evidence that provides inferential support to the non-moving party's position is not necessarily sufficient to resist a summary judgment application.

(Were there gaps in the evidential support for the non-moving party's position, that would be an independent basis for summary dismissal of its claim as a matter of law.) 55 Merit, though, cannot require the non-moving party to prove its case on a balance of probabilities.
That is the standard of proof to be met at trial.
56 As indicated above, establishing lack of merit should not require the moving party to prove its case to some standard higher than the balance of probabilities.
57 An issue has merit, and should be decided at trial, if the issue cannot fairly and justly be decided on the summary judgment record.
That, again, is what Hryniak v Mauldin teaches at para 49.
When is it not fair and just to decide an issue on the record?
At this point, I depart from safe consensus.

58 It would not be fair and just to decide an issue if, on the record, in light of both the evidence of the moving party and the evidence of the non-moving party, the decision-maker is not satisfied that the moving party has satisfied its case on the balance of probabilities.
On the record, the moving party's evidence cannot be fairly and justly found to be more likely than the evidence of the non-moving party.

59 It would not be fair and just to decide against the non-moving party if, on the record, the non-moving party had a “real chance of success” or genuine chance of success on the issue, as rule 7.3 suggests: Hercules Managements Ltd v Ernst & Young, [1997] 2 SCR 165 at para 15
Guarantee Co of North America v Gordon Capital Corp, [1999] 3 SCR 423 at para 27.
From the perspective of the moving party, the question is whether it has shown that the non-moving party does not have a real or genuine chance of success at trial.
60 On this approach, the moving party bears no standard of proof higher than the balance of probabilities.
The question is whether, on the record, the probative value of the non-moving party's evidence is so low that it does not preclude the inferences sought by the moving party.
In that sense, the non-moving party's likelihood of success must be “very low:”Whissell Contracting Ltd v Calgary (City), 2018 ABCA 204 at para 2; Rotzang v.
CIBC World Markets Inc at para 15.
The current uncertainty relates to the description of the standard governing the assessment of the merits of the non-moving party's case as opposed to the ultimate burden borne by the moving party.
61 A typical example of when deciding an issue on the record would not be fair and just would concern conflicting affidavit evidence on an important issue.
The record itself may not permit a finding that one account should be preferred over the other.
Both the non-moving party's claims and the moving party's claims are in affidavit form.
There is no basis for choosing between the two accounts.

There are no objective indicia, no foundations in the evidence that would permit a decision-maker to find that the non-moving party does not have a real or genuine chance of success at trial, a chance of success at least equal to the chance of the moving party.
To obtain an evidential foundation for finding that one set of claims has greater weight than the other, further evidence is needed, such as through viva voce evidence and trial.
See 776826 Alberta Ltd v Ostrowercha at para 11; Price-Goulet v Transamerica Life Canada, 2017 ABCA 156 at para 8 (“The key is whether viva voce evidence is required to resolve the dispute”).
Rotzang v CIBC World Markets Inc at para 68.
See also Nafie v Badawy, 2015 ABCA 36 at para 106; Rensonnet v Uttl, 2014 ABCA 304 at para 10; Charles v Young, 2014 ABCA 200 at paras 3–5; Nieuwesteeg v Barron, 2009 ABCA 235 at paras 9–11.

Thus we read in Cuthbert at para 28 that [28] Summary judgment is not possible if opposing parties' affidavits and evidence conflict on material facts because a chambers judge cannot weigh evidence or credibility on a summary judgment application … and in Stefanyk v Sobeys at para 15: In other words, is the record such that it is fair and just to decide summarily if the moving party has proven the case on a balance of probabilities?

That generally comes down to deciding if there is any material issue of fact on which a trial is justified, or whether the chambers judge can make any required fact findings from the summary dismissal record in a fair and just manner.

A trial may be the preferred and proportional procedure where there is a reasonable expectation that a better evidentiary record will be created by a trial, for example because there are disputed issues of material fact, or issues of credibility, that cannot fairly be resolved summarily.
62 However, summary judgment is not precluded just because affidavits conflict.

Decision-makers have some latitude for fact-finding and assessing the chance of success at trial even in the face of conflicting affidavit evidence—if the record provides a foundation for substantially discounting the probative value of a party's claims.
Facts may be found and chance of success determined despite conflicting affidavit evidence if, for example
(i) the conflicts do not concern essential or material facts
(ii) the conflicts do not concern facts, but only litigants' opinions—especially legal opinions—about the facts (often affidavits contain thinly disguised argument as opposed to facts)

(iii) a party's affidavit evidence contains internal conflict or contradiction, including evidence that supports an opponent's factual allegations—such evidence would amount to admissions against interest
(iv) a party's affidavit evidence is inconsistent with evidence provided in Questioning on affidavit; or
(v) issues can be resolved on the basis of evidence that is not in dispute.
See Sandhu v Siri Guru Nanak Sikh Gurdwara of Alberta, 2015 ABCA 101 at para 81 and Janvier v 834474 Alberta Ltd, 2010 ABQB 800, Macklin J at para 15.

63 Furthermore, the weight of affidavit evidence may properly be found to be reduced if, for example, the evidence is not consistent with other evidence and known circumstances: Compton Petroleum Corporation v Alberta Power Ltd, 1999 ABQB 42 at para 14; see N.
V.

Reykdal & Associates Ltd, 2000 ABCA 330 at para 5; Janvier v 834474 Alberta Ltd at para 15; Faryna v Chorny, 1951 CanLII 252 (BC CA), 1951 CarswellBC 133, [1952] 2 DLR 354, O'Halloran JA at para 8 (CarswellBC).
Common sense need not be abandoned in the face of an allegation in an affidavit.
Allegations are not entitled to weight just because they are included in an affidavit.

64 Finally, claims in an affidavit have no weight if the statements are “self-serving,” in the sense of being “merely conclusory,”“argumentative,” or having no evidence supporting the claims made besides the claims themselves; that is, if the claims are “bare assertions” or “mere assertions.” See Guarantee Co of North America v Gordon Capital, [1999] 3 SCR 423 at para 31.

65 If, on the record and despite conflicting affidavits, a decision-maker has a foundation for concluding that there is no real or genuine chance that the non-moving party would be able to establish its claims, that the weight of the non-moving party's claims is so impaired that the decision-maker can find that the moving party has established its claims on a balance of probabilities, then the decision-maker may grant summary judgment to the moving party.
66 These reflections are consistent, I suggest, with the “road map” for summary judgment set out by Master Schlosser at para 17 of 1214777 Alberta Ltd v 480955 Alberta Ltd, 2014 ABQB 301.
Summary Judgment is still available in actions set for a jury trial In Wenzel v.

Further, I accept the approach adopted in both Manitoba and Ontario, which promotes access to speedy justice through summary judgment, while protecting the jury mode of trial for those matters that actually proceed to trial.

It follows that I do not accept the Defendant's contention that the Plaintiff's summary judgment application is precluded by the order of Yamauchi J directing that this matter proceed to trial before a jury.
I agree with the Plaintiff that the right to a jury trial does not preclude the bringing of a summary judgment application.

Shifting Onus and Conflicting Evidence (and where it can come from) In First Calgary Holdings (Alb) Corp. v.
Metropolitan Ventures Inc., 2015 ABQB 54, 2015 CarswellAlta 108 (Master), the defendants applied for summary dismissal of the plaintiff's claim.
The plaintiff did not file an affidavit that supported its claim; the plaintiff submitted that the documents produced and excerpts from the questioning of the applicants

(defendants) (there was no cross-examination of the defendants on their affidavits filed in support of the application) showed that the defendants' affidavit evidence in support of the application was unreliable, and that the application must therefore fail.
The defendants submitted that without cross-examination on the affidavits, the content of them should be accepted by the Court.

Master Robertson said, at paragraph 68: 68 In my view the resolution of this application rests on whether “the record permits a fair and just adjudication”, based upon the approach indicated by the Alberta Court of Appeal in Windsor v.
Canadian Pacific Railway, 2014 ABCA 108, 2014 CarswellAlta 395.

If the affidavit evidence put forward in support of the application does not appear to be true, or there is a reasonable basis for doubting the veracity of the affidavit evidence on material points of fact, the onus does not shift to the respondent to reply.
Only when the applicant has met its obligation does the onus shift to the respondent, as described in Pioneer Exploration Inc. v.
Euro-Am Pacific Enterprises Ltd., 2003 ABCA 298 at para.
18 and 19, Murphy Oil Co. v.
Predator Corp., 2006 ABCA 69, and Tottrup v.
Clearwater, 2006 ABCA 380 at para.
The learned Master then addressed the absence of cross-examination on the affidavits: 76 The defendants say that neither Mr.
Tomanik nor Mr.
Luppi were cross-examined on their affidavits, and therefore their affidavit evidence should be accepted by the Court.
77 However, citing Beier v.
Proper Cat Construction Ltd., 2013 ABQB 351 at para.

61, First Capital says that the defendants have not demonstrated that their position is “unassailable” and “so compelling that the likelihood of success is very high.” Since the evidence is not clear, and may not be accurate, … the affidavits cannot be relied upon for summary dismissal.
If it is shown that their evidence may not be true because of inconsistencies they themselves have presented, their position cannot be described as “unassailable”.
78 Nonetheless, the defendants say First Capital cannot take this position without cross-examining.
79 They refer to section 23 of the Alberta Evidence Act.
That section addresses presenting contradictory evidence to a witness who is in cross-examination.
Before giving proof of a contradictory statement, where the witness has not already admitted that he made the statement, the witness is to be asked whether he made the contradictory statement.
It assumes that there actually is a cross-examination in which this would be done.

It does not appear to apply here so as to require a cross-examination take place where this witness has previously given evidence under oath in the same proceedings that contradicts his later evidence, and the issue before the court is not whether his evidence is true—that is, the court is not weighing his evidence—but whether there is some basis for concluding that his evidence should be weighed by a trial judge.
80 Counsel for the defendants also relies on the Rule in Browne v.
Dunn, and says that on this summary judgment application his clients have not been given an opportunity to explain their prior inconsistent statements.

Accordingly, the statements should not be referred to, and the evidence in their affidavit should be treated as uncontroverted and simply accepted by the Court regardless of their prior inconsistent testimony in the same proceedings.
81 I drew to counsel's attention (as had counsel for First Capital) that I had recently concluded that the Rule in Browne v.

Dunn does not apply in summary judgment applications, because it is a rule that applies to allow the proper weighing of evidence, and evidence is not weighed at a summary judgment application: Chandos Construction Ltd. v.
Buildtech Framing Inc., 2014 ABQB 597.
82 Furthermore, the realities of a trial are simply not the same as they are on a chambers application, as counsel for First Capital pointed out.

In light of the fact that the previous inconsistent statements were given under oath in these proceedings, and they were clearly identified in First Capital's brief, there could have been a request for an adjournment for a further affidavit by either Mr.
Luppi or Mr.
Tomanik, or both, to provide an explanation, but there was none.

These deponents are not third party witnesses who may no longer be available to swear new affidavits; they are the litigants instructing counsel, and who are trying to persuade the Court to dismiss the claim as against them.

There is not the same prejudice here as there is at trial when a witness has long left the witness stand, and then some prior allegedly inconsistent statement that he made, but to which he was not referred in his evidence, is raised in order to call his credibility into question or to prove that his evidence was wrong.
In that case, the witness has not been given an opportunity to explain.
83 As well, no suggestion was made here as to what Mr.
Luppi's and Mr.
Tomanik's explanations might possibly be. … 85 In my view, a part of a party's duty to “put its best foot forward” is its duty to allow relevant information to be placed before the court.
It cannot object to relevant evidence, and then argue that the evidence is not before the court because the other side did not compel it to provide it.
The court is entitled to consider whether evidence, or a topic of enquiry, is relevant when the issue comes before it, not just on an application to compel.
86 First Capital had been met with the objections based on relevance at questioning.
Conducting a cross-examination on an affidavit simply to get the same objections would have been pointless.
87 Objections based on relevance at questioning can backfire on the party making the objection.
A party who objects to questions by the opposing party may find himself estopped from tendering evidence on the same topic at trial, having taken the position that it was irrelevant at questioning.
The objection may be binding on the objecting party at trial if it is not challenged by the opposing party.
But his objection does not bind the opposing party from continuing to assert that the evidence is relevant.

Master Robertson concluded: 97 All of this leaves the evidence in a very unsatisfactory state for a summary dismissal of the claim against the individuals. … 98 The burden on an applicant for summary judgment is to present a case that is “unassailable”.
If it appears to be unassailable, the respondent can provide evidence that demonstrates that it is not.
99 However, where the respondent can demonstrate that the applicant's own evidence is not “unassailable”, the onus does not shift to the respondent to tender any evidence.

100 As explained above, the questioning can be relied upon to show discrepancies in the applicant defendants' own evidence, and the documents listed in the parties' affidavits of records may be referred to for at least the limited purposes of showing that they exist and are authentic, and that they have been transmitted.
101 The application for summary judgment dismissing the claim against some of the defendants is dismissed.
In Mackey v.

Squair, 2015 ABQB 329, Justice Topolniski discussed summary judgment applications and the onus of proof: 21 Rule 7.3 of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010 permits a party to apply for summary judgment on all or part of a claim where there is no merit to a claim or part of it, or where the only real issue is quantum ….
22 A party's position is without merit if the facts and law make the moving party's position unassailable and entitle it to the relief it seeks.

In this regard, “unassailable” means if it is so compelling that the likelihood of success is very high: Access Mortgage Corporation (2014) Limited v Arres Capital Inc, 2014 ABCA 280 at para 45 (Access Mortgage).

23 The Supreme Court of Canada and Alberta Court of Appeal have mandated a cultural shift to promote timely and affordable access to our civil justice system which affects applications for summary judgment: Hryniak v Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, [2014] 1 SCR 87 (Hryniak)
Windsor v Canada Pacific Railway Ltd, 2014 ABCA 108, 371 DLR
(4th) 339 (Windsor).
Today, if the Court is able to reach a fair and just determination on the merits on a motion for summary judgment then there is no meritorious issue which requires a trial.

Windsor at paras 12-13 and 49 indicates there are three criteria to apply Rule 7.3 and order summary judgment; if the summary judgment application: 1. allows the judge to make the necessary findings of fact, 2. allows the judge to apply the law to the facts, and 3. is a proportionate, more expeditious and less expensive means to achieve a just result.

24 The supporting principles governing summary judgment applications are described in Beier v Proper Cat Construction, 2013 ABQB 351 at paras 66–69, 564 AR 357, and reiterated in several appellate authorities including Stout v Track, 2015 ABCA 10 at para 53, 9 Alta LR
(6th) 341 and Access Mortgage at para 45: 1.

The onus of proof is on the moving party who must present the facts, which in combination with the applicable law, make its position unassailable if the non-moving party does not contest the facts and the law.
The non-moving party has no legal or persuasive burden to discharge although that may practically place him at risk.
The Court may not make findings of credibility and resolve contested facts.
However, controversy over nonmaterial fact is irrelevant.
The Court considers the evidence before it the not that which might later be adduced.
In Amack v.
Wishewan, 2015 ABCA 147, the Court commented on the meaning of the phrase “no genuine issue for trial” after the Supreme Court of Canada's decision in Hryniak v.
Mauldin: 26 Rule 7.3(1)(b) allows a court to grant summary judgment to a defendant where there is “no merit” to a claim.
Where the claim is by a plaintiff, it is referred to as summary judgment; and where it is by a defendant, it is typically referred to as summary dismissal.
The point is that for purposes of this Rule, summary judgment includes summary dismissal.

Following the recent Supreme Court of Canada decision in Hryniak v Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, [2014] 1 SCR 87 [Hryniak], this Court has held that summary judgment can be granted if a disposition that is fair and just to both parties can be made on the existing record: Windsor v Canadian Pacific Railway Ltd., 2014 ABCA 108 at para 13, 572 AR 317 [Windsor]
Maxwell v Wal-Mart, 2014 ABCA 383 at para 12.
This does not, however, detract from the requirement that there be “no genuine issue for trial”: Hryniak, supra at para 34
Windsor, supra at para 13; 776826 Alberta Ltd. v Ostrowercha, 2015 ABCA 49 at para 11 [Ostrowercha]
Can v Calgary (Police Service), 2014 ABCA 322 at para 10, 315 CCC

Rather, the two concepts are themselves linked, as noted in Hryniak, supra at para 49: • There will be no genuine issue requiring a trial when the judge is able to reach a fair and just determination on the merits on a motion for summary judgment.
This will be the case when the process
(1) allows the judge to make the necessary findings of fact
(2) allows the judge to apply the law to the facts, and
(3) is a proportionate, more expeditious and less expensive means to achieve a just result.
Justice Yungwirth put it this way in Robinson v.

Lewis, 2015 ABQB 385: 25 In relation to an application for summary dismissal pursuant to Rule 7.3(1)(b), Read J confirmed in the case of Harding v Hudsons Canadian Hospitality Ltd, 2015 ABQB 38 at para 9, [2014] AWLD 1488, that summary judgment is no longer to be denied solely on the basis that the evidence discloses a triable issue.
She confirmed that the question is whether there is in fact any issue of merit that genuinely requires a trial.
Affidavits in Summary Judgment Applications In H2 Canmore Apartments LP v.

Cormode & Dickson Construction Edmonton Ltd., 2023 ABKB 659, Justice Marion discussed what should, and should not, be in an affidavit filed in a summary judgment application: [18] It is appropriate in a well drafted affidavit to describe an allegation to provide the reader with context to better understand the evidence in the affidavit, but the statements must not go beyond that purpose and amount to inadmissible advocacy: Kissel at para 62, citing Alberta Treasury Branches v Leahy, 1999 ABQB 185 at para 84.

[20] As per McDonald, [McDonald v.

[21] It is also important, again, to remember the summary judgment context.

Given that the applicant has both the threshold and ultimate burden to establish that summary judgment is appropriate and that there are no genuine issues for trial, the court must be careful in considering a pre-emptive motion to strike evidence.
For example, the court must be alive to the fact that only the initial elements of a defence must be proven in order to trigger the duty of the respondent to put its best foot forward.
In some cases, this may require an applicant affiant to open themselves up to questioning by simply saying: “the allegations against me are not true”.
Courts must be careful about striking, as a bald or bare assertion, a factual statement required to put the applicant over the threshold burden.
[22] Further, Courts must be wary of requiring an affiant to provide detailed supporting facts to support a negative proposition.
For example, where it is alleged a defendant did X, it may not be reasonable to expect an affidavit to say more than: I did not do X as alleged.
It may not be reasonable to expect an affiant to provide detailed evidence of everything they did do that was not X.
In some instances, a lack of detailed back-up to a conclusory statement in an affidavit should be addressed in the context of all the evidence.
This point is particularly relevant where an applicant for summary dismissal is responding to broad or conclusory allegations in a Statement of Claim.

Legal Conclusions or Legal Opinion in Affidavits [23] Conclusions are the function of the court and affidavits should be confined to evidence: Alberta (Human Rights Commission) at para 6; Rau at para 19.
To the extent a lay witness with no legal expertise ventures into providing legal opinions, it is trite that such opinions are also inadmissible.

Opinion Evidence in Affidavits [24] The general rule is that witnesses may not express opinions, because opinion evidence is presumptively inadmissible: R v DD, 2000 SCC 43 (CanLII), [2000] 2 SCR 275 at para 49
Kon Construction Ltd v Terranova Developments Ltd, 2015 ABCA 249 at para 20
White Burgess Langille Inman v Abbott and Haliburton Co, 2015 SCC 23 at paras 14-15.

[25] There are at least two exceptions to this rule: (1) the compendious statement of facts exception; and (2) the witness with expertise exception: O'Kane v Lillqvist-O'Kane, 2021 ABQB 925 at para 6.

[26] The first exception was summarized in O'Kane [footnotes omitted]: [8] The leading case on the admissibility of lay opinion evidence under the compendious statement of facts exception is Graat v R.
The Supreme Court of Canada admonished courts faced with lay opinion evidence not to place too much weight on the “tenuous, and frequently false, antithesis between fact and opinion.
The line between “fact” and “opinion” is not clear.” The Court went on to prescribe a principled approach.
The Court explained that “[a]dmissibility is determined, first, by asking whether the evidence sought to be admitted is relevant.
This is a matter of applying logic and experience to the circumstances of the particular case.

The question which must then be asked is whether, though probative, the evidence must be excluded by a clear ground of policy or of law.” [9] The Court in Graat admitted lay opinion evidence from police officers as to whether the accused was too drunk to drive.

The lay opinion evidence was neither excluded by a clear ground of policy nor law because it fell under what is known as the “compendious statement of facts” exception to the rule against opinion evidence.
Under the compendious statement of facts exception, the opinion functions as a shorthand for expressing all of the small facts that are implicit in the opinion.

For example, the conclusion that a person is drunk may be taken to be comprised of the factual observations that an ordinary person would use to conclude that a person was drunk, such as slurred words and a lack of coordination.
[10] Following Graat, leading texts have distilled four criteria for admitting lay evidence under the compendious statement of facts exception that have, in turn, been accepted by courts.
Lay opinion evidence may only be accepted if:
(1) the lay witness is in a better position than the trier of fact to form the conclusion
(2) the conclusion is one that persons of ordinary experience are able to make
(3) the witness, although not expert, has the experiential capacity to make the conclusion; and
(4) the opinions being expressed are merely a compendious mode of stating facts that are too subtle or complicated to be narrated as effectively without resort to conclusions.
[11] The four criteria are sometimes styled the “lay evidence rule.” [27] The second exception was addressed by the Court of Appeal in Kon Construction.
In that case, the Court of Appeal identified three types of witnesses with expertise, at para 35:
(a) Independent experts who are retained to provide opinions about issues in the litigation, but were not otherwise involved in the underlying events.
This is the category of expert witness contemplated by White Burgess and Mohan.
(b) Witnesses with expertise who were involved in the events underlying the litigation, but are not themselves litigants.
An example is the family physician in a personal injury case who is called upon to testify about his or her observations of the plaintiff, and the treatment provided.
(c) Litigants (including the officers and employees of corporate litigants) who have expertise, and who were actually involved in the events underlying the litigation.
[28] The Cormode Employee Defendants argue that they fall within the third category: litigants with expertise who were involved in the underlying litigation.

In Kon Construction, the Court of Appeal said this about these types of witnesses: [40] Secondly, it is generally not necessary to qualify the last class of witnesses with expertise as “experts” under the Mohan procedure.
As parties to the litigation they are entitled to testify, and generally they will have the most direct and relevant evidence about the issues.
The truth finding function of a trial requires that their evidence be received.

Since they were often only involved in the underlying events because of their expertise, it makes no sense to hold that they cannot explain why they acted as they did, if they stray into their expertise.
Their opinions explain why they acted as they did.
Since these witnesses are available for pre-trial questioning, formal advance notice of their opinions or their evidence is not needed.

[29] It may be difficult in determining exactly when such witnesses stray outside of their expertise, or when they are giving opinions that are not based on their involvement in the underlying events.
If it is not clear, it may be more appropriate for such issues to be dealt with as in the context of all the evidence on the summary judgment application.

Where it is clear that such witnesses are giving opinions outside of their expertise or are given opinions that are not based on their personal involvement in the matter, then such evidence may be inadmissible.

This jurisprudence states that where resolving such disputes entails weighing evidence, summary judgment normally ought not to be granted.

11 There are some exceptions to this general rule, for example: (i) where the chambers judge/master assumes that the evidence of the non-moving party is correct, (as was done in Sherwood Steel, supra).

(ii) where the evidence of the non-moving party is either destroyed by cross-examination on affidavit or the introduction of other evidence rendering that party's evidence completely non-credible: Janvier v.
834474 Alberta Ltd., 2010 ABQB 800.

(iii) Where the conflicting evidence is on matters which are irrelevant to the ground upon which summary judgment is being sought (for example, where there is conflicting evidence as to which driver caused a collision between two automobiles but the summary dismissal application is being brought on a limitations defence).
12 No exceptions apply here.
In Goodswimmer v.
Canada (Attorney General), 2017 ABCA 365, 2017 CarswellAlta 2299, 60 Alta.
L.R.
(6th) 226, the Court said: 38 The appellants argue that the case management judge erred in granting summary relief in the face of conflicting affidavits.
They argue that the only way to resolve disputed issues of fact is with a trial.

There are admittedly cases that point out the dangers of attempting to resolve disputed issues, especially those that rely on findings of credibility, based on conflicting affidavits and documents that would support either party's position.
39 The modern summary judgment case law, however, marks a shift away from seeing the trial as the default method of proving disputed facts.
Hryniak v Mauldin at para.

4 confirms that a trial is not needed to resolve disputed facts if a summary judgment motion can achieve a fair and just adjudication, and that the prospect of the trial judge obtaining a better appreciation of the evidence at a trial should not be overemphasized.

Not every conflict in the evidence precludes the chambers judge from drawing inferences from the admitted facts, the undisputed evidence, the conduct of the parties, and the corroborating evidence (such as documents with objective reliability): Sandhu v Siri Guru Nanak Sikh Gurdwara of Alberta, 2015 ABCA 101 at paras.
The Alberta Rules permit a judge to make findings of fact on an application for summary judgment: Windsor v Canadian Pacific Railway Ltd., 2014 ABCA 108 at para.
40 The mere fact that there might be some conflicting evidence on the record does not mean that a “fair and just adjudication” is not possible.
The case law was summarized in Shefsky v California Gold Mining Inc., 2016 ABCA 103 at para.
113, 31 Alta LR (6th) 1, 616 AR 290: 113 Not every piece of disputed evidence requires a trial.
For example, a “bare denial” or bald allegation does not raise a triable issue: Canada (Attorney General) v Lameman, 2008 SCC 14 at para.
11, [2008] 1 SCR 372; Goldman v Devine, 2007 ONCA 301 at para.
Floden Services Ltd. v Solomon, 2015 ABQB 450 at para.
23, 24 Alta LR (6th) 76; Confederation Trust Co. v Alizadeh, [1998] OJ No 408 (QL) (Gen Div).
Nor does a self-serving affidavit unsupported by other evidence: Guarantee Co. of North America v Gordon Capital Corp., [1999] 3 SCR 423 at pp.
Nor does evidence that flies in the face of the balance of the record: Dagher v Glenn, 2016 ABCA 38 at paras.
30–2; Pioneer Exploration Inc.
(Trustee of) v Euro-Am Pacific Enterprises Ltd., 2003 ABCA 298 at para.
25-6, 27 Alta LR (4th) 62; Rogers Cable TV Ltd. v 373041 Ontario Ltd.
(1994), 22 OR (3d) 25 (Gen Div); Klein v Wolbeck, 2016 ABQB 28 at para.
26; Pizza Pizza Ltd. v Gillespie (1990), 75 OR (2d) 225 at p.
253 (Gen Div).

Whether there is truly a “genuine issue requiring resolution at a trial” requires a nuanced balancing of the weight and perceived reliability of the evidence, the importance of the issue, the likelihood of there being a better record at trial, and any other relevant considerations.
There are other manifestations of this principle, including Leis v Leis, 2014 ABCA 36 at para.
45, where the affidavit said to raise a conflict was “unsupported or outright contradicted by the litigation history”, and Lydian Properties Inc. v Chambers, 2009 ABCA 21 at paras.
2, 22-3, 100 Alta LR (4th) 39, 457 AR 211 where the conflicting evidence was not material to the outcome.
41 The presumption against deciding summarily based on conflicting affidavits is primarily concerned with situations where the conflict raises issues of credibility.
None of the historical evidence in this case raises issues of credibility.
Assertions by those who actually participated in the settlement negotiations that are plainly contradicted by the contemporaneous documents do not necessarily bar summary disposition.
Further, the presumption against deciding summarily based on conflicting affidavits assumes that the affidavits are relevant and admissible.

Where the identified disputes are not on matters of fact, but are really legal opinions, inferences, or subjective views on the interpretation of documents, there is not necessarily an impediment to a summary disposition.
In Liberty Mortgage Services Ltd. v.
Shaw, 2024 ABKB 92, Justice Aloneissi said: [39] Summary judgment is not limited to cases where the facts are not in dispute: Weir-Jones at para 21.
Put otherwise, not every conflict in evidence gives rise to a genuine need for a trial: Weir-Jones at para 38.

That said, some factual disputes can create a need for trial, like conflicts of evidence on material issues or conflicts of evidence that require findings of credibility to be resolved: Weir-Jones at paras 35 and 38.
[40] Conflicts between affidavit evidence may require credibility findings to resolve.

It is an error to disregard conflicting affidavit evidence entirely when that evidence could, if assessed for credibility, have a material impact on the outcome of the case: LRS v SSD, 2020 ABCA 206 at paras 17 and 19 citing to Nieuwesteeg v Barron, 2009 ABCA 235.
[41] However, conflicts in affidavit evidence do not necessarily preclude summary judgment.
The circumstances in which facts may be found in despite conflicting affidavit evidence were described by Bielby JA in Sandhu v Siri Guru Nanak Sikh Gurdwara of Alberta, 2015 ABCA 101 [Sandhu]: 1.
Where the conflicts in the evidence do not concern essential facts.
Where the apparent conflict is a conflict of opinions or interpretations, rather than a factual conflict.
Where the issues can be resolved based only on facts that are not disputed.

Where one party relies on several affidavits which contain internally conflicting evidence, including some evidence which agrees with or supports the opposing party's evidence and thus amounts to an admission against interest.
Sandhu at para 81.
[42] In R Floden Services Ltd v Solomon, 2015 ABQB 450 [Floden], Justice Renke added an additional category: 5.
Where the issues can be resolved on the basis of admissible evidence other than the conflicting affidavit evidence.
Floden at para 21 citing to Compton Petroleum Corp v Alberta Power Ltd, 1999 ABQB 42 [Compton] at para 14 and N V Reykdal & Associates v 571582 Alberta Ltd, 2000 ABCA 330 at para 5 [Reykdal].
[43] Furthermore, not all affidavit evidence is equally weighty.
In Floden at para 22, Justice Renke listed the circumstances in which a Judge may properly give less weight to particular affidavit evidence: 1.
The Judge is satisfied the deponent was attempting to engineer circumstances which precluded being tested on credibility (e.g. by avoiding questioning): Sandhu at para 83.
The affidavit evidence is “destroyed by cross-examination”: Janvier v 834474 Alberta Ltd, 2010 ABQB 800 at para 15 [Janvier].
The evidence is not consistent with other evidence and known circumstances: Compton at para 14; Reykdal at para 5; Janvier at para 15.
[44] Affidavit evidence that is general, vague, or superficial may also be given reduced weight: Geophysical Service Inc v Falkland Oil and Gas Ltd, 2020 ABCA 21 at para 61
MNP Ltd (Eco-Industrial Business Park Inc) v Symmetry Asset Management Inc, 2023 ABKB 429 at para 87.
Affidavit evidence that is self-serving and otherwise unsupported can be given no weight and does not give rise to a genuine need for trial: Guarantee Co of North America v Mr.
Tayloron Capital Corp, 1999 CanLII 664 (SCC), [1999] 3 SCR 423 at 436-437 [Mr.
Tayloron] at 436-437.

Other descriptions of this type of evidence include a “bare denial”, a “bald assertion”, or having no “air of reality”: Goodswimmer v Canada (Attorney General), 2017 ABCA 365 at para 40 citing to Lameman at para 11 and Floden at para 23
Fitzpatrick v The College of Physical Therapists Alberta, 2020 ABCA 164 at para 22.
Consider Application to Strike after Hearing Applications to Amend In Condominium Corp.
No.
970365 Alberta Ltd., 2012 ABCA 26, 2012 CarswellAlta 58, 519 A.R.
L.R.

(5th) 1; leave to appeal refused 2012 CarswellAlta 1698, 2012 CarswellAlta 1699 (S.C.C.), Chief Justice Fraser said, at paragraph 3: 3 MCAP applied under Rule 159(2) of the former Alberta Rules of Court (Old Rules) seeking a summary judgment dismissing all the appellants' claims against MCAP.
Prior to hearing the summary judgment application, the chambers judge dealt with and granted, with the consent of counsel for MCAP, an outstanding application to amend the Statement of Claim.
Once that was concluded and the amendment allowed, he dealt with the summary judgment application on the basis of the Amended Amended Statement of Claim.
This is the proper procedure and one that ought to be followed as a matter of good practice.
That is to say, outstanding applications to amend pleadings should be resolved prior to a chambers judge's considering a summary judgment application on its merits: Elbow River Marketing v.
Canada Clean Fuels Inc., 2011 ABCA 258 at para.
In light of the above statement, one might want to approach with caution Justice Graesser's statement in L.
Alberta, 2011 ABQB 771, 2011 CarswellAlta 2262.
In that case, an application for summary judgment was brought before a pending amendment application was brought.
Graesser, J. said, at paragraphs 45-46: 45 The Crown cites Elbow River Marketing v.
Canada Clean Fuels Inc., 2011 ABCA 258 on this point.
There, the Court of Appeal determined that it was “reversible error” for the chambers judge, [2011] A.J.
No.
545, to deal with summary judgment in the face of a motion to amend pleadings.
It also held that it was “not in a position” to deal with the summary judgment on the merits with what amounts to unsettled pleadings and an equally unsettled evidentiary foundation”.
I take those comments to be case specific, and not a determination that in no case can summary judgment proceed in the face of a motion to amend the pleadings, or if the pleadings are not settled.
46 Each case should be dealt with on its merits.

Sometimes, it will be inappropriate to proceed with summary judgment; where the motion or uncertainty in pleadings affects other issues but not the issue on which summary judgment is sought, the summary judgment motion might proceed.
P.L.'s summary judgment application falls in the latter category: the trespass and unlawful confinement causes of action are not affected by the decisions referenced in paragraph 43 of these reasons.
In 926 Capital Corp. v.
Petro River Oil Corp., 2016 ABQB 194, 2016 CarswellAlta 575, Master Prowse considered an amendment application before determining an application for summary judgment.

Master Prowse's decision was appealed, and Justice Strekaf, in dismissing the appeal, said: 14 The general rule where an application to amend pleadings and an application for summary judgment are heard concurrently is that the amendment application should be heard first.
The Status of Pretrial steps when summary judgment is sought In Patrick Burns Memorial Trust (Trustee of) v.
P.

Burns Resources Ltd., 2015 ABQB 378, Justice Macleod considered the question of whether the taking of pre-trial steps (e.g., production of records, questioning) should be allowed pending the hearing of a summary dismissal application.
Master Prowse had ruled that those proceedings should not be permitted.
Justice Macleod disagreed that there should be an automatic stay of such proceedings.
His Lordship said: 7 The appeals are allowed for the following reasons.

Parties to litigation may bring an application for summary judgment or summary dismissal prior to and regardless of whether or not they have taken the pre trial steps of questioning and document production.

The question raised in this instance is whether or not the default position, in the face of such proceedings, is that the obligations or powers under Part 5 of the Alberta Rules of Court [Rules] are stayed or held in suspense.
8 The starting point in this analysis has to be the Rules themselves.

As our Court of Appeal has said in Canadian Natural Resources Ltd v ShawCor Ltd, 2014 ABCA 289 at para 30, the Rules have a status comparable to a statute and must be read in their entire context and in their grammatical and ordinary sense, harmoniously with the overall scheme of the legislation.
9 Part 5 makes an affidavit of records mandatory (rule 5.5).
Rule 5.17 confers the right of questioning upon a party.
The rights and obligations under Part 5 had accrued.
The Statement of Defence was filed on September 27, 2012.

10 The only rule dealing with the modification or waiver of any right or power under Part 5 is rule 5.3 which confers upon the Court the right to modify if a) a person acts or threatens to act in a manner that is vexatious, evasive, abusive, oppressive, improper or tediously lengthy or, b) the expense, delay, danger or difficulty in complying with a rule would be grossly disproportionate to the likely benefit.
11 There is nothing in any other part of the Rules which would suspend the operation of Part 5 in the face of a summary judgment application.
12 The Respondents cite Wenzel Downhole Tools Ltd v National Oilwell Varco, Inc, 2010 ABCA 381.
That case merely affirms that there is no necessity to file an affidavit of records or engage in full discovery before an application for summary judgment.

But that decision makes it clear that the case management judge was correct in taking all matters into consideration before allowing an adjournment of a summary judgment application pending further questioning and production.

The case of Solis v del Rosario, 2014 ABQB 310 is of no assistance because it dealt with whether or not questioning of a person be adjourned pending the decision on a summary judgment application which already had been reserved.
The judge properly evaluated the situation and concluded that not allowing the questioning was the most effective manner in which the “claims will be resolved”.

13 It is true that a party cannot oppose an application for summary dismissal using the argument that some evidence in support of its claim may arise during questioning or document production and one is obligated to put one's best foot forward in a summary application.

But when, as in this case, the Defendants have all of the knowledge and all of the documents related to the Plaintiff's claim the situation cries out for an analysis of what disclosure is necessary or reasonable before the summary dismissal application goes ahead.
This, presumably, would be included within the Court's inquiry as to whether or not the rights or powers under Part 5 ought to be modified.

If the exercise of powers or rights would not meaningfully add anything to the relevant question at issue in the application, the Court has the power to attenuate the rights or obligations, particularly if the expense and delay would be grossly disproportionate to any benefit.
However, to conclude that the rights and powers under Part 5 should be suspended without any analysis is, in my view, to ignore the plain and ordinary meaning of rule 5.3.

While a respondent to an application for summary judgment may not be entitled as of right to the full penalopy of powers under Part 5, the Court before attenuating those powers must engage in some sort of cost benefit analysis.
14 This is a case where the factual underpinnings of the Plaintiff's case and the evidence as to those facts are within the knowledge and possession of the Defendants.
In my view, the request to question two of the Defendants and to review the content of the affidavit of records was not unreasonable and accordingly the decisions of the Master are set aside.

15 After the questioning of the two Defendants are completed, including the questioning on the Affidavit of Records, they may apply further to the Court for modification of any powers or rights under Part 5 of the Rules.
16 In arriving at this decision I whole heartedly agree that the judiciary should be actively managing litigation to ensure meaningful access to justice.
In doing so a more robust approach may often be warranted in pretrial proceedings.
However that can best be achieved when cases are assessed individually.
Timing of Summary Judgment Applications with Class Proceedings Applications In P.
Alberta, 2014 ABCA 404, 2014 CarswellAlta 2152, 7 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 629, the plaintiffs applied for certification of their action under the Class Proceedings Act.
The defendants applied for summary judgment on the basis that the claim was brought out of time.

The learned Chambers judge granted the summary judgment application, and then made a provisional ruling on the Class Proceedings application in case the summary judgment ruling was reversed on appeal.

The plaintiffs appealed the summary judgment decision and provisional ruling as they contended that the learned Chambers judge should have certified the proceedings before ruling on the summary judgment application.
The Court of Appeal ruled that the order in which the applications are determined is within the discretion of the judge.
At paragraphs 18–23, the Court said: 18 As already noted, this ground has—as the appellants have framed it—two aspects.
They say, first, that the chambers judge should have deferred hearing and deciding on Alberta's summary judgment application until deciding on certification.
And, secondly, they argue that summary judgment should not have been granted at all, since whether the ultimate limitation period applied here was a “triable issue”.
19 The appellants assert (but really do not argue) that this sequencing of dispositions is preferable.
Indeed, they say that the jurisprudence shows that limitations issues are “overwhelmingly” decided by a full trial, rather than by summary judgment.
Yet, the briefest review of the case law demonstrates that this is not so.

Subject to the Rules of Court (which, by operation of section 41 of the CPA, apply to class proceedings), and to a court exercising its case management discretion to direct otherwise, a party defending against an action may apply at any time for summary judgment.
Usually, an application for certification will be heard first: Hoffman v Monsanto Canada Inc, 2002 SKCA 120 at paras 28-29, 220 DLR
(4th) 542; Kwicksutaeineuk/Ah-Kwa-Mish First Nation v British Columbia (Agriculture and Lands), 2009 BCSC 1593 at paras 59–62, 84 CPC

This is principally the effect of the short timeframe contemplated by the CPA for obtaining certification of a class proceeding.2 20 The appellants say that this timeframe amounts to a statutory “direction” that all other matters are to be held in abeyance pending certification.
This is incorrect.

Proceeding with a certification application first is “primarily a matter of convenience rather than necessity”: Kowch v Gibraltar Mortgage Ltd, 2013 ABQB 317 at para 10, 536 AR 112 (Master in Chambers).

The CPA does not preclude a judge from exercising his or her discretion to hear and decide a summary judgment application prior to certification on the basis that it is an efficient and cost-effective way of disposing of an issue that might bring an end to the litigation altogether.
It does not matter whether the purportedly unmeritorious claim is sought to be advanced as a class proceeding or not.
Trying unmeritorious claims is per se unreasonable, because it imposes an unnecessary and often onerous burden upon parties and our system of civil justice: Hryniak at paras 23–28
Canada v Lameman, 2008 SCC 14 at para 10, [2008] 1 SCR 372
Windsor at para 13
Beier v Proper Cat Construction Ltd, 2013 ABQB 351 at paras 56–71, 564 AR 557 [Beier]
Orr v Fort McKay First Nation, 2014 ABQB 111 at paras 24–26.
21 Simply put, a class proceeding is just one procedural mode of advancing a claim.
The mere fact that a claim is advanced by way of a class proceeding does not endow it with special status allowing it to survive where the same claim would otherwise be doomed.
More particularly, it remains subject to all the tools furnished by Part 7 of the Rules of Court for resolving claims without a full trial, including summary judgment.

As the Supreme Court observed in Bisaillon v Concordia University, 2006 SCC 19 at para 17, [2006] 1 SCR 666, “[t]he class action is … a procedural vehicle whose use neither modifies nor creates substantive rights[.]… It cannot serve as a basis for legal proceedings if the various claims it covers, taken individually, would not do so[.]” (See also Stevenson Estate v Bank of Montreal, 2011 SKCA 51 at para 12, 371 Sask R 198

Thorpe v Honda Canada Inc, 2011 SKQB 72 at para 29, 373 Sask R 71; and Thorpe v Honda Canada Inc, 2009 SKQB 488 at para 14, 357 Sask R 1.) 22 The foregoing applies with equal force where the summary judgment application is based upon the expiry of a limitation period relative to the claim of a proposed representative plaintiff: Stone v Wellington County Board of Education, 1999 CanLII 1886 (ONCA) at para 10, [1999] OJ No 1298 (QL) [Stone].

Where a proposed representative plaintiff's claim is shown to be time-barred, there is no good reason for permitting the issue of certification to continue consuming judicial and litigants' resources.

Indeed, there is good reason for not doing so, since the representative plaintiff must be a member of the class: Section 2(1) of the CPA.3 Allowing a representative plaintiff's clearly time-barred claim to proceed further would defy the Legislature's intent that the class proceeding be brought only by someone with a personal stake in the outcome: Stone at paras 9-10
Hughes v Sunbeam Corp (Canada) Ltd
(3d) 433, 165 OAC 68 at para 15, leave to appeal refused [2002] SCCA No 446 (QL).

23 While the chambers judge in this case actually expended the time needed to hear and provisionally decide the certification application after having heard the summary judgment application, concerns about costs to litigants and to the civil justice system nonetheless arise here given the appellants' argument that limitations should have been determined by a full trial.
Further, the chambers judge's decision as case manager to order the applications as he did is entitled to substantial deference.
That decision was not appealed.

And, in any event, it was not unreasonable for him to exercise his discretion by hearing and deciding on Alberta's summary judgment application before deciding on the appellant's certification application.

Ostrowercha, 2015 ABCA 49, 2015 CarswellAlta 155, the defendant applied for summary judgment dismissing the plaintiff's claim; the summary judgment application was dismissed by the learned Chambers judge.

The Court of Appeal said, at paragraph 7: 7 His [the Chambers judge's] decision was an exercise of discretion.

He submits the proper construction of that subrule requires an affidavit swearing positively to those matters.

That interpretation is made clear, he argues, by placing the word “either” after the first “that”, such that the rule would read: The application must be supported by an affidavit swearing positively that EITHER

27 To respond to the plaintiff's evidence, the defendant must produce evidence on which the court can make a ruling on whether to grant the plaintiff summary judgment.
As Master Funduk said in Tucson Properties Ltd v.

In some cases it might be found within the evidence of the plaintiff.
In some cases it might be found in a cross-examination on affidavit.
By whatever means the evidence comes before the court, there must be evidence which lends some support to the defences raised.
If there is no evidence to support the issues the defendant raises in his defence, there is nothing for the court to weigh.
The scales tip entirely in one direction, that direction being in favour of the plaintiff.
If there is some evidence to support the issues the defendant raises, the court must then weigh that evidence and decide whether the plaintiff's claim is beyond all doubt.

If, after weighing the evidence supporting the defendant's position, the court is satisfied beyond all doubt that the plaintiff is entitled to judgment, then judgment should be given for the plaintiff.

If, however, after weighing the evidence supporting the defendant's position, the court is not satisfied beyond all doubt that the plaintiff is entitled to judgment, then the matter must proceed to trial.

They say this even though both the facts and the law are clear.
All that is required is an application of the law to the facts, which requires the exercise of judicial discretion.
There is nothing in rule 159 which prevents such a judicial exercise.
In its earlier formulation, rule 159 was restricted to actions in debt with liquidated damages.
That is no longer the case. . . . . .

Given that both the facts and law are clear, I cannot see how a court would be assisted by requiring a trial to take place merely because the matter involves wrongful dismissal and an exercise of judicial discretion. . . . . .

People are entitled to their day in court but not their decade.

A summary judgment procedure is swift, cheap and efficient, with the same neutral evaluation before an imparital judge.

In Wild Rose School Division No.
