339 (Q.B.), a contractor (Pratch) sued a school division and an engineering firm (Bearden) for damages resulting from a fire at a construction project.
The engineering firm filed a third party notice against the school division.

The contract between the school division and Pratch required Pratch to obtain a policy of insurance for the very type of loss which formed the subject matter of Pratch's claim against the school division.
The school division applied for summary judgment dismissing the third party proceedings.
An issue arose as to whether the court could rely on the pleadings as evidence of what claim was being made by the contractor.

The engineering firm which filed the third party notice contended that the court could only look at the filed affidavits, and that if the type of claim was not disclosed in the affidavits, the court could not look at the pleadings to ascertain the nature of the claim (that information was essential so that the court could determine if the claim fell within the contractor's insurance obligation).
Sanderman J. held that he could rely on the pleadings as evidence of the nature of the contractor's claim.
At pp.

343-44, his Lordship said: Bearden takes the position that the affidavits relied upon by the School Division do not establish to the degree required that the claim of Pratch is caught by the covenant to insure in the construction contract in existence between Pratch and the School Division.
Bearden asserts that there is no positive statement establishing this fact.
Therefore there remains unresolved a genuine question of fact and consequently a genuine question of law.
Put simply, Bearden submits that there is nothing in the affidavit that indicates that that which is claimed by Pratch against the School Division falls within the ambit of the covenant to insure.
There is nothing from Pratch that asserts this in a conclusive manner.
Bearden submits that the court is left in the position of not knowing what the covenant to insure relates to.

Absent this information being provided in a positive fashion in that affidavit, Bearden takes the position that the application must be dismissed in its entirety regardless of the analysis that the court has found compelling.

Bearden insists that the court cannot look at the pleadings filed by Pratch in order to determine whether or not there is evidence before the court that indicates with a degree of particularity what Pratch's claim is for.
Bearden takes the position that the court is restricted to looking at the affidavit evidence filed on behalf of the parties in relation to this application.
I disagree with the position taken by Bearden.
Pratch is not involved in this application.
No materials have been filed on behalf of Pratch.
Pratch is a major participant in this lawsuit.
It is through Pratch's statement of claim that Bearden has asked for indemnity or contribution from the School Division.
The document that allows Bearden to make this claim is Pratch's statement of claim.
It is the defining document.
Not to be allowed to look at it for the purposes of deciding this application would be foolish and irresponsible on the part of the court.
It is presumed that the pleadings of a party set out with precision the claim made or defence offered.
They must be taken to set out the position of the party filing them with the court.
The court must be able to rely upon pleadings as being an accurate assertion of the position of the party filing them unless they are amended.
To come to some other conclusion would be sheer folly.
The pleadings of a party delineate with particularity the remedy being sought.
A court's jurisdiction to grant a remedy is limited by the pleadings of the party.
The remedy granted cannot go beyond that which is sought in the pleadings… Surely, the court must be able to rely upon the pleadings of a party when attempting to ascertain what a claim is for.
When one reads clause 17 of the statement of claim of Pratch, it is obvious what is being claimed.
Pratch is claiming for “expense in the amount of $297,059.81 to repair and replace direct physical damage to property in the course of construction, installation, reconstruction or repair”.
One could not but come to the conclusion that this was work contemplated by the construction contract between Pratch and the School Division.
It is caught by the covenant to insure.
It is not necessary for a positive assertion of this to be placed in the affidavit filed in support of this application.
The court must be able to rely upon the pleadings of the party that Bearden joins in its claim against the School Division.

She therefore moves for summary judgment.
Unfortunately I have concluded that I should not give her that remedy.

The issue is quantum and quantum is disputed, so therefore the issue is whether there is a genuine triable issue as to any part of quantum … So therefore for these reasons I have come to the conclusion that on each part of the claim of the plaintiff there is a genuine issue to be tried, not in the sense of liability but in the sense of quantum.

(a) allows the judge to make the necessary findings of fact

13 In this case the reasons under appeal stated the test for summary judgment as being whether the moving party's position was “unassailable”, and stated it would be unassailable if it is so compelling that the “likelihood of success [at trial] is very high”: reasons at para.
This statement of the law was extracted from the concurring reasons in Can v Calgary Police Service, 2014 ABCA 322 at para.
20, 584 AR 147, which extracted that test from the earlier reasons of the author in Beier v Proper Cat Construction Ltd., 2013 ABQB 351 at para.
The obiter dicta in Can do not accurately state the law.
Under the rules of stare decisis, decisions of the Court of Appeal reflect the law of the province.
The binding ratio decidendi of a Court of Appeal decision, however, is to be found in the majority reasons.
Obiter dicta in concurring and dissenting reasons do not reflect the law, and they should not be followed to the extent that they are inconsistent with binding authority.
14 First of all, it is now established that there is only one civil standard of proof and it is proof on a balance of probabilities.
The rule was definitively stated in F.H. v McDougall, 2008 SCC 53 at para.
40, [2008] 3 SCR 41: “… I think it is time to say, once and for all in Canada, that there is only one civil standard of proof at common law and that is proof on a balance of probabilities”.

That is the standard the summary judgment rule engages when it talks about “merit”: proof on a balance of probabilities. “Unassailable” and “very high likelihood” are not recognized standards of proof.
15 Secondly, the test for summary judgment is stated in the binding cases like Hryniak v Mauldin and Windsor v Canadian Pacific Railway.
Summary judgment is one procedure for deciding whether the moving party has proven its case on a balance of probabilities.
Summary judgment is the appropriate procedure where the record is such that a fair and just disposition can be made on it: 776826 Alberta Ltd.
(c.o.b.
Budweiser Motorsports Park) v Ostrowercha, 2015 ABCA 49 at paras.
In other words, is the record such that it is fair and just to decide summarily if the moving party has proven the case on a balance of probabilities?

That generally comes down to deciding if there is any material issue of fact on which a trial is justified, or whether the chambers judge can make any required fact findings from the summary dismissal record in a fair and just manner.

A trial may be the preferred and proportional procedure where there is a reasonable expectation that a better evidentiary record will be created by a trial, for example because there are disputed issues of material fact, or issues of credibility, that cannot fairly be resolved summarily.

16 It follows that a plaintiff cannot resist summary dismissal merely by raising a “doubt”, although the plaintiff is not required at that stage to prove its case on a balance of probabilities: McDonald v Brookfield Asset Management Inc., 2016 ABCA 375 at para.
The plaintiff can obviously resist summary dismissal by showing that the applicant has not, at that stage, proved its defence on a balance of probabilities.

(above), for example. i)—Weight and Probative Value 14 In its ordinary sense (and I have in mind The Concise Oxford Dictionary meaning) “to weigh” is to “estimate relative value or importance”, or, “to consider with the view to choice, rejection, or preference”.
In the trial context this usually means an estimation of probative value.
In the trial context, weight has to do with ranking admissible evidence to find facts or to decide whether one fact is more or less probable than a competing fact.
In this case, I do not have to decide between competing facts.
There are no facts in dispute.
There are no questions of admissibility in this case. ii)—Weight and Admissibility 15 Weight and admissibility are two different things.
Admissibility has to do with whether you can consider evidence, or even hear it at all.
Like truth or the quality of being unique, admissibility does not admit of degree. iii)—Weighting Factors 16 There may be another sense in which evidence might be weighed.
Bardal (below) sets out a non-exhaustive list of factors for determining the length of reasonable notice.
It might be said that ranking the factors (by attaching more weight or importance to length of service than to age, for example) is, in some sense, weighing or weighting evidence.

However, (and subject to what follows), the law of reasonable notice is so well travelled, the determination is largely a question of attaching equal weight to what the decided cases tell us are the important points and then applying the decided cases to them like an algorithm.
There might be an unusual case that takes us outside this exercise.
But this is not one of them. iv)—Summary Judgment 17 A master (or for that matter, a judge), in a summary judgment application is playing a very different role from a trier of fact at a trial.
18 Masters, or chambers judges, hearing summary judgment applications are not acting as “triers of fact”.
They determine the sufficiency of the evidence to make a summary disposition.
The Court is saying: “If the matter were to go to trial, this would be the result”.
The Court is reaching its decision that a matter need not go that far on a level of certainty that is usually (and perhaps necessarily) higher than balance of probability certainty.
And this is done on the assumption that both sides are putting their best case forward.

19 If the weight of evidence is in question at a summary judgment application, it might be necessary to see the witnesses and send the evidence for “forensic testing at trial”: 776826 Alberta Ltd. v Ostrowercha, 2015 ABCA 49.
20 Conflicts in the evidence usually mean that the matter must go to trial.

It is not an option to resolve conflicts in the evidence at a summary judgment application, unless the parties agree and the matter is being heard by a master (section 9(3)(b) of the Court of Queen's Bench Act), or unless the conflict has been resolved in some other fashion.
21 The distinction is subtle but important.

In Orr v Fort McKay First Nation, 2014 ABQB 111, Brown J. said: [17] The line between weighing evidence, and deciding that the evidence merits granting (or not granting) summary judgment, may seem elusive when it is considered that both parties to a summary judgment application will typically put evidence before the master in order to show that the test is (or is not) met.
Again, Harvey CJ's decision in Polson Iron Works, [1915] A.J.
No.
106 offers guidance: The order under consideration is perhaps the nearest approach to determining the rights of parties by trial that the rules authorize the Master to make.
But in reality, he is not trying the rights of the parties.
He is determining that there is no real issue to be tried.

It is only when such a situation is found to exist that the Master is authorized to give a judgment … (Polson Iron Works at 235.) [18] In short, while masters may not weigh evidence to resolve disputed or contentious questions of fact, they may examine the evidence to determine whether an issue remains to be tried or to otherwise determine (by applying the facts to the law) whether a party's position is so compelling that the likelihood it will succeed is so high that it merits granting summary judgment.
(Janvier v 834774 Alberta Ltd, 2010 ABQB 800 at para 15.) I recognize that, at some level, all evidence—even extremely compelling evidence—requires weighing.
(Brown, “The Possibility of “Inference Causation”: Inferring Cause-in-Fact and the Nature of Legal Certainty”

(2010) 55 McGill LJ 1 at 31–35.) To carry that proposition to its logical conclusion would, however, defeat the constitutional purpose served by appointing masters of facilitating the administration of justice.
This conundrum need not be resolved here.

It suffices for present purposes to reiterate that masters may not carry out the weighing of evidence contemplated in Ontario's Rule 20.04(2.1), which is the first reason why the guidance in Hryniak v Mauldin regarding the standard of review is inapplicable to an application for summary judgment under Rule 7.3.
22 The question is whether this case meets the threshold for summary determination.

Nine Energy Canada Inc., 2018 ABQB 898, 2018 CarswellAlta 2553, 78 Alta.
L.R.
210-014, Justice K.

Nixon concluded that “the assessment of damages for pay in lieu of reasonable notice is not appropriate for summary judgment” (paragraph 11) (see the annotation “Masters' Jurisdiction” under this rule).
However, in Rudichuk v.
Genesis Land Development Corp., 2019 ABQB 133, the defendants brought an application for summary dismissal of the plaintiffs' wrongful dismissal claim.

Justice Marriott discussed summary judgment applications relating to wrongful dismissal claims: [28] The party moving for summary judgment has the burden of proving, by adducing their own evidence, that there is no genuine issue for trial on a balance of probabilities: Weir-Jones at paras 32, 47
Windsor at para 13
Stefanyk v Sobeys Capital Incorporated, 2018 ABCA 125 (CanLII) at para 4 [Stefanyk]
Murphy Oil Co Ltd v Predator Corp, 2006 ABCA 69 (CanLII) at para 25 [Murphy Oil].
[29] Once the moving party has met its burden, the responding party must then demonstrate from the record that there is a genuine issue for trial: Weir-Jones at para 47.
This may be done in a number of ways, including that “the responding party may adduce evidence to persuade the court that there remains a genuine issue to be tried”: Murphy Oil at para 25.
[30] The Court of Appeal noted in Weir-Jones that there is “no symmetry of burdens”: at para 32.

Once the party moving for summary judgment has established the factual elements of its case on a balance of probabilities and that there is no genuine issue requiring a trial, then the respondent must “only demonstrate that the record, the facts, or the law preclude a fair disposition”: at para 32.

[31] Summary judgment is still possible even when there is some conflict in the affidavit evidence of the opposing parties, provided it is possible to fairly resolve the dispute summarily: Weir-Jones at para 47. “The key is whether the necessary findings of fact can be made on the record.

The chambers judge may make inferences of fact based on the undisputed facts before the court, as long as the inferences are strongly supported by the facts”: Malhotra at para 31, citing Guarantee Co at para 31.
The Court only assesses credibility and weighs evidence at trial, not when considering an application for summary judgment.

However, the Court may properly reduce the weight of affidavit evidence for several reasons including when the judge is satisfied that “the evidence is not consistent with other evidence and known circumstances”: Malhotra at para 33.

Furthermore, the conflict between the affidavits may not be on essential facts, or the issues may be resolvable based on the portions of the affidavits which are not in conflict: Sandhu v Siri Guru Nanak Sikh Gurdwara of Alberta, 2015 ABCA 101 (CanLII) at para 81, leave to appeal to SCC refused, 36426 (13 August 2015).
[32] As stated above, it is well established that the party bringing the motion for summary judgment bears the onus to prove that there is no issue of merit requiring trial.
What is less clear is which party bears the onus for proving or disproving Genesis' just cause defence.
[33] The parties appear to disagree as to which party bears the onus with respect to just cause.

The Plaintiffs concur with Master Robertson, who held that even in an employee's application for summary judgment, “the primary burden is on the employer to prove that there was just cause” if he raises it as a defence.
This follows the principle that “he who asserts must prove” unless there is a specific reverse onus: Rudichuk at paras 27–29.

[34] Genesis disagrees, citing a wrongful dismissal summary judgment decision of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, which held: “[t]he onus is on a Plaintiff to establish that there is no triable issue with respect to its claims or any defence raised with respect to those claims”: Lewis v Lavern Heideman & Sons Ltd, 2015 ONSC 3752 (CanLII) at para 43.

However, this statement in Lewis is, in my view, simply the condensed version of the plaintiffs' and moving party's initial onus of establishing wrongful dismissal, a further two part process that is fully described in Anderson v Cardinal Health, 2013 ONSC 5226 (CanLII) which Lewis cites for authority.
[35] As held in Anderson, the onus rests on the non-moving employer to establish their defence of mitigation against the employee's claim.
It is then up to the employee to counter the alleged defence with sufficient evidence to demonstrate that the defence is not a genuine issue requiring a trial: Anderson at para 7.

Although the onus is on the moving party to show that the issue of the defence can be determined on a summary basis, the non-moving party must first establish that there is merit to its alleged defence.
Recent case law confirms that this is the approach taken by the Ontario Superior Court of Justice: Merritt v Tigercat Industries Inc, 2016 ONSC 1214 (CanLII) at para 25
Edmond v Algonquin College, 2018 ONSC 1898 (CanLII) at para 95
Visaggio v Joynt-Dent Inc, 2018 ONSC 1911 (CanLII) at para 123.

[36] In East Winds Caribbean Limited Partnership v Reti, 2016 ABQB 536 (CanLII) at para 42, Master Hanebury clearly described the onuses and evidentiary burdens on each party as follows: … it is important to note that this [the test for summary judgment] does not affect the established legal burdens.

If an applicant discharges the initial evidentiary burden imposed upon it on a balance of probabilities, the evidentiary burden then falls to the respondent to show that there is arguable merit to the case and that there is a compelling reason that it should go to trial.
Only when the applicant has met its initial obligation does the onus shift to the respondent to reply, and the legal or persuasive burden is on the applicant throughout.
[37] The reasoning behind this assignment of onus is two-fold.
First, as identified by Master Robertson, absent guidance in a specific rule or statute, the general rule is that “he who asserts must prove”, and that the moving party needs evidence.
Otherwise, the moving party may have to prove a negative in response to a defence raised by the other party, “which is normally next to impossible”: Garry v Canada, 2007 ABCA 234 (CanLII) at para 8
Slater v Burgoin, 2001 ABCA 213 (CanLII) at para 13.

[38] Second, in response to the significant economic and self-worth consequences to an employee who is terminated for cause, the law has developed to protect employees in these vulnerable situations, in part by placing the onus to prove just cause on a balance of probabilities on the employer: Molloy v EPCOR Utilities Inc, 2015 ABQB 356 (CanLII) at para 140.
It would not, therefore, be reasonable to strip the employee of the protection of an employer's onus simply because the employee applies for summary judgment.
[39] In Hryniak, the Supreme Court recognised the importance of the summary judgment procedures (in appropriate cases) for access to justice: at paras 1–6.
Contrary to the intent of the Court, wrongfully dismissed employees would be discouraged from making use of summary judgment if the just cause onus was reversed.

The employer's rights are still protected, because, to succeed at summary judgment, the employee must still rebut the evidence in support of just cause to the extent that they can show that just cause is not an issue of merit that requires a full trial to justly determine.

[40] To conclude, in the case at bar, the Plaintiffs, Rudichuk and Scott, bear the onus of proving, on a balance of probabilities, that there is no genuine issue for trial with respect to their employment contract, and whether Genesis wrongfully terminated their employment contract.

Once the Plaintiffs have satisfied this burden, it is up to Genesis to demonstrate from the record enough evidence in support of its defence of just cause to show that there is a dispute that cannot be justly resolved by summary judgment.

If Genesis is successful in the preceding step, then the Plaintiffs, to be successful in their summary judgment application, bear the burden of countering Genesis' just cause evidence to demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that there is no issue of merit for trial.
In Kubersky v.
Pomeroy (Pomeroy Group), 2021 ABQB 173, 2021 CarswellAlta 499, 25 Alta.
L.R.
(7th) 354, affirmed 2021 CarswellAlta 3387 (Q.B.) (Master), Master Schlosser concluded that a Master did have jurisdiction to grant summary judgment in a wrongful dismissal action.
The learned Master said: [3] It might be worthwhile to begin by clearing up a few misconceptions about Summary Judgment.
From a Master's perspective, the law is in an unsatisfactory state.
Much of the problem stems from the decision in Coffey v Nine Energy Canada Inc.

That case holds that neither a Master nor a Judge can weigh evidence in Chambers (Master's because of the constitutional impediment) and, consequently, a wrongful dismissal case must proceed at least to a summary trial.
The learned Justice in that case acknowledges that there are at least nine decisions against this position (at paras 14, 15): listing seven Masters' decisions and two Judges' decisions.

To that list we can add Bier v Proper Cat Construction Ltd, 2013 ABQB 351 at paras 63, 64 per Wakeling (then) J which holds out wrongful dismissal as an example of a type of case suitable for Summary Judgment.
And there are others. … [16] In S.B.I.

(at para 57) Justice Lieberman, writing for the Court, said: The Master would be exceeding his jurisdiction if he assessed damages in the sense that he weighed evidence to arrive at an amount … Here, however, there was no weighing of evidence … .
The damages in that case were essentially liquidated damages.

[17] In the Coffey decision at first instance (2017 ABQB 417), Master Farrington declined to determine pay in lieu of notice and found that a claim for damages and the counterclaim were not suitable for summary disposition.
His decision was affirmed on appeal (2018 ABQB 898).
The appeal decision came out before Weir-Jones and Hannam, at a time when there was division in the decided cases about the approach to Summary Judgment and the correct test to be used.
It is the appeal decision that gives us trouble.
[18] Coffey makes a number of pronouncements: 1.
That it is inappropriate to weigh evidence at a Summary Judgment application whether it is before a Master or a Judge (para 45); 2.
Weighing evidence is outside the jurisdiction of the Master and beyond the scope of the Summary Judgment rule (para 41); and 3.
A Master is precluded by Section 9 of the Court of Queen's Bench Act and Section 96 of the Constitution Act from weighing evidence in reaching a determination of damages (para 21).
[19] First of all, (and with respect) these pronouncements fail to grasp the ‘elusive distinction’ between summary disposition and trial referred to in paragraph 13, above.
Summary disposition is neither a trial nor an adjudication (in the Section 96 sense).

Second, and perhaps understandably, the case failed to anticipate the path of the law both in terms of the approach to summary disposition and the appropriate test to be used; though I acknowledge that the appeal decision did not turn on the correct test to be used (Coffey, para 20).
As such, it now conflicts with the leading authorities from the Court of Appeal.
Third, and again with respect, no stock can be placed in the constitutional pronouncements made in that case.
Much of the dicta in Coffey seems to be premised on the assumption that summary disposition is an adjudication.
Summary disposition does not try the rights of the parties.

A Master hearing a summary disposition application is not weighing evidence in an adjudicative sense as a Judge would at trial. … [29] The truth of the matter is that there is no one type of case that is now inherently unsuitable for summary disposition.
There is no one type of case that requires a summary trial.

The analysis has to be performed on a case-by-case basis according to the principles set out below, and, to the extent that I am forced to choose between the conflicting decided cases, I am not persuaded that the Coffey decision properly decides the central issue raised by the Court.
My vote goes to the opposite team.
See also: Nixdorf v.

Broadstreet Properties Ltd., 2017 ABQB 132, 2017 CarswellAlta 297 (Master), where Master Robertson similarly concluded that a Master does have jurisdiction to hear a plaintiff's application for summary judgement in an action for wrongful dismissal (paragraphs 3-4 and 32-33).
Must Defence Referred to in R.
7.3 Be in Statement of Defence?
The answer seems to be “no”.
In Bartle & Gibson Co. v.
Spicer (1982), 35 A.R.
324 (Q.B.), Master Funduk says at pp.

332-33: Although Rule 159(2) states a defendant must satisfy the court that he has a good defence on the merits it does not necessarily follow that it must in all events be a defence which has been raised by the pleadings.
The question the court must address is whether the defence might succeed with an amendment.
Counterclaims May Not Prevent Summary Judgment Counsel for the defendants submits that summary judgment on the debt claim should not go because of the counterclaim.
A counterclaim does not without more prevent a plaintiff from getting a summary judgment on his claim.
It depends on what is advanced in the counterclaim.
If a counterclaim advances a defence of legal set-off or equitable set-off it may prevent a summary judgment going.
That is because legal set-off and equitable set-off are defences.
These defences are raised in a counterclaim (rather than a statement of defence) because rule 93(2) requires it.
However, it does not follow that because legal set-off and equitable set-off are raised by way of counterclaim that all counterclaims are defences.
They are not.
A counterclaim which does not raise legal set-off or equitable set-off is at best a “procedural set-off”, which is not a defence: Abacus Cities Ltd. v.
Aboussafy (1981), 29 A.R.
McBride v.
Kolenko (1990), 115 A.R.
348 (Master), at 351, per Master Funduk.
Similarly, a set-off claim does necessarily defeat a summary judgment application.
One must always go back to the rule.
The fact a defendant raises a claim of set-off in his pleading does not of itself mean summary judgment should not be granted to the plaintiff.
A claim by the defendant, whether raised in a statement of defence or a counterclaim, still must meet the test imposed on a defendant by Rule 159 if summary judgment is to be avoided.
What it comes down to is that a pleading is not evidence …Bank of Montreal v.
Rolseth (1986), 66 A.R.
381 at 387 (Master).
Summary Judgment for Part of Claim In some cases it is appropriate to give summary judgment for part of a claim with the balance of the claim going to trial: Steeplejack Services (Canada) Ltd. v.
Access Scaffold and Ladder Co.
Master).
The cases where that is appropriate are situations where the defendant will be liable for one or the other, that is, the lesser or the greater.
It is a two possibilities situation.

Summary judgment for part of a claim is not appropriate where it is a three possibilities situation, the three possibilities being: (a) no liability; (b) liability for the lesser amount; (c) liability for the greater amount.
See, for example, Rajani v.
Mandel Group Inc.
Master), p.
312 on this point.
Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce v.
Godziuk (1996), 182 A.R.
145 (Master), at 148, per Master Funduk.
In Borhaven v.
Brookwood Catering, 2002 ABQB 79, 2002 CarswellAlta 79, 306 A.R.
308, the plaintiff applied for summary judgment for the minimum amount of damages she expected to be awarded in the action.
The plaintiff alleged that she required the money to alleviate financial hardship.
Burrows, J. held that Rule 159 (6.1) (now R.
7.3) does not permit such an order.
At pp.
310-312, His Lordship said: Her [the plaintiff's] goal, in this application, is to obtain some relief from that financial hardship before the trial of this action.
She argues that unless her application succeeds, the financial pressures weighing upon her may force her to accept a settlement for an amount far less than is just.
She submits the defendants should be required to make a partial advance payment of her damages because it is obvious they will eventually be found liable to her for substantial damages. . . . . .
Of these cases, only Chernichen v.
Armitage[(1991), 122 A.R.
387 (Alta.
Q.B.)] dealt with the subject in a context similar to the present case.
There the defendant had admitted liability.
Côté J.A. sitting in the Queen's Bench, said: When the Plaintiff's counsel here argues that she is obviously going to get an assessment at least X dollars, he has a good point.
Unfortunately, however, Alberta still has the common-law rule which says that damages are to be assessed once and for all, and does not provide for a compulsory payment on account.
It is obvious from what I have said that I do not read Rule 159 on summary judgment, which was really designed for totallydifferent matters, as extending to that sort of thing.
Rule 159 (6.1) was enacted in 1999. … In my view, even with the addition of subrule (6.1), Rule 159 still does not provide for a compulsory payment on account.
It may be helpful to read and understand Rule 159 as a whole Subrule

(1) sets out three situations where an order under the rule may be granted: a) where there is no defence to a claim b) where there is no defence to a part of a claim, and c) where the only genuine issue is as to amount.
Subrule (6) adds a fourth situation: d) where the only genuine issue is a question of law.
The order granted will depend on which situation exists.
Where there is no defence to a claim, the court may order summary judgment (subrule (3)).
Where the only genuine issue is as to amount, the court may order an assessment (subrule (5)).
Where the only genuine issue is a question of law, the court may order the trial of that issue (subrule (6)).
Subrule (6.1) applies in the remaining situation—where there is no defence in respect of part of claim or in respect of an amount less than the full amount of the claim.
Where there is a defence as to the other part of the claim, the court may order summary judgment for the first part and a trial for the second.
Where the only genuine issue with respect to the other part of the claim is as to amount, the court may order summary judgment for the first part and an assessment for the second.
But, in my view, subrule 6.1 has no application where, for the whole of the claim, the only genuine question is as to amount.
This is the situation which Ms.
Borhaven has sworn she believes exists in this case.
Subrule (5) applies in that situation.
It would require that an assessment be directed.
It does not contemplate summary judgment being granted for a portion of the damages to be assessed—not even a portion clearly small enough to be certainly less than the eventual assessment.
In my view in this case none of the situations which Rule 159 contemplates is present.
There are genuine issues as to liability and amount in this case… There is no part of Ms.
Borhaven's claim for which there is clearly no defence.
An order under Rule 159 (6.1) cannot be granted.
Counsel referred to Ontario cases where summary judgment for part of a claim was granted in circumstances similar to this case: Moore v.
Vandenbosch, [1989] O.J.
No.
H.C.); Johnson v.
Gen.
Div.).
The Ontario Court of Appeal commented on those cases in Ford Motor Co. of Canada v.
Ontario (Municipal Employees Retirement Board) (1997), 36 O.R.

The headnote in that report summarizes the position in Ontario as follows: Partial summary judgment under Rule 20 of the Rules of Civil Procedure [Ontario's summary judgment rule] should only be granted where the evidence establishes that there is no genuine issue for trial in respect of a discrete claim. … Had the legislature intended that Rule 20 be used to grant partial summary judgment based on the probable minimum value of a plaintiff's claim, or plain need, it would have said so.
Rule 20 was not intended to serve that purpose.
I have reached the same conclusion regarding Alberta Rule 159 (6.1).
In DIRTT Environmental Solutions Ltd. v.
Falkbuilt Ltd., 2021 ABQB 252, 2021 CarswellAlta 979, 26 Alta.
L.R.

730, Justice Sidnell gave this summary of the law relating to partial summary judgment applications: [35] Distilling the comments and concerns from the cases referred to above, in my view, I must answer the three main questions, set out below, in the affirmative to find that partial summary judgment is an appropriate application to pursue in this case:
(a) Can the issue to be determined on a partial summary judgment application be bifurcated from the remainder of the issues that will proceed to trial?
The determination of whether the issue can be bifurcated should be considered with the answers to the following four exploratory questions in mind:
(i) Is the issue to be determined on the partial summary judgment application intertwined with those proceeding to trial?
(ii) Where there is more than one defendant, is the issue to be determined on the partial summary judgment application inextricably linked to the claim against the other defendant(s)?
(iii) Is the record available on the issue to be determined at the partial summary judgment application as extensive as it would be at trial?
(iv) Is there a danger of duplicative or inconsistent findings of fact or any res judicata on issues to be determined at trial?
(b) Will the partial summary judgment application advance the action as a whole?
To access whether there will be any advancement, the following two exploratory questions can be asked:
(i) Will the partial summary judgment application achieve efficiencies in the litigation given that other issues will be proceeding to trial?
(ii) Will the partial summary judgment application deal with the issue expeditiously and not cause unreasonable delay to the main action?
(c) Will partial summary judgment significantly advance access to justice, and be the most proportionate, timely and cost-effective approach?

[36] If the partial summary judgment application is appropriate based on affirmative answers to these three questions, then I can proceed as set out in Weir-Jones, if the record permits the necessary findings of fact and application of the law to determine the matter summarily.
In JBRO Holdings Inc. v.
Dynasty Power Inc., 2022 ABCA 140, additional reasons 2022 ABCA 258, the Court of Appeal said: [49] Under r 7.3(1), a party may apply for summary judgment in respect of all or part of a claim.
Partial summary judgment is expressly contemplated by the words of the rule.
Provided the issue can be decided discretely and fairly, partial summary judgment may be granted: Baim, paras 10-11.

[50] While partial summary judgment (for example, granting summary judgment against a single defendant) may run the risk of duplicative proceedings or inconsistent findings of fact, resolution of an important claim against a key party could significantly advance access to justice, and be the most proportionate, timely and cost effective approach: Hryniak, para 60.
It must be demonstrated that partial summary judgment would achieve a just result: see Stankovic v 1536679 Alberta Ltd, 2019 ABCA 187, para 54, 88 Alta LR (6th) 1.

[51] If the record allows the judge to make the necessary findings of fact and apply the law, then the summary procedure should be used unless there is a substantive reason to conclude that summary disposition would not achieve a just result: Weir-Jones, para 25.
Personal Knowledge This is an application by the plaintiff for summary judgment.
This application is not an interlocutory motion so without more the only evidence that is admissible is that which complies with r.
Aside from that, r.
159(1) requires that the affidavit be by a person “who can swear positively to the facts”.
Either way, belief with grounds and source, opinions or conclusions are not admissible.

Although paragraph 5 of Tarangle's evidence is a “positive” statement of facts, that is, not a belief, the balance of his evidence clearly discloses that he does not have personal knowledge about any alleged sale by Kettleson to the defendant.
Even if the evidence is couched positively it does not necessarily follow that the mandate in rules 305(1) and 159(1) has been observed.
The rules cannot be evaded by couching the affidavit as if the witness has personal knowledge when he does not …Silver Recovery Systems of Canada Ltd. v.
WMJ Metals Ltd.
252 at 253-54 (Master).
Mr.
Justice Sanderman said in Wild Rose School Division No.
Bert Pratch Construction Co.
339 (Q.B.), at pp.
342-43: … affidavits that are to be used in order to give summary judgment pursuant to rule 159 must positively state the facts that are to be relied upon.
Information received and a belief based upon the advice of others is not sufficient to support such an application.
The individual swearing the affidavit to be relied upon must positively swear to the facts that would support the relief questioned.
Deposing to one's belief is not sufficient.
However, one should note the contents of the annotation “Use of Hearsay in Final Applicatons” under Rule 13.18.
In Kam's Sand Coating Ltd. v.
Mearford Energy Services Inc., 2000 ABQB 434, 2000 CarswellAlta 658, 267 A.R.
355, Veit J. said, at pp.

363-364: The traditional view of the evidentiary basis for an application for summary judgment is accurately reflected in rule 159: a party applying for summary judgment must submit an affidavit by any person who can swear positively to the facts, verifying the claim.

In combination with rule 305, the duty is, therefore, to present evidence from someone who does not rely on information and belief; to put it another way, the evidence in support of an application for summary judgment cannot be hearsay evidence.

This standard for the quality of evidence required for a summary judgment was consistently applied until the traditional view of hearsay evidence was reformulated by the Supreme Court of Canada in the late 1980s and early 1990s.
The implications of the Supreme Court of Canada's decisions for civil practice were addressed by Mason, J., in [Alberta Treasury Branches v.

201 (Q.B.)] where he approved the following summary, which I also adopt: An affidavit may now contain statements of the deponent that are based on information and belief, if this prima facie inadmissible hearsay evidence falls within the common law exceptions to the hearsay rule.

The question to be asked is whether the evidence sought to be admitted meets the common law exceptions to hearsay, which are now governed by the criteria of necessity and reliability … In 1059028 Alberta Ltd. v.

Capio Oilfield Services Ltd., 2016 ABQB 234, 2016 CarswellAlta 734 (Master), Master Schulz said that the supporting affidavit does not have to specifically contain the words “swears positively”: 9 Given the wording of Rules 7.3 and 13.18(3), must the supporting affidavit contain the magic words, swears positively, or is this another way of stating that the evidence must be based on personal knowledge?
In my opinion, it is sufficient if the evidence tendered by the Applicant is based on personal knowledge.
The magic words are not necessary, but evidence on personal knowledge is necessary, particularly in light of Rule 13.18(3).
10 Must the supporting affidavit swear specifically that one or more of the three grounds listed in Rule 7.3(1) has been met?
The words in Rule 7.3 are not intended to be a trap for the unwary litigant, but instead are meant to set out the substance of what must be proved to be successful in a Rule 7.3 application.
Swearing (positively or otherwise) that there is no defence or merit to the claim is giving an opinion on the ultimate issue.
It is the job of the Court to give an opinion on the ultimate issue, not that of the affiant.
It is the job of the affiant to provide the Court with the evidence to form an opinion on the ultimate issue, based on the merits as shown in the supporting evidence and any defences raised.
Enforcing a Settlement In Varsanyi v.
Mityok, 2002 ABQB 720, 2002 CarswellAlta 957, 324 A.R.
186, 5 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 181 (Master), the plaintiffs alleged that a settlement had been reached and applied for summary judgment to enforce it.
Master Laycock summarized the law as follows (at p.

186): Canadian authorities suggest the following procedural guidelines: 1 Where settlement has been reached and incorporated in a final judgment a new action must be brought to set aside the judgment based on such allegations as fraud, mistake of law or fact.

Where a settlement is reached but not incorporated into a final order and the plaintiff reneges on the alleged settlement and proceeds with the action, the court may grant a stay of proceedings so as to enforce the settlement or allow the defence to be amended to plead settlement, or conclude that there was no settlement or that it was unenforceable and allow the action to proceed.
Where a settlement is reached but not incorporated into a final order and the defendant reneges, the plaintiff may apply for final judgment enforcing the alleged settlement agreement.

On such an application the court may grant what is in effect a summary judgment or if triable issues are raised about the settlement, the court may direct a trial of an issue in the same action or require that a separate action be commenced to prove and enforce the settlement agreement.
If the court concludes that there was no settlement or that it is unenforceable, the plaintiff is left with the original action.

Standard of Review on Appeal The standard of review on an appeal of a summary judgment decision made by a Court of Queen's Bench Justice de novo from a Master's Order is correctness on questions of law and palpable and overriding error on questions of fact.
On a summary judgment decision, which is discretionary, great deference is given.
Shuchuk v.
Wolfert (2003), 15 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 5 (C.A.) at 7, per Ritter J.A.
The above paragraph from Shuchuk v.
Wolfert was quoted with approval in 732311 Alberta Ltd. v.
Paradise Bay Spa & Tub Warehouse Inc., 2003 ABCA 362, 2003 CarswellAlta 1733, 339 A.R.
L.R.
(4th) 17, at 19, per curiam.
In Enokhok Development Corp. v.
Alberta Treasury Branches, 2011 ABCA 322, 2011 CarswellAlta 2034, 68 Alta.
L.R.
(5th) 126, the Court said, at paragraph 12: 12 The standard of review on an appeal of a decision to refuse summary judgment is correctness on questions of law.

For questions of mixed fact and law, and fact alone, the standard of review is palpable and overriding error, unless the error of mixed fact and law involves an error relating to an extricable principle of law, in which case correctness applies to that extricable legal question: Poliquin v.
Devon Canada Corporation, 2009 ABCA 216, 454 A.R.
416 at paras.
Summary judgment should only be granted if the matter is factually and legally beyond doubt.
If facts are disputed or if the law is unclear, then the chambers judge can exercise his discretion and decline to grant summary judgment.
Provided the judge hearing the matter applied correct law, his or her findings are accorded deference.
In Orr v.
Fort McKay First Nation, 2014 ABQB 111, Mr.
Justice Brown said, at paragraphs 15, and 20-21: 15 In my judgment, the direction in Hryniak v.

Mauldin regarding the standard of review to be applied to a decision upon an application for summary judgment is not applicable to an application for summary judgment under Rule 7.3 of the Alberta Rules of Court (AR 124/2010). … … 20 The Supreme Court's direction in Hryniak v.

Mauldin regarding the deference to be shown to the motions judge on an application under Ontario's Rule 20 for summary judgment therefore does not apply to first-instance decisions on applications for summary judgment brought under Alberta's Rule 7.3—irrespective of whether that decision was taken by a master or a judge—for summary judgment.
It does, however, apply to decisions on applications for judgment by way of a summary trial under Alberta's Rule 7.5 (which decisions must always be taken by a judge, and not a master).
21 The hearing of the appeal from the decision of Master Smart in this matter is therefore de novo, and the standard of review which I am to apply to his decision remains, notwithstanding Hryniak v.
Mauldin, correctness.
Granting Summary Dismissal as part of denying a Summary Judgment Application In Pyrrha Design Inc. v.

Plum, 2016 ABCA 12, 2016 CarswellAlta 165, the plaintiff (Pyrrha Design) and the defendant (Plum and others) entered into a settlement agreement relating to a dispute which had arisen between the plaintiff and the defendants.
The plaintiff subsequently sued the defendants, alleging that the defendants had breached the terms of the settlement agreement.
The plaintiff brought an application for summary judgment.

The defendants “did not formally cross-apply for summary dismissal, although they requested this relief in their written brief filed in response to the appellant's [plaintiff's] application.” The summary judgment application of the plaintiff was dismissed and “[t]he chambers judge concluded that the matter could be dismissed on a summary basis because this was the most efficient and proportionate way to proceed, and that it was fair and just to proceed on the existing record.” On the issue of whether “the chambers judge erred in granting summary dismissal of the appellant's claim in the absence of a formal application by the respondents”, two of the three Court of Appeal justices ruled that no error had been made, and said: 8 It is incontestable that a chambers judge possesses inherent jurisdiction to control its process: De Shazo v Nations Energy Company Ltd, 2006 ABCA 400 at para 12, 401 AR 142
MacMillan Bloedel Ltd v Simpson, [1995] 4 SCR 725 at para 33, 130 DLR

This jurisdiction is also expressly granted by s 8 of the Judicature Act, RSA 2000, c J-2, which provides the court with power to grant any appropriate remedy that is appropriate in the discrete circumstances of a case: Nafie v Badaway, 2015 ABCA 36 at paras 97-98, 11 Alta LR
(6th) 1; Bank of Montreal v Valerio, 2009 ABQB 578 at para 30, 480 AR 393.
9 Rule 1.3(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court is to like effect when it states that the Court may do either or both of:
(a) give any relief or remedy described or referred to in the Judicature Act; or
(b) give any relief or remedy described or referred to in or under these Rules or any enactment.

Rule 1.3(2) specifically states that a “remedy may be granted by the Court whether or not it is claimed or sought in an action.” 10 And, quite apart from avoiding the multiplicity of actions—the mischief sought to be avoided by s 8 of the Judicature Act and R 1.3 of the Alberta Rules of Court, a proposition for which there is also ample case authority—the chambers judge properly adhered to the urging of the Supreme Court of Canada in Hryniak v Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, [2014] 1 SCR 87 to the effect that courts are obliged to resolve legal disputes in the most cost-effective and timely method available, provided the process selected ensures fairness between the parties.

Here, the chambers judge is to be commended, not criticized, for pursuing a cost-effective, timely final resolution to this litigation which was fair and just to the parties, as it simply serves no one's interest to permit continuation of protracted and costly litigation when it can be properly disposed of summarily and entirely.

11 This Court has expressly advocated a modern approach, involving the broad interpretation of summary judgment rules, in order to comply with the Supreme Court's recognition in Hryniak at para 2 that “a culture shift is required in order to create an environment promoting timely and affordable access to the civil justice system”: Windsor at para 13.
The motions court must determine “whether the issue of law can fairly be decided on the record before the court”: Tottrup v Clearwater (Municipal District No 99), 2006 ABCA 380 at para 11, 401 AR 88.
12 The respondents concede that it would have been preferable to file and serve a formal application for summary dismissal.

However, having reviewed the record in these proceedings, we agree with the respondents that the appellant had sufficient notice of the respondents' position with respect to the merits of the appellant's claim and, further, that there is no suggestion that the appellant was taken by surprise or that any prejudice resulted from the procedure followed, because: • In its statement of defence, the respondents expressly plead that the allegations made against them by the appellant were “entirely without merit”. • The respondents filed written submissions 11 days in advance of the special chambers application in which they specifically asserted that they had not breached the terms of the settlement contract and in those submissions, twice expressly requested that the action be dismissed in its entirety, on a summary basis. • After receiving the written submissions and notice of the respondents' intention to seek summary dismissal, the appellant did not object in any fashion to this informal demand for summary dismissal although it conceded that the submissions were read, and recognized that these materials would also be read, in advance of the special hearing date, by the assigned chambers judge. • Additionally, the respondents had signed a consent order which allowed the appellant to file a surrebuttal brief for the application, which was in fact filed and which specifically responded to the respondents' written submissions, including addressing the evidence given by Ms.
Hardy at the comprehensive cross-examination on her affidavit.

13 The appellant fairly concedes that it did put its “best foot forward” before the chambers judge and did argue that its interpretation of the contract, when compared to the photographic evidence proffered at the special hearing, rendered unassailable the conclusion that the respondents had breached the settlement contract.

14 The chambers judge reached an opposite conclusion and found that on the same evidence and having regard to her “interpretation of the settlement contract”, there was no merit to the appellant's claim.
The gravamen of the appellant's summary judgment claim was that the photographs proved breaches of the settlement agreement.
In turn, the essence of the respondents' summary dismissal argument was that the photographs did not support this claim and there had been no breach of the settlement agreement.
The outcome either way depended on the chambers judge's assessment of the settlement agreement and whether the photographs proved that the agreement had been breached.

If the appellant put its “best foot forward” on its summary judgment application, as it was required to do, we are not persuaded that it could have proffered any additional evidence or made any different arguments had the respondents formally applied for summary dismissal.

15 Nor do we see any merit to the appellant's objection that the respondents failed to formally comply with R 7.3(2), which dictates that an application for summary dismissal must be supported by an affidavit swearing positively that one or more of the grounds for summary dismissal have been met, or by other evidence to the effect that the grounds for summary dismissal have been met.
16 In the present case, Ms.
Hardy's affidavit sworn on May 30, 2014 and filed on June 2, 2014 satisfies the substance of R 7.3(2) in that it contained the evidence upon which the respondents relied in seeking summary dismissal.
In essence, the appellant's submissions in this regard are a complaint of form over substance.
We find that the respondents met the substance of R 7.3(2) and the underlying basis for it.
17 In our view, the appellant was not prejudiced by the respondents' failure to file and serve a formal notice of application for summary dismissal.
The appellant urged the chambers judge to do exactly that which was done, but clearly does not agree with the result and now complains that it was an unfair process.
The failure to file and serve a formal notice of application may, in some circumstances, prejudice the opposite party.
The essence of the Rule is to protect litigants from ambush or litigation surprise.
On the record before us, there was neither.
Accordingly, we conclude that the chambers judge did not err in granting summary dismissal in the absence of a formal application by the respondents.
